Late-night transfer fallout sparks Chelsea-Monaco row

BBC News Wed, 02 Sep 2026 14:48:09 GMT

Lamine Camara (left) and Folarin Balogun (right) will not be moving to the Premier League from Monaco

One source with connections to both Chelsea and Monaco said the clubs had "played with fire and got burned".

Indeed, the late-night transfer drama that involved Folarin Balogun, Everton, Monaco, Lamine Camara and Chelsea saw all parties lose out.

Camara - a 22-year-old Senegalese international midfielder - had been a target for Chelsea as they prepared for the £125m sale of Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City.

But Monaco were adamant he was going nowhere for the fee Chelsea were willing to pay.

"I've been speaking to them for the last 10 days," said Monaco sporting director Thiago Scuro said.

"At around 16:00 BST yesterday we got contact from Chelsea. The answer was the same: no."

Instead, the Ligue 1 club had allowed United States international striker Balogun, 25, to fly to Merseyside to complete a £40m move to Everton. According to Monaco, Camara had agreed to stay with the club.

With three hours remaining of the transfer window, Chelsea were content with their midfield options, despite the sale of Fernandez, after failing with enquiries for Camara and Roma's Manu Kone.

But issues with Balogun's Everton medical presented an opportunity for Chelsea.

"Of course, Chelsea saw an opportunity," Scuro added.

"'Monaco need money, Balogun is struggling there, let's go and try.' Chelsea called us and said: 'Maybe we can be the solution.'

"At that moment, we had to open the door to discussions."

Negotiations were back underway with Monaco at 20:00 BST and a £47m fee was agreed shortly after.

Meanwhile, Everton failed to find alternatives to Balogun and revived their move with minutes before the deadline.

Chelsea had completed all the necessary paperwork for Camara and did not need to submit a deal sheet - a request to the Premier League for additional time to complete a transfer, post the deadline.

But the plug was pulled. Monaco acknowledge Camara was disappointed after he had spoken to manager Xabi Alonso, passed a medical and signed a contract until 2033.

"What happened was that around 22:00 BST our time, maybe a bit earlier, Everton realised there was no issue and decided they were ready to sign the contract [for Balogun]," Scuro told reporters on Wednesday afternoon.

"As soon as we received that information, we came back to Chelsea and said there was no deal. Because that's also fair. It's part of the game."

Chelsea were left furious, claiming Monaco informed them in writing that the deal would not proceed rather than communicating the decision by phone.

Monaco thought - by signing a deal sheet, five minutes before the 23:00 BST deadline, to allow Everton extra time to complete the transfer of Balogun - they had secured the sale they needed to help comply with Uefa's financial regulations.

The Ligue 1 side were under pressure to generate 150m euros in player sales this summer, and had raised 106m euros from departures.

Balogun left Everton's Finch Farm training ground without signing for the club

Another twist was still to come.

In the early hours of Tuesday morning, the former Arsenal striker had a change of heart which saw him leave Everton's Finch Farm training ground without signing for the club.

Scuro claims Balogun felt he was mistreated while at Everton's training ground, something the Premier League club disputes.

"We had to respect his decision," Scuro added.

"We found solutions, challenged the medical assessment and worked through the issues.

"I don't want to create a war with Chelsea or Everton.

"My role is to protect Monaco and act in the club's best interests. That's what I've done since I arrived.

"It's not about being loved by people outside the club. It's about doing what Monaco needs."

Scuro says it is possible Monaco will look at selling other players to countries whose transfer window remains open in order to acquire the funds they need.

The Monaco chief is open to welcoming back both players. Camara has already returned to training and is set to feature in their upcoming match away at Paris St-Germain on Friday night.

"I really understand because a player can get excited by conversations with a coach and by everything a club like Chelsea can offer," Scuro continued.

"This is not the end of the world. It's one opportunity. For a player with his level of talent, I'm very confident he will soon have even better options and offers than the one he had yesterday."

According to sources close to Camara, Liverpool also retain a long-standing interest in a future deal.

Lamine Camara has scored six goals and supplied 11 assists in 75 matches for Monaco

Chelsea had been considering Camara as an option to replace Fernandez for the final 10 days of the window.

Of course, the Londoners could have forced a deal through sooner but it might have meant overpaying because, as sources had previously explained, Monaco saw Camara as not for sale throughout the majority of the window - barring those few hours on Tuesday evening - but for "exceptional" offers.

Chelsea were blindsided by the collapse of the deal and there was little they could have done to revive it or sign an alternative before the deadline.

They did, however, have the option of cancelling Fernandez's move to Manchester City but opted not to do so out of a sense of "professionalism".

Chelsea wanted a midfielder to replace Fernandez but there was never any desperation as the club only wanted to do so on its own terms.

Alonso sees captain Reece James primarily as a midfield option, alongside Moises Caicedo, Romeo Lavia and new signings Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco within his 27-man squad.

Yet injuries to Caicedo and Henderson, coupled with James' workload, meant full-back Malo Gusto was used in midfield during the 4-3 victory over Brighton, a match in which Chelsea recorded 25.6% possession, their lowest figure since records began in 2003-04.

Alonso could have selected Barco, 21, who came on as a second-half substitute, but the club want to carefully manage the signing from Strasbourg as he returns to the Premier League after a short-lived spell at Brighton.

There remains debate over whether Chelsea have sufficient depth and quality in midfield, with the club retaining the option of revisiting a move for Camara or another midfielder in January.

They could also look to strengthen other positions having been left delighted at making a net profit in the transfer market while adding quality.

Chelsea signed World Cup winner Emiliano Martinez, France international Maxence Lacroix and club-record £117m signing Morgan Rogers, as well as experienced striker Danny Welbeck and full-backs Pep Chavarria and Marco Palestra.

It's now on the manager and squad they have built to attempt to match Chelsea's ambitions on the pitch, starting with Sunday's trip to champions Arsenal.

Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics

BBC News Wed, 02 Sep 2026 14:26:39 GMT

Throughout the summer Andy Burnham's been attempting to cultivate a new style of communicating with a steady stream of social media videos designed to speak directly to the public.

But alongside his digital push, the prime minister still has to master one of Westminster's weekly traditions; the political back and forth that is Prime Minister's Questions.

To some it might seem outdated in a modern media world, but the exchange across the despatch box is still deemed vital by many in Westminster as a moment of scrutiny; a chance for the public to peer into Parliament's workings and a crucial factor in setting the mood among backbench MPs as they watch – and judge – the performance of party leaders.

So the debut of a new prime minister matters.

Burnham took his place in the House of Commons chamber to raucous cheers from the packed Labour benches and struck a confident tone from the start, clearly keen to maintain the sense of optimism he's promised the country.

His initial exchanges with Kemi Badenoch were vaguely jocular. The Conservative leader started with a joke about the prime minister's stamina after a marathon Commons' session on Tuesday when he took questions for more than three hours; there was laughter from MPs and a cautious smile from Burnham.

But if there was an early twinkle in the eye of either party leader their exchanges soon slipped into more familiar territory, trading barbs over tax and borrowing with Badenoch making claims of profligate government spending.

Burnham, despite his promises to end what he's called political "point scoring" was soon pointing the finger at the Tories for their economic record, referencing the budget of former Prime Minister Liz Truss while promising he'd deliver fiscal discipline.

He's not the first prime minister to pledge a new style of politics only to find it hard to dodge the adversarial nature of PMQs.

David Cameron said he'd end "Punch and Judy politics" when he became Tory leader only to find himself in regular political knockabouts across the despatch box.

But while the political barbs continued it's clear that Burnham is a more comfortable communicator than his predecessor. His real challenge will be delivering more than a change in tone.

The backdrop to his first few days as prime minister with Westminster in full swing has been the increased cost of borrowing – a global trend but one to which the UK is exposed and which looks likely to limit the chancellor's room for manoeuvre at the budget come the end of October.

Burnham has promised a transformational government but he's facing many of the same challenges as Sir Keir Starmer, with difficult decisions on defence spending, welfare and social care - to name just a few - hurtling towards him.

These are the pressure points his political opponents will seek to exploit, as evidenced by Badenoch's approach at Prime Minister's Questions when she quizzed him over plans for taxes, spending and borrowing.

Burnham pointed to his early actions in office, cutting VAT on domestic electricity bills and business rates for pubs and music venues as a sign of his priorities, but he gave little more away – leaning back on another familiar refrain that prime ministers don't write budgets from the despatch box.

In reality, it would be unfair to expect much more in the way of detail about Burnham's plans for the economy during his very first session of PMQs, but these are questions his government will eventually have to answer.

And what is clear is that despite the promise of a more consensual style of politics, when it comes to the substance there are sharp ideological differences across the Commons.

Burnham's diagnosis for the country's problems centres on privatisation and deindustrialisation over recent decades, as well as Brexit.

Badenoch disagrees, pointing instead to high taxes and spending as constraints on economic growth.

While Burnham's early weeks in office have seen a shift in style with a summer tour around the country and heavy social media presence, the economic arguments between him and his political opponents remain, and now Westminster is back in session there will likely be a clamour for more detail about his planned direction.

Today's Prime Minister's Questions is a taste of what's to come.

As well as smart communications, the choices the prime minister makes against a tricky economic background will take careful navigation if he's to deliver the optimistic future he's promised.

Letby 'boyfriend' doctor named as court order lifted

BBC News Wed, 02 Sep 2026 13:49:17 GMT

The doctor described during Lucy Letby's trial as her "boyfriend" can now be identified.

Mark Deakin, who died in July aged 53, had been protected by a court anonymity order that has now been lifted.

Deakin worked alongside Letby, now 36, at the Countess of Chester Hospital during the period in which she murdered seven babies and attempted to murder seven others in 2015 and 2016.

Deakin, who was married, continued his medical career after leaving the Countess of Chester, later working as a consultant at Alder Hey Children's Hospital in Liverpool.

There have been reports that Deakin died shortly after learning that he had been sacked after it was found he had breached patient confidentiality in text message exchanges with Letby.

It is understood that he had been unwell. An inquest into the circumstances surrounding Deakin's death will now be opened.

Details of Deakin's personal interactions with Letby were revealed during the Thirlwall inquiry into how the nurse's murders were able to take place.

The inquiry heard that the pair had exchanged more than 1,000 Facebook messages and that Deakin helped Letby secure a placement at Alder Hey hospital after she was suspected of murdering babies.

Deakin told the inquiry he had been "misled" and "maybe manipulated" by Letby and that he was tricked into giving her information about babies she had attacked.

He added that it "had been a massive mistake" to help Letby and said he had "a lot of regrets".

The inquiry is due to publish its findings on 15 September.

Letby - who has always maintained her innocence - is serving 15 whole life prison terms. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) is conducting a review of Letby's convictions.

At her criminal trial - the longest murder trial in UK history - Deakin gave evidence in relation to several babies. He was granted special measures as well as anonymity. These allowed him to give evidence from behind a screen so that Letby, the public gallery, and the media were prevented from seeing him.

Deakin's evidence provided detail of some of the emergency calls and resuscitations which he and Letby were jointly involved in. Their long nights of text messaging were laid bare and many of the messages shown to the jury.

When he was sworn in, on the first occasion he testified, Letby burst into tears, in what was the first display of emotion from her during the trial.

During her cross-examination, Letby was forced to deny that Deakin was her boyfriend, though she did accept that they had gone on a trip to London together.

The prosecuting barrister, Nick Johnson KC, said Letby "tried to get out the back of the dock" when the doctor first came to the witness box.

Letby said: "Yes, because I felt unwell."

Johnson said: "No, it's because you didn't like hearing your boyfriend giving evidence, did you?"

Letby said: "That's unfair."

Prosecutors also went through a WhatsApp message exchange between Letby and a friend who had teased her for being "flirty" with Deakin.

Johnson said: "She knew you were sweet on Mark, didn't she?"

Letby said: "What do you mean, sweet?"

Johnson said: "That you had a crush on him."

"No," said Letby.

"There was nothing between me and that Mark."

Johnson told the court that Letby told her friend she had received a "strange message" from the doctor.

Her colleague responded: "Did you? Saying what? Go Commando [laughing face emoji]."

While some media reports have described him as "a key witness", Deakin was one of many former colleagues of Letby's whose joint testimony helped to build the prosecution case against her, and none of the convictions rested solely on his evidence.

Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night

BBC News Wed, 02 Sep 2026 13:20:11 GMT

It is not just the wildfire burning in the bond markets, with many countries facing interest rates at multi-decade highs.

The markets lending money to governments appear to be changing more fundamentally too.

Over summer, the message has been made clear: countries will have to pay more to borrow cash.

The immediate reason is the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and renewed hostilities between the US and Iran, which has pushed up inflation and, in turn, raised expectations of higher interest rates in the world's major economies.

Markets had assumed tensions would subside, and so too would oil and gas prices, ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

It was wishful thinking, based on the hope that US President Donald Trump would want the conflict in the Middle East resolved well before Americans go to the polls.

But that has not happened, leaving markets pricing in higher energy prices, a chronic Gulf crisis, higher inflation for longer - and so higher interest rates.

But that is only part of the story.

The bigger picture is rising demand for borrowing across the world - and not just from governments. Big tech companies are turning to the same bond markets to raise hundreds of billions of dollars for investments in AI data centres.

Over $219bn (£162bn) of debt has already been issued this year by the US "hyperscalers" such as Google, Amazon and Meta, nearly a third of it in currencies other than the dollar, including sterling.

The total issued last year was $93bn, while before that it averaged less than $40bn a year. Some expect the tech giants to raise $400-$500bn from the bond markets this year. These are staggering sums, raising competition in the market and pushing up the price for governments.

Looking east, there is another major borrower: Japan.

It has the highest debt burden, relative to its GDP, of the major economies and is the biggest single lender to the US government. Until recently its central bank's interest rate was zero, but that has crept up to help combat rising inflation.

As a result, its government bond yields have been pushed to 30-year highs. The declining value of the yen complicates things, but the bottom line is that there is a change afoot in the global flow of money.

The biggest factor pushing up rates is the credibility of the borrowing plans set out by major countries. The increase is not based on fears about countries "going bankrupt".

But it is based on the brutal market equation that if a country wants to borrow more, and to do so without a credible plan, especially if there are doubts over the stability of a given government, it should expect to pay a higher rate.

Influential economists lean on different factors. Mohamed el-Erian told me the AI competition in bond markets was the biggest new factor.

Lord Jim O'Neill, says the recent action has been caused by uncertainty about US policy, and in particular efforts by the US Government to try to manage down surging yields.

This brings us to the UK. The profound and rolling instability of multiple prime ministers, chancellors, policy U-turns and the seeming inability to push through major structural change in this country over the past decades, has attracted a premium.

It was part of Sir Keir Starmer's strategy to try to take on boring reforms and offer markets stability in a bid to lower borrowing costs.

It was a shock to many in the markets that despite a landslide majority, Labour could not push through plans to cut Britain's welfare bill. This added to the ups and downs in the gilt markets - the trade in British government debt.

Actually, there are signs of green shoots in the underlying economy. Economic growth has been faster than peers so far in 2026, despite the energy price spike.

Measures of consumer confidence have ticked back up again. The PM is hoping to build on these signs to help rebuild the economy.

But the ongoing rout in global bond markets raises serious questions about the coherence and detail of Burnham's broader plans.

"More public control" and more support for those struggling with the cost of living sounds like a plan for more spending, while the former could turn off potential investors looking at the country.

Burnham's former economic adviser, Lord O'Neill, told me yesterday that the PM's 10-year plan, expected in November, needs to set out how he will tackle "excessive spending".

Lord O'Neill believes showing investors he can be decisive on the state pension or the welfare bill will give him breathing room to focus on his favoured infrastructure investments.

As interest rates tick up, the trade offs facing the prime minister only get more difficult.

About 700 prisoners to be freed on 1 October under revised early release plans

BBC News Wed, 02 Sep 2026 13:10:19 GMT

About 700 eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on the morning of 1 October and some 2,550 will have been released by the end of the year, the government's revised early prison release plan shows.

The new plan, signed into law and published online, shows Andy Burnham's government kept the promised original schedule of how and when offenders will leave jail, aside from delaying the start date by a month and excluding specific offences from the programme.

Under the original plan, offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months would have been eligible from 2 September to walk out of jail after serving a third of that time.

In the Commons on Wednesday, Burnham said he understood the "anguish" of victims and "listened to what they were saying".

"I came in and asked for changes to the early release scheme, and we excluded rape, grooming, and child sex offences," the prime minister added.

Prisoners will now qualify for their earlier release from 1 October and officials estimate that around 700 will walk out of the prison gates that day.

From 13 October, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months.

Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity, with the latest Ministry of Justice figures showing the number of available spaces across the male prison estate at its lowest this year, with about 1,500 free spaces.

Under the original plan, prisons and probation services had almost six weeks to prepare this second group following the first releases, but they now have less than a fortnight.

The rest of the estimated 4,500 releases will then be phased in following the dates below. Some 1,400 more offenders were due to be released under the original plans before revisions made after certain offences were excluded.

The estimated numbers are Ministry of Justice calculations:

The offenders serving the longer sentences, which do not become part of the scheme until next year, include more dangerous criminals who would have previously expected to spend two-thirds of their sentence behind bars.

Under the new rules this group will instead leave jail at the halfway point.

The ministerial order lists all of the 71 crimes that are exempt from the earlier release scheme, including manslaughter, rape, and sexual and grooming offences.

Prisoners on a special form of extended sentence and those on life terms are excluded from the scheme.

On Tuesday, the government explained it was creating more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.

An investment of £110m, which is set to come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the Ministry of Justice said.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris told the BBC being released did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.

Norris also said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

Attacks families not told 'stalker' had violent past

BBC News Wed, 02 Sep 2026 12:40:13 GMT

Families of the Nottingham attacks victims said police did not tell them a man who had taken an interest in them had a history of violence when he attempted to visit them.

Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, on 13 June 2023. He tried to kill three others.

Grace's father, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, said he was told in 2025 that a man had visited his GP surgery in London. Emma Webber, Barnaby's mother, said he had also travelled to Somerset, but neither were informed of the man's history of mental ill health.

Nottinghamshire Police said it had received a complaint and referred the matter to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

The IOPC confirmed it had received a referral of a complaint from Nottinghamshire Police in relation to information the force allegedly withheld from the families of Calocane's victims about a potential witness who had tried to contact them.

Kumar told the BBC he was informed by Nottinghamshire Police in 2025 that a man from Nottingham, who had taken an interest in his family and the Webber family, had visited his surgery in London.

He said police gave little to no details about the man, with no mention of his past mental health history.

"They [the police officers] said it was a very lowbrow thing. There was no assessment of risk to me or my family," he added.

"They didn't mention the word 'risk'."

Kumar said it was only recently, as a result of ongoing investigations into Nottinghamshire Police, in relation to the attacks, that he was informed of further details about the man by the IOPC.

"Later, we found out from the IOPC that this guy was on the Prevent register, that he had been sectioned a few times or that he was known to be a violent offender," Kumar said.

"I'm angry. Don't place my wife, don't place my other child at risk. Do these people not realise the tragedy we've been through?

"Just be transparent. That's all we wanted."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4, Grace's mother, Dr Sinead O'Malley-Kumar, said she was "absolutely flabbergasted" that police were aware of the man's behaviour in December 2024, but did not inform families until about a year later.

"And what's more concerning is that, as victims, we weren't given the proper information," she added.

"We do not know what this man looks like. Should he ring on our doorbell? Should he come to our place of work again?

"The information has been minimal."

The Times reports Barnaby Webber's parents were not told for 18 months that a stalker had travelled to Somerset to try to find them.

Emma Webber, the mother of Barnaby Webber, said in a social media post she was "furious".

"Now we learn that another mentally ill man with a fixation on us and the Nottingham case travelled to Somerset, including our home town, seeking out victims' families; and the police chose not to tell us," she said.

A spokesperson for the IOPC said it was "assessing the referral" from Nottinghamshire Police to decide what further action was required.

"After originally receiving information from Nottinghamshire Police we spoke to a potential witness in January 2025 in connection with our investigation concerning the force's interactions with Calocane prior to the attacks," the spokesperson added.

"It was unclear whether Calocane was the suspect for the matters that had been reported to police by the witness and the information was assessed as not relevant to our inquiries.

"We did, however, make the force aware of the information provided by the witness so it could take the appropriate safeguarding measures.

"We recognised that the families should have been updated that we'd spoken to this witness at the time and acknowledged that in a recent update to them.

A Nottinghamshire Police spokesperson said: "We received a complaint and due to the nature of the complaint referred the matter to the IOPC on August 24 and are awaiting their response.

"Unfortunately, we cannot comment any further at this stage while an investigation is underway. We have updated the complainant throughout the process."

Calocane pleaded guilty to three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility, and to three counts of attempted murder in November 2023.

He was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order in January 2024. A public statutory inquiry, which is examining the lead-up to the attacks and decisions taken in the aftermath is set to resume in September.

What later emerged was a series of failings by authorities, including the police and mental health services - which Calocane was known to - prompting calls for a statutory public inquiry.

The Nottingham Inquiry heard from more than 100 witnesses as the lead-up to the attacks, the investigation that followed and the aftermath were examined.

More than 900 killed in Gaza this year despite ceasefire, Hamas-run health ministry says

BBC News Wed, 02 Sep 2026 11:51:46 GMT

More than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, according to latest figures from the territory's Hamas-run Ministry of Health.

It brings the total number of Palestinians killed in the Strip since the 10 October ceasefire was declared to more than 1,300, including 301 children, the ministry says.

Hamas and Israel agreed to halt the war after accepting US President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan. That plan included a suspension of "all military operations, including aerial and artillery bombardment".

Since then, BBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos which show the impact of Israeli strikes on locations including a beachside cafe, tents where displaced people have been sheltering, and a reported funeral procession in central Gaza.

Recent months have been some of the most deadly according to the figures, with more than 100 people recorded killed each month between April and August.

The health ministry attributes the deaths directly to Israeli military action, but does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

The UN considers the figures reliable, and experts have told BBC Verify that their independent analysis is consistent with the ministry's data.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) disputes the ministry's figures. It told BBC Verify there is "no basis to assume" that all those listed were killed as a result of IDF activity.

It said it operates in "a precise manner to remove threats and protect its troops and Israeli civilians, in accordance with the agreement", and that it works to mitigate any civilian harm "to the greatest extent possible".

At the start of this year Israeli media reported that an Israeli security official acknowledged more than 70,000 people had been killed in the Gaza war, which it said included more than 20,000 combatants.

From the start of the ceasefire agreement on 10 October to the end of that month, the ministry recorded 251 deaths. Since then the deadly Israeli attacks have continued every month. The highest monthly death toll this year was recorded in July, when 152 people were killed including 21 children, according to the figures.

The IDF says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".

It also says it has killed hundreds of military operatives since October.

Conflict monitoring group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (Acled), which uses official statements, media reports and social media to verify attacks, says it has recorded around 200 Israeli strikes during the ceasefire that have reportedly killed Hamas operatives or other armed "militants" in targeted strikes.

Acled said this includes commanders involved in planning the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the war and killed around 1,200 people with 251 taken hostage.

Hugh Lovatt, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank, said "Gaza has seen a ceasefire in name only" since last October. He said the Israeli military has continued its almost daily air and drone strikes, and "though it claims to be targeting Hamas or imminent threats, it is Gaza's civilians that have continued to bear the brunt".

This could now be a "central stumbling block" in international efforts to implement Trump's ceasefire deal, he added.

The IDF told BBC Verify it "remains committed" to the ceasefire agreement and that there have been "continued violations and threats posed by Hamas and other terror organizations" in Gaza.

Warning: The following segment of this story contains graphic content which some readers might find distressing.

BBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos of attacks in Gaza carried out since the ceasefire.

In one, emergency services are seen attending to people in the aftermath of a strike at a beachside cafe in Gaza City on 18 August, where six people were killed, according to the health ministry. The next day nine people, including a 13-year-old, were reportedly killed in a strike on a police headquarters in the al-Tuffah neighbourhood.

The IDF said it was targeting Hamas commanders and terrorists in the two incidents and that "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".

One of the deadliest single incidents in July was a strike on a reported funeral procession in Nuseirat. Seven people were killed and 22 injured, according to the Al-Awda Hospital where casualties were taken. Several verified images show nine people covered in blood lying on the street. Two people appear to still be alive and are being treated by bystanders.

The IDF said it was targeting a "significant military operative" of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad group who was involved in the 7 October 2023 attacks.

In a strike on an apartment block on the western edge of Gaza City overnight on 1 August, a pregnant woman, her husband and their young son were killed, according to local reports. Verified footage showed the body of an unborn baby in the rubble.

A man searching the ruins said he had heard a strike overnight and saw smoke coming from the building. "I broke the door and went up and I found dead bodies scattered," he said. The IDF said it had targeted an acting Hamas commander.

UN agency Unicef has also reported more than 300 children have been killed since the ceasefire. The aid organisation has been tracking all available reports of incidents affecting children in Gaza, including via UN personnel on the ground.

James Elder, Unicef global spokesperson, said the number of child deaths was "absurd and devastating".

He added that hundreds more have been injured. "A ceasefire that paints such a grim picture can only be failing children."

Unicef and other humanitarian organisations operating inside Gaza have also reported Israeli strikes on their workers since the ceasefire. This includes two water truck drivers contracted by Unicef killed in April by Israeli fire at the Mansoura water filling point in northern Gaza.

The IDF said its soldiers "identified suspects approaching" the Yellow Line area during the incident, who were later identified as UN contractors who had not "coordinated in advance". Unicef said the drivers were carrying out routine water trucking operations with "no changes in movement or procedures".

Aid Worker Security Database, whose figures have been cited by the UN and UK government, told BBC Verify it has recorded 22 aid workers killed in Gaza since 10 October 2025.

Independent research group Airwars works to identify civilian deaths from a range of open sources including news agencies, NGOs and social media, matching names it finds to those published by the health ministry.

Director Emily Tripp told BBC Verify the ministry's data on death tolls is consistent with its own tracking and research, and that it recorded more than 60 deadly incidents in July.

"This is the highest number of fatal incidents we've seen in a month since the ceasefire," Tripp said. "Our own findings point to an increasing number of civilian harm incidents a month."

Professor Michael Spagat from Royal Holloway, University of London, is the chair of Every Casualty Counts, a charity that studies death tolls in wars. He told BBC Verify that the figures recorded by the health ministry are "testable" because it publishes names, ages and ID numbers of the dead.

He said that since April, the monthly death toll in Gaza has been roughly double what was seen in December. "July was the worst month but even August's lower toll is still high compared with the November to March period," he added.

Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West

BBC News Wed, 02 Sep 2026 11:47:11 GMT

Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine.

"That's a secret. A military secret."

Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging.

And that, I suspect, is the point.

Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine.

It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares".

Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like.

We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK.

But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe.

Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport.

Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe".

Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK?

Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference.

So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks.

"If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks."

Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine.

The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind.

For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine.

Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure.

"I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on.

Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war".

"War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference.

He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys.

"We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them."

There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip.

Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon?

There's nothing in the diary. Not yet.

But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms.

BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel expanding positions

BBC News Wed, 02 Sep 2026 05:03:09 GMT

The drive on the highway by the Mediterranean in southern Lebanon, near the border with Israel, is scenic and, these days, desolate. Crops lie abandoned and buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes, too many to count, are in ruins.

Near the town of Naqoura, a Lebanese military checkpoint, painted in the white-and-red colours of the national flag, is the last visible sign of the state's presence. Soldiers are positioned behind concrete walls, but the road is empty. A few minutes further south, around a dozen Israeli flags indicate the start of occupied territory. Unless authorised by Israel, no-one can enter.

This part of the country is the heartland of Lebanon's Shia Muslim community, from which Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed militia and political party, gets most of its support. It has seen three invasions by the Israeli military in wars against the group in the last two decades alone. The most recent started in March, after Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel following the killing of the Iranian supreme leader, at the start of the US and Israel's war against Iran.

Last month, a BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, known as Unifil, which is one of the only ways to visit the area under Israeli control. There, as it did in Gaza, Israel has flattened entire villages, and air strikes and demolitions have continued even after a ceasefire was announced in June.

Led by Finnish troops who are part of Unifil, the convoy was escorting civilians to and from Christian villages near the border. Those communities were spared from Israel's attacks and invasion during the war and, with the surrounding areas now under occupation, are now cut off from the rest of the country. Our presence was allowed by the Israeli military through a deconfliction mechanism with the UN.

The strip of land currently controlled by Israel constitutes around 5% of Lebanese territory and, in some places, extends 10km (six miles) from the border. Driving along the wall that separates the two countries, we saw service roads built by Israel after the invasion, intense movement of Israeli soldiers and residential buildings that were being used by them. Some were covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones.

We also heard Israeli surveillance drones in the sky and explosions in the distance, possibly from demolitions being carried out by Israel in villages that are under occupation.

In a visit to occupied southern Lebanon last month, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said he had instructed the military to "take all necessary steps to prepare for a long-term presence in the area". Israeli officials say their goal is to establish what they call a "security zone" to protect communities in northern Israel from rockets and drones that have been fired by Hezbollah from southern Lebanon, as well as a possible ground invasion.

According to Unifil, the Israeli military has established four new bases in the invaded areas, bringing the number of such positions to nine. Israeli forces had remained in five points after invading southern Lebanon during the previous war against Hezbollah in 2024, in violation of the deal that ended that conflict.

"In the past months, we've seen the consolidation and fortification of Israeli positions, construction of protective infrastructure, and other engineering works," Kandice Ardiel, a Unifil spokeswoman, said. "We have [also] observed what appear to be Israeli civilian personnel carrying out demolition and engineering activities in support of military activities in south Lebanon."

Human rights groups say some of Israel's actions in southern Lebanon amount to the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure, a possible war crime. Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese remain displaced, without knowing when, or if, they will be able to return.

In response to our questions, the Israeli military said the buildings that had been destroyed were used by Hezbollah for military purposes, and that it operated in accordance with international law. It did not respond to other specific questions about its actions in the occupied areas.

In June, the US and Iran announced a preliminary deal aimed at ending their conflict, which included a cessation of the violence in Lebanon. Since then, a Lebanese intelligence official told me, Lebanon's military has recorded more than 5,000 violations of the deal by Israel, including air strikes, drone attacks, shelling and near-daily incursions of Israeli soldiers into Lebanese territory beyond the area under occupation, the so-called Yellow Line.

As it does in Gaza, the Israeli military justifies some of its attacks in Lebanon as operations against what it describes as immediate threats. In many cases, however, it is not clear how immediate these alleged threats are or if there is any threat at all. Hezbollah, which is considered a terrorist organisation by countries including the UK and the US, has not carried out attacks against Israel since the ceasefire came into force, but has targeted Israeli troops operating inside Lebanese territory.

"[The Israelis] are expanding their presence [in Lebanon]. They've [also] been setting areas ablaze, demolishing houses while the bombing continues, despite the ceasefire," the Lebanese intelligence official said. "It's clear that they don't want anyone to go back [to those villages] in the coming year, or even years. This isn't only about Hezbollah. This is about preventing people from returning."

Israeli officials have conditioned a withdrawal from Lebanon on Hezbollah's disarmament, something the Lebanese government cannot deliver without the group's consent. Hezbollah, observers say, is still a significant military force despite the setbacks in the recent wars. Both countries have held direct talks that resulted in a framework agreement brokered by the US: Israel would pull out of certain areas, called "pilot zones", where Lebanese army soldiers would be deployed and Hezbollah's disarmament would be verified.

Hezbollah opposes the efforts – the group's leader, Naim Qassem, called them "surrender with humiliation" last week – and says any discussion about its weapons should only happen after a full Israeli withdrawal. Israel, for its part, has claimed that the Lebanese national military, which rejects the use of force against the group saying this could pit Lebanese against Lebanese, has not done enough.

The plan has seen no progress, and there is no expectation of any significant change before the Israeli election at the end of October.

"The idea of the 'pilot zones' seems to be dead until the context changes," a European diplomat familiar with the situation told me. "It seems we're heading to a Gaza-like situation. The Israelis are entrenching themselves... and are here to stay, for now."

Kids eat free and loyalty points - six ways to eat out but not break the bank

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 23:26:38 GMT

The price of eating out can be hard to swallow while the cost of living remains high, with more than a third of Brits cutting back on going to restaurants, according to YouGov's latest Dining Out report.

Restaurateurs say the rising cost of food, energy, wage and tax bills mean they've had to put up prices, with some top chefs campaigning for government help.

Many eateries are offering incentives to get diners through the doors. Here are some ways to save money on meals out.

Many restaurants offer points, freebies, discounts and birthday treats to keep customers coming back.

One of the most well-known is the Pizza Express Club. Regular diners can progress through a bronze, silver and gold system unlocking perks from free dough balls to hot and soft drinks on the house.

Nando's uses a chilli system for its loyalty programme, while other schemes such as Tastecard offer discounts at hundreds of eat-in and takeaway venues in exchange for an annual fee.

Restaurants often want to fill seats outside of peak lunch and dinner hours so opting for earlier or later sittings can be rewarded by a cheaper bill.

Apps such as First Table, which operates across 21 UK cities, as well as Ireland, New Zealand and Australia, give diners 50% off food when they book a participating restaurant's first or last dining slot. In exchange, diners pay a small booking fee.

EatClub is another, giving walk-ins up to 50% off the whole bill at thousands of venues when they redeem an offer within its app. The biggest discounts are at off-peak times.

Shokofeh Hejazi, director of foresight and innovation at global trends agency The Food People, says earlier dining appeals because it tends to be quieter and calmer, people drink less and it allows them to get home sooner.

Meeting up for breakfast also tends to be a bit more wallet-friendly as it's usually just one course and diners get the same catch-up time with friends and family, she adds.

In the school holidays, many places will entice families through their doors by offering free or £1 meals for kids eating with paying adults.

These range from big chains such as TGI Fridays, cafes at supermarkets including Morrisons and Asda, and even garden centres like Dobbies.

While some tie-in with school holidays, other deals are all year round.

Many new restaurants will offer discounts in a bid to encourage diners to try them out and spread the word that they've opened for business.

These are known as "soft launches" and can run for several weeks. They're a cost-effective way of trying a higher-end restaurant without such a hit to the wallet.

Keep track by signing up to newsletters that list upcoming openings in the local area.

Hejazi says some restaurants are extending the period before they fully open to garner more buzz, while others are making their soft launch pricing permanent for quieter days such as Mondays.

People shouldn't assume they're priced out of fine dining-type venues because "there's access points for everybody in a lot of these places", she says.

Supermarket loyalty points from those weekly shops add up over time so why not put them toward a meal out?

For example, each 50p earned in Tesco Clubcard points can be exchanged £1.50 in vouchers to spend at participating Prezzo Italian venues. The chain is just one of Tesco's restaurant partners.

Finally, there are plenty of options to take away food for free or at a fraction of the usual price.

Surplus food apps such as Too Good To Go, or Olio, allow customers to bag goodies that would otherwise go to waste.

It's a bit of a gamble - you don't always know precisely what you'll be getting.

But there's money to be saved on items needed to buy anyway, that's more cash left over for when you do decide to dine out.

Saturn has a big, weird decagon around its south pole

New Scientist September 02, 2026

Saturn has a new, odd weather pattern resembling a decagon near its south pole. This may have formed due to a large storm nearby, but researchers aren’t totally sure.

The pattern has clearly defined sides shaped by powerful winds, looking like a decagon – a geometric polygon with 10 sides and 10 angles – from above. It is similar to a hexagonal weather pattern first seen at the planet’s north pole more than 40 years ago.

Saturn’s rings may have formed after a huge collision with Titan

“[But] the one at the north is a bit smaller,” says Amy Simon at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland. The south pole pattern also seems to be moving a bit more with the rotation of the planet.

Advertisement

The feature was first spotted by amateur astronomers in 2024. Simon and her colleagues then examined images taken by the Hubble Space Telescope from 2023 to 2025. “We confirmed the existence of the decagon with absolute clarity,” says team member Agustín Sánchez-Lavega at the University of the Basque Country in Spain.

It is unclear exactly when the pattern formed, with no spacecraft having orbited Saturn since 2017. “It most certainly wasn’t expected,” says Simon. “The hexagon has been there for decades, but this is something new.”

The decagon measures about 13,000 kilometres across, slightly wider than Earth. It is thought to result from a large atmospheric wave shaped by wind from a powerful jet stream that meanders near the planet’s south pole.

Its formation may be linked to a large nearby storm, although the exact cause is a bit of a mystery. “It’s a very complicated fluid dynamics sort of thing,” says Simon. “It’s telling us something about what’s going on deeper below the clouds.”

The rings of Saturn are normally thought to be flat, but measurements by the Cassini spacecraft show that some of their particles fly hundreds of thousands of kilometres above and below the thin main discs

Andrew Ingersoll at the California Institute of Technology says the discovery highlights that Saturn is a dynamic, changing world. “It’s very interesting to see these features,” he says.

No similar pattern has been observed on any other planets, although Jupiter does have an arrangement of cyclones at its poles. “People didn’t really predict that such an organised, polygonal pattern would exist on another planet,” says Ingersoll.

We don’t know how long the pattern will last. Other telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope, are poised to study it in more detail, but many scientists are vying for access to those. “We’ll look as frequently as anyone will let us,” says Simon.

Adam Kucharski would like to point out he did not win big at a casino

New Scientist September 02, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

An epidemiologist walks into a casino – what happens next? Feedback is tempted to say he wins the black spot, or some other top-quality pun, but our editor is giving us a long, hard stare, so we had better get on with it.

Epidemiologist and mathematician Adam Kucharski was recently bemused to learn that the internet is making up stories about him. Two posts on X, the site formerly known as Twitter, told the same tale: that he had walked into a casino for the first time in his life and won “500K”. The currency wasn’t specified in one instance, while in another, it was US dollars.

Advertisement

One of the X posts even seems to quote Kucharski directly: “One evening I made 500K at a casino. I had never gambled before – but I’d spent my whole life studying probability theory, and I decided to test one formula in practice.” This quote apparently came from Kucharski’s debut popular science book The Perfect Bet (2016).

So far, so people making stuff up on social media. But mark the sequel: these stories at one point made their way into the AI Overview hosted at the top of Google Search when Kucharski looked up “kucharski 500k” – “with some extra AI invented detail”, as he points out. The overview added that Kucharski has made a “lifelong study of roulette dynamics” and that he won by “applying probability theory and physics-based insights to roulette wheels, similar to the principles studied by Claude Shannon”.

Feedback genuinely has no idea what that last bit is about. Shannon was a researcher who laid the theoretical groundwork for digital circuits and modern cryptography. He wasn’t known for spread-betting on roulette.

Yet again, AI systems are readily poisoned with nonsense from somewhere else – and that’s assuming the original X posts were written by humans in the first place, which nobody should assume at this point. It’s a particularly insidious example because Kucharski did write a book about gambling strategies, so the story is plausible enough to pass an initial sniff test: one needs actual knowledge of Kucharski’s life and work to know that it’s not true.

We will give the last word to Kucharski’s wife, entrepreneur Emily Kucharski. Responding to the claim that he had won half a million of some currency or another in one night, Emily said, simply, “If only this were true”.

How big does an ocean wave need to be to tower over a roadside model of a carrot? This was our question on 29 July, after we saw a wave forecast from New Zealand’s weather service, claiming that “combined wave heights in eastern offshore waters could reach or exceed the height of the Ohakune Carrot”. The Ohakune Carrot proved to be a 7.5-metre-tall fibreglass sculpture placed outside the town of Ohakune to commemorate its carrot-growing industry.

The issue, Feedback felt, was whether or not the Ohakune Carrot was sufficiently well-known in New Zealand that it could be safely used as a unit of wave height. For instance, certain British landmarks could probably be used in a similar way in British weather forecasts, like the London Eye or Blackpool Tower, but was the Ohakune Carrot the New Zealand equivalent? Current and former residents of Aotearoa have now weighed in on this point.

“As an Aotearoan/NZer who hasn’t lived there in over 13 years,” writes Kirsten Cameron, “my immediate reaction and I imagine that of most in Aotearoa/NZ: Yeah quite high. The actual height is irrelevant, it’s enough information to know it’s high enough to be a problem!” Feedback isn’t sure we agree: depending on what kind of watercraft you are using, a 7.5 m wave might be trivial or dangerous. We recently had to transfer between a cruise ship and a zodiac boat, and we can assure you that a swell of a metre or so was enough to turn this into a tricky operation.

On which note, “third-generation NZer” Brenda Solon makes a much more dramatic point. “It occurred to me that while the Carrot might be only 7.5m tall, Ohakune is 582m above sea level,” she writes. “That would be a dangerous ocean wave indeed that could reach its top.” Fortunately, she notes, “this wave didn’t eventuate”, hence she is alive to email us with this thought.

Finally, and with a certain inevitability, Simon Bird suggests that a suitable unit of height for London-based phenomena would be the Camberwell Carrot. Initially, Feedback’s literal-minded brain protested: the notable thing about the Camberwell Carrot, as featured and indeed smoked in Withnail and I, was its width, not its length or height. Then we realised that Simon wasn’t talking about physical height.

Over the years, Feedback has encountered a number of examples of nominative determinism related to trees. Who can forget research forest products technologist Marlin E. Plank, or Tree Hunting author Paul Wood?

A couple more examples have trickled into our inbox over the past few months. First, Andy Maloney directs us to an article in The Guardian about volunteers who are trying to grow 8 million native trees in Scotland. Inevitably, these virtuous activities are being supervised by Roz Birch.

Meanwhile, Janet Dowle tells us: “I have just had a flyer put through my letterbox from a tree surgeon called Edward Wood.”

Ambitious sci-fi novel imagines a universe where time flows backwards

New Scientist September 02, 2026

Under StoryChloe BenjaminTinder Press (UK); G. P. Putnam’s Sons (US)

One of the big books of 2026, Under Story by Chloe Benjamin, has a wonderful premise. What if there were an identical universe to ours, except that time runs in the opposite direction? And what if we could cross over from this universe to the “anti-universe” and then back again?

This is a human, warm and extremely ambitious book. Our hero, fungi expert Laurel Salter, having suffered a devastating loss, takes a job as a kitchen steward at an Antarctic research station. She makes friends with other workers and becomes fascinated with a strange light display in the distance called the “anomaly”. We gradually come to realise that this light display could potentially be a crossing place to the anti-universe.

Everything ramps up when Laurel’s ex-husband, a physicist named Eli Rosen, shows up to investigate the anomaly. Laurel wasn’t expecting him; they are barely on speaking terms.

Alert: a few mild spoilers ahead, but only because I need to explain what was (for me) a problem.

Laurel’s story, and the way we go back and forth from the present-day Antarctic to her past and the heartbreak that happened, is all well done in the first half of the book. Arguably, it could have been edited – this is a long book – but if you don’t mind a languorous pace, and a lot of focus on side plots and side characters, then no biggie.

There’s a lot of science – about physics, Eli’s speciality, and also about fungi, Laurel’s speciality – arguably too much. Either way, all the science served to set me up for a book that was going to feel scientifically robust… which brings us to the nub of my problem.

Of course, in a novel, universes can have time running backwards for some things but not others

Eli and Laurel cross over to the anti-universe, for heartfelt reasons I won’t go into. There, they duly find that time runs backwards. Politics, wars and so on happen in the reverse order to those in the regular universe. For example, Donald Trump is president before Barack Obama. People are born in their graves, very old, and get physically more robust throughout their lives before, near the end, shrinking into tiny people, then being pushed back into their mother’s wombs. So far, so backwards. Interesting, too. Babies slipping back into their mothers! Newborns being very old people, waking from death!

However. Some things in this universe go backwards, but a heck of a lot goes forwards. Characters drive to places in a regular way as they de-age. They eat food and digest it after eating, not vice versa. They have sex in a normal manner (in a pivotal sex scene, the man ejaculates at the end of the sex, not at the start). They go on holiday at the start of a trip, enjoy it, then go home. Conversations begin, take place and end, with questions answered and so forth – all very much in the order you would expect in a regular universe.

Free newsletter

Of course, in a novel, universes can have time running backwards for certain things but not others; authors may do exactly as they please. But for whatever reason, I ended up worrying over the physics, and that ruined things. (I look forward to hearing what physicists think of this book.)

Anyway, once you start worrying that the central logic of a book doesn’t really hang together, it does tend to dampen enjoyment. Nonetheless, I still read to the end, and I enjoyed a lot of my journey forwards in our universe, and (partly) backwards in the anti-universe, and there is a lot of beauty in the story Benjamin weaves. She is clearly very talented.

The Other ValleyScott Alexander HowardAtlantic Books

This is a good example of a book where the central premise may make literally no sense – the valleys oneither side of a central valley are either ahead of it in time, or behind it – but it doesn’t matter one whit because the writer never bothers to explain what’s going on, but instead pulls you along so firmly that physics is the last thing you’re worrying about.

Emily H. Wilson is the author of the Sumerians series (Inanna, Gilgamesh and Ninshubar, all published by Titan) and she is currently working on her first sci-fi novel. She is a former editor of New Scientist and you can follow her on Instagram @emilyhwilson1

Designer floating homes may be the future as sea levels rise

New Scientist September 02, 2026

Floating FuturesAlessandro Gandolfi

Imagine a city where suburbs float on water. Floating homes already exist in coastal communities in places like the Philippines and Vietnam. Now, high-income nations facing dangerous sea-level rise are looking to those examples.

Among them is the Netherlands, where over a quarter of the land is below sea level and around two-thirds of it is at risk of flooding.

Advertisement

This photograph shows floating houses in the IJburg district at the edge of Amsterdam, the largest Dutch city. The image comes from Floating Futures, a new series by photojournalist Alessandro Gandolfi.

The affluent, relatively high-density IJburg community comprises 158 waterside homes, 55 of which are floating. Residents are connected by bridges and roads, and most houses have a boat outside instead of a car.

Simply raising the dykes is no longer enough against the rising waters, Gandolfi writes in his photo essay. “Experts warn that mastering water’s whims is an illusion. The answer, they say, lies in a shift of mindset – the philosophy of meebewegen: not fighting against water, but learning to live with it.”

The homes at IJburg aren’t houseboats or retrofitted vessels like the ones lining Amsterdam’s canals, but architect-designed homes intended to encourage community living. They are built to be sustainable, with rooftop solar panels and careful management of sewage and other waste.

But their biggest difference from other houses will always lie below, in their watery foundations.

Humans can see water, so can fish see air?

New Scientist September 02, 2026

Mike FollowsSutton Coldfield, West Midlands, UK

Neither water nor air is normally visible because they are largely transparent. What we actually see are boundaries between different media or particles suspended within them.

A fish can see the water’s surface from below, just as we can see it from above, because light is reflected and refracted where water meets air. This is due to the difference in refractive index between the two media. The effect is most noticeable when the surface is rippled, as the changing angles produce shifting reflections. The same principle applies to air bubbles in water or droplets of water in air: it is the boundary between the two media that is visible, not the medium itself. When viewed close to perpendicular to the surface, a perfectly calm water surface can become almost invisible, allowing you to look directly into the other medium, almost as if you were immersed in it.

Advertisement

Refraction also produces “Snell’s window”: rather than seeing the entire world above the surface, a fish sees it compressed into a circular window about 97 degrees across. Outside this window, the surface acts as a mirror because of total internal reflection, reflecting the underwater world back to the fish. Someone standing above the surface outside this window wouldn’t be directly visible, a fact often exploited by anglers.

A fish can see the water’s surface from below because light is reflected and refracted where water meets air

Similarly, when you are underwater wearing a mask or goggles, you can’t really see the water itself, just as you can’t see the air on land. You know you are underwater because of the different environment: buoyancy, the altered landscape and the underwater flora and fauna.

Visibility underwater is often poorer than in air because suspended particles scatter light. Even in exceptionally clear water, light is gradually absorbed with depth. Longer wavelengths, such as red light, are absorbed first, leaving mainly blue light to penetrate to greater depths, which is why the underwater world becomes increasingly blue.

So, in much the same way that we don’t normally see the air around us, fish don’t normally see the water around them. Instead, they see objects in the water and the boundaries where water meets something else, particularly the water’s surface.

If the sun suddenly disappeared, how long would life on Earth last?

New Scientist September 02, 2026

If the sun suddenly disappeared, how long would life on Earth last, from humans and plants to subterranean bacteria?

Anthony WoodwardPortland, Oregon, US

It depends what is meant by “disappeared”. If it means the sun and its mass being deleted by some god-like entity, then 8 minutes later, Earth would stop orbiting and move off in a straight line towards the boundary of the solar system at 107,000 kilometres per hour. So would the other planets. Eventually, Earth could catch up with Jupiter moving at about 47,000 km/h. Earth might even become another moon of Jupiter, now the most massive body in the solar system. All life would have frozen to death before we reached the hazards of the asteroid belt.

Advertisement

If “disappeared” means we no longer see the sun because the sun has stopped emitting light and heat (but its mass remains), then 8 minutes later, photosynthesis stops. But there would be little immediate change. After all, life on Earth is accustomed to the dark of night.

The surface of Earth would cool rapidly. Within a week, surface water would be frozen and most plants and animals would begin to die. Any water deep below the ice would remain liquid for decades, so some aquatic animals could live for years feeding on detritus.

If the sun disappeared, Earth would simultaneously be obliterated by the cataclysmic event that caused it to disappear

Less than 0.001 per cent of life on Earth doesn’t depend on photosynthesis. Such organisms, typically found in the depths of the oceans, could survive until even those depths froze.

But humans are inventive, with access to huge amounts of energy in the form of fossil fuels and nuclear power. Our cities shine so brightly they are visible from space. We would light and heat our homes. We could create vast greenhouses to grow the plants we like to eat, and even enough grass to feed cattle for meat and milk. Of course, such use of energy requires the money and political control of wealthy people. Those who can’t afford it would starve.

Hillary ShawNewport, Shropshire, UK

If humans aren’t around, temperatures fall below freezing everywhere within a week and all bodies of water ice over. Plants are dormant, later to die when their cells freeze, and land animals die of thirst if the cold hasn’t claimed them.

Within a year, all water bodies except deep oceans have frozen solid, killing all life in them. After two years, atmospheric nitrogen will rain out (which condenses at -196°C), as will the oxygen (-183°C). All surface land life and soil bacteria are now dead. Life clings on in deeper oceans, which take 1000 years to freeze almost solid, although most higher oceanic life has starved by then. The last survivors are tubeworms at oceanic vents, where the ocean may not ever totally freeze as Earth’s geothermal heat continues for millions of years.

But if there is no liquid water to lubricate plate tectonics, Earth’s plate system may partially seize up. This causes less frequent, but catastrophic earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Maybe some deep sea vent life won’t survive this.

With humans, given a year’s warning, we might construct underground shelters for billions. We would need geothermal power at an unprecedented scale, and intensive farming, maybe “vertical farms”. Many people in low-income countries would still be unable to secure a place, unless they mounted a mass invasion of higher-income countries. Then most humans would die in the total world war that ensues, and most shelters wouldn’t get built. Psychological issues would be numerous, from lack of access to nature to the need for strict totalitarian control.

On the day the sun goes out, we buy some time by quickly burning the forests, which will die anyway, creating a massive greenhouse effect. Maybe then, after a year, average global temperature is a balmy 0°C and the oceans may not have frozen. We then need to give the population hope and a purpose, so we build a huge “Noah’s Ark” spaceship. This will take as many different life forms as possible with less than 1 billion humans on a long voyage with no clear destination, just a desperate search for another suitable planet, knowing many generations will pass on board before we find one.

Andrew WardWotton-under-Edge, Gloucestershire, UK

If the sun suddenly disappeared, Earth would simultaneously be obliterated by whatever cataclysmic event caused it to disappear. Possibly delayed by 8 minutes.

The legendary snow leopard comes up against harsh realities in remarkable book

New Scientist September 02, 2026

The Ghost of the MountainsKulbhushansingh SuryawanshiGranta Books (UK); Riverhead Books (US)

Like many large carnivores, the snow leopard is eclipsed by an outsize reputation, which makes it almost impossible to separate the animal from the story. The solitary, largely silent cat is often spoken of as being not there – a shadow, a ghost – with its ethereal presence, in the Buddhist heartlands of the Himalaya, bordering on the spiritual.

When Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi first proposed studying the cat, his professor dismissed the idea, because, he said, his student would never see one. Yet two decades on (and a handful of sightings later), Suryawanshi has produced a wonderful book, The Ghost of the Mountains, about this most unknowable of animals.

Advertisement

During the Pleistocene ice age, the snow leopard’s distribution probably stretched from Portugal to Siberia. But their range contracted with the ice, and they are now confined to 12 countries in Central Asia and the Himalaya, across some of the world’s highest mountain ranges. Unlike wolves, say, or lynxes, they are the only large carnivores to be exclusively adapted to mountains. Their dusky coats, spotted with dark rosettes, vanish against boulders and scree. Relative to their body size, their tails are longer than that of any other cat, helping them balance, while wide nostrils warm the air they breathe. Genetic adaptations let them cope with the thin air.

The leopard becomes his way of penetrating the complexity and fragility of all we stand to lose

Suryawanshi is equally well equipped to study them, combining profound patience, a lifetime of mountaineering and a deep passion for this enigmatic animal. This is just as well: it is hard to imagine a more punishing environment for fieldwork. The snow leopard inhabits 3 million square kilometres of mountains. The peaks soar to over 8000 metres and the weather can turn on a dime. His teams must deal with hypothermia, blizzards, bears and rivers in spate. One friend dies of a heart attack, a complication of altitude sickness. Another, who worked to protect the mountains from mining, is found dead, his death unexplained.

Until Suryawanshi began his work, less than 1 per cent of the snow leopard’s habitat had been properly surveyed. Yet it is impossible to conserve something if you cannot show that it is there.

As far as we know, a snow leopard has never harmed a human, the only big cat to hold this “noble record”. Yet this still hasn’t endeared the cats to the herders that share their hills. As I wrote in my own work on wolves in Europe, conservation achieves little without a meaningful, concurrent approach to coexistence. Killing snow leopards is illegal, but that doesn’t stop poaching.

Yet predators aren’t the only threat to these livelihoods. When mining companies prospect for mineral deposits in the Gobi desert, Suryawanshi’s team discovers that under Mongolian law, holders of traditional land rights can form nature reserves by demonstrating the biodiversity of the land. Working with herders, procuring funds for them to build corrals to keep their goats safe, the team sets about changing the narrative of the snow leopard, and ultimately enables the formation of the Tost-Tosonbumba Nature Reserve. It is those who live there, Suryawanshi understands, who are the land’s most vital custodians.

Writing about the snow leopard inevitably means writing about naturalist and writer Peter Matthiessen. In 1973, he was invited by the naturalist George Schaller to accompany him to the Inner Dolpa on the Tibetan plateau of Nepal, on a search for the snow leopard. Matthiessen never sees one, but his book about the journey did much to cement the animal’s mythology as both remarkable carnivore and potent symbol of the untamed and the ineffable.

A wolf’s 1000-mile quest makes for epic and empathetic reading

For Suryawanshi, too, the snow leopard is his way into these places. But if for Matthiessen the elusive animal becomes a cipher for the mystery at the heart of oneself, for Suryawanshi, the quest is far more tangible. The snow leopard becomes his way of penetrating the complexity and fragility of ecosystems and human cultures, and all we stand to lose.

One of the great merits of the book is its story of conservation from a non-Western perspective. Two decades ago, when Suryawanshi began his work, the snow leopard was little studied and the majority of researchers were Westerners. In one illuminating chapter, he explores the downlisting of the snow leopard from “endangered” to “vulnerable” in 2017 by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Whether such a downlisting is merited depends on estimating the population, a Herculean task, and so decisions become politicised. While Western scientists broadly support the downlisting, claiming a conservation success, local scientists fear it will embolden those who want to develop the mountains. Suryawanshi brings a rare, much needed reminder that “political and racial bias” remains in how the wider academic community sees local researchers.

“If there is still a mystery left in the Himalaya,” says one mountain ranger, early in the book, “then it is the snow leopard.” Something similar could have been claimed for Everest, but the mountain is now “for tourists”, says one mountaineering instructor. A boom in wildlife tourism risks similar commodification of snow leopards. With dedicated guides and telemetric equipment, they are now easier to find and Suryawanshi has a certain disdain for photographers lined up to grab a photo of the ghost. Yet tourists bring money to communities and add weight to the idea that these animals and their habitats carry intrinsic value worth protecting.

In the end, Suryawanshi writes, “whether local livestock herders chose to live with snow leopards would depend on their own stories”. Towards the end of the book, an ancient male snow leopard lies down outside a mountain village. Decades earlier, a herder would have killed him on the spot. But now the villagers see him differently. They leave out meat, and when he dies, they bring him into the village and give him a funeral. People can change, if their concerns are understood. It is a remarkable moment in a remarkable book about this most inscrutable of animals.

The Tiger: A true story of vengeance and survival by John VaillantAn outstanding book about our relationship with carnivores, this tells the story of a man-eating Siberian tiger and those tasked with hunting it down. As pacy as a thriller, it examines how we see carnivores – and how they see us.

The Velvet Queen a documentary directed by Marie Amiguet and Vincent MunierIn a modern reworking of Peter Matthiessen’s quest, wildlife photographer Vincent Munier invites writer Sylvain Tesson to join a search for the snow leopard in Tibet. A deep meditation on the value of the wild.

Lone Wolf: A journey into the wild heart of the Alps by Adam WeymouthForgive me for plugging my book, but my 1600-kilometre hike in the footsteps of a GPS-tracked wolf could work as a companion to Suryawanshi’s, exploring similar issues of wilderness and coexistence – but in Europe.

Adam Weymouth is a writer based in Kent, UK
