Why the extremes of climate breakdown will continue to take us by surprise

New Scientist September 02, 2026

For some in the northern hemisphere, 2026 has been the summer the climate threat became real. It has, at times, felt like one long, rolling crisis, bringing drought, energy shortages, failed harvests, deadly wildfires – and relentless heat.

There’s much we can do to adapt to these extremes. Our cover feature this week reveals how we can train our bodies to cope better in the heat, both by hacking our circulatory systems and rethinking our summer habits.

We would be fools not to prepare our infrastructure now for future severe weather and its fallout. To that end, more must be done to protect our water supplies, shift our farming practices and cool our buildings.

Advertisement

But climate change is a fickle beast. It is a big, global, slow-moving crisis. We know glaciers are slowly melting – as our reporter Alec Luhn saw first-hand – seas are warming and temperatures are rising. Yet it also emerges as a sudden, disastrous event, in the form of a storm, a flood or a heatwave.

We are getting better at spotting when these violent lurches in the system will take place. Satellite imagery, sensors, floating buoys and computer models can chart everything from the next storm to the coming monster El Niño. Sometimes, we will get a warning months before an event. But other times, as we saw tragically in Nepal and Tibet last week, severe events strike too suddenly to avoid disaster.

This summer has underscored how much climate breakdown can take us by surprise

The scale of these shocks means that just learning to predict and prepare for them isn’t a long-term solution. This summer has rightly brought much more focus on how we can adapt to live with future extremes. But it has also underscored the alarming potential for climate breakdown to take us by surprise with its speed and severity.

The urgent task is to reduce emissions, and fast. Limiting warming to well below 2°C – as the world has collectively promised – offers the chance of a future we can adapt to. Let’s hope this roiling summer has rekindled enthusiasm for that gargantuan task.

Wellington Zoo euthanises elderly giraffe a week after putting down chimp

New Zealand Herald September 02, 2026

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Wellington Zoo has euthanised an elderly giraffe just days after having to put down a chimp who was injured in a troop fight.

Zahara, the “matriarch” of the giraffe herd, was farewelled on Tuesday by keepers after her degenerative arthritis became too severe.

Known as “Queen Z”, the 22-year-old had lived longer than the average life expectancy for giraffes in human care, Te Nukuao Wellington Zoo staff said in a social media post.

“Earlier this year, Zahara was observed with increasing lameness during training sessions. X-rays taken at the time showed evidence of progressive joint disease and lameness in at least two limbs. Sadly, this type of degenerative arthritis is common in aged zoo giraffes,” the zoo’s post said.

Zahara had been managing well on pain medication but in the past week had started showing “increasing signs of discomfort”.

“She had also developed pain in her mouth and was reluctant to eat, which is a worrying sign in a giraffe, considering how much they need to eat.

“Zahara’s prognosis was not positive, and the decision was made to euthanise her to ensure she was no longer in pain.

“It’s heartbreaking to say goodbye to any of the animals at Te Nukuao, and Queen Z had a place in so many people’s hearts – staff and visitors alike. We will miss her terribly.”

Zahara’s death was announced about a week after the zoo posted about the death of 11-year-old chimp Kitwe.

Kitwe, named by the late conservationist and chimp expert Dr Jane Goodall, was involved in a fight with other members of the chimp troop, and was assessed by the primate and veterinary teams afterwards.

“The decision was made to euthanise him due to the extent of his injuries,” the zoo said.

“Fights and displays of aggression are behaviours common in chimpanzee troops and this is a natural part of chimp life, whether they’re living in the forest or in human care.

“Understanding this is part of chimpanzees’ nature does not make the loss of Kitwe any easier on our team, and we are all feeling this loss, especially the primate team who care for the chimps every day.”

“He was the sweetest boy with the goofiest smile, and he will be greatly missed by everyone at the zoo and across our community of visitors.”

It is not the first time Wellington Zoo has had to euthanise animals after aggression.

In 2019, the zoo put down its troop of baboons after a breakdown in their social structure.

Zoo staff explained at the time the baboons would have killed each other, but could not be rehomed, kept in isolation or reintroduced into different troops.

The then-primate team leader said the troop was stable for a long time, but when its hierarchy began falling apart the fighting became more frequent and the baboons started suffering worse injuries.

“In the end, it led to a complete disestablishment and non-existence of any hierarchy within that group,” she said.

Other recent deaths of animals at the zoo have been caused by old age and health issues, with the latest being Fernando the capybara, whose health and quality of life plunged after the death of his breeding partner, Dia.

In April, 18-year-old Sumatran tiger Bashii was also euthanised after developing kidney disease, a common issue for elderly cats.

Christopher Luxon’s bed tax U-turn is the third ‘rock’ for councils to swallow

New Zealand Herald September 02, 2026

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has abandoned plans to look at introducing a bed tax for tourist accommodation. Photo / 123rf

Promised a loaf of bread and given a rock.

That’s how Mackenzie District Mayor Scott Aronsen described Christopher Luxon’s rapid U-turn on a bed tax.

The Prime Minister had promised to explore this in a signed deal with Auckland Council, and in deals about to be signed in other parts of the country, including Queenstown-Lakes and the Mackenzie District.

But this would have undermined Luxon’s most important election message of no new taxes – is it a levy or a tax? – so out the window it was flung. There will be other options, he said, without naming any.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown put the U-turn down to election season and Luxon being in “temporary survival mode”. Brown seemed pragmatic about picking up the bed levy conversation post-election with whoever ends up occupying the Beehive.

Then came the 4% cap on council rates (except for water infrastructure, and from 2029). At least this was long signalled rather than sprung from nowhere.

It’s also politically potent, given its unsurprising popularity with ratepayers (voters), but it’s another rock in councils’ bread supply.

The vast majority already have rates higher than 4% as they try to plug infrastructure deficits that, in some districts such as Queenstown-Lakes, are only going to come under increasing pressure from fast-tracked housing projects.

“Local government only gets 10% of the country’s tax take but councils are responsible for about a third of all public infrastructure investment in New Zealand,” Local Government NZ president Rehette Stoltz said.

“Councils can’t be expected to deliver more infrastructure, support growth and meet communities’ expectations with fewer levers – the maths just doesn’t add up and something will have to give.”

At least these were announced. The third in the rocky trifecta is the under-the-radar raiding of the International Visitor Levy (IVL).

The IVL was established in 2019 to help pay for the burden foreign tourists placed on tourism infrastructure they used, and the conservation jewels they visited.

It started as $35 each for about 60% of foreigners (Australians and some Pacific nationalities are exempt), but since October 2024 it has been $100.

This should have seen the IVL cashflow triple for money-starved biodiversity and infrastructure work. The Department of Conservation is an estimated $1.65 billion a year short of what it needs to meet its biodiversity objectives. Cost pressures from international visitors on conservation land are estimated to be at least $96 million a year, while on tourism infrastructure, it’s at least $150m a year.

But facing financial squeezes, the Government engineered a funding switch, swapping IVL cash for Crown funding in the tourism or conservation portfolios while keeping overall spending at a standstill.

“This will generate positive fiscal headroom by ‘backing out’ an equivalent amount of existing Crown funding,” Treasury said.

This doesn’t mean none of the IVL is being used for its intended purpose. Budget 2025 documents show $90m a year being set aside for additional tourism and conservation spending – $35m for the former and $55m for the latter – while keeping $131m a year from 2026/27 as extra fiscal breathing space.

It’s also notable that the IVL’s tourism spend isn’t about helping to cope with tourist numbers, but boosting those numbers. Most of it – $19.5m – is for Tourism New Zealand marketing, while $5m is for the Major Events Fund.

The latest annual performance report for the IVL suggests the anticipated IVL pot has grown by $10m a year.

Budget 2025 had the pot at $837m over the four years to 2028/29, but the annual report – published in June this year – has it at $877m; $27m of that has been committed to administrative costs, while $248m is committed for additional spending in conservation and tourism ($124m each).

That leaves about $580m over four years, including $141m a year from 2026/27 – more than enough to cover what a bed tax might have brought in for interested councils.

Auckland Council has estimated $27m a year from a levy of 2.5% to 3%, while in Queenstown a $10-a-night bed tax could bring in $60m a year.

Whether using IVL revenue in this way would be supported by the governing parties is another matter.

Act leader David Seymour has already tried, unsuccessfully, to garner support from National and New Zealand First in this year’s Budget for a Local Tourism Dividend: $1 from central to local government for every commercial guest night in their area.

Based on 2026 numbers, it would generate $40.6m a year overall, including about $8.2m for Auckland, $4.9m for Queenstown and $2m for Rotorua, for the likes of local roads, public toilets, or council-owned public spaces and events infrastructure.

The advantage, Seymour says, is that it would avoid the bureaucracy of setting up and administering an accommodation levy, as well as the inevitable higher prices that would be passed on to tourists or picked up by hotels.

It would also be fairer, given the disparity over the tax take from central government compared with local government, relative to infrastructure burden.

And if it came from the IVL, it would channel that money towards what it’s meant to be used for, restoring some of the Government’s integrity points lost from the bed tax U-turn.

The disadvantage, and the likely reason his coalition partners didn’t support it, is the tens of millions of dollars a year that the Government wouldn’t be able to spend or would have to cut from somewhere.

It’s not dissimilar to moving income tax brackets with inflation to account for bracket creep. It passes the fairness test but it would also deprive the Government of a bunch of tax cash.

This is the advantage of the bed tax. The money wouldn’t come from the Crown but from tourists, assuming it’s passed on to the customer.

Act has already said it would veto any bed tax, which requires legislative change (and a parliamentary majority) to implement.

The middle ground then is a continuation of growing tension between local and central government, along with either reduced local services or higher debt.

Derek Cheng is a senior journalist who started at the Herald in 2004. He has worked several stints in the press gallery team and is a former deputy political editor.

Wellington City Council will hold a byelection in the city’s Northern ward on December 11, four months after the unexpected death of councillor Tony Randle.

Nominations have today opened for candidates to stand in the seat to serve the rest of the term before the 2028 local elections.

Randle, a second-term independent councillor, died of heart complications at Wellington Hospital on August 9, aged 65.

Retiring Labour Rongotai MP Greg O’Connor has announced he is “seriously considering” a tilt at the seat, after his parliamentary career was cut short by the abolition of his electorate and missing out on a candidacy bid elsewhere.

O’Connor yesterday told the Herald he was still thinking about it, and planned to spend the next few days with his family following his valedictory speech yesterday.

Also interested in a run is former Northern ward councillor John Apanowicz, who said he has unfinished business on council after being the only councillor who ran in the October elections not to return.

Former Independent Together candidate and anti-Tiaki Wai campaigner Guy Nunns has also announced his intention to stand, seeking the position to scrutinise the water entity from within the council.

The Northern ward is the largest council ward in the capital, except for the Māori Ward, with approximately 36,000 enrolled electors.

The byelection will be conducted by postal vote, and people who are enrolled can expect to receive their voting packs in the mail from November 9.

Nominations for prospective candidates close at midday on Thursday, October 1.

Voting will open on November 9 and close at noon on December 11.

Early estimates suggest the byelection could cost $250,000, a council spokesman said previously, citing the increased cost of postage as a key inflationary factor.

Auckland former teacher trial: Man testifies against his alleged child sex abuser

New Zealand Herald September 02, 2026

The ex-teacher denies the offending.

An Auckland man who says he was sexually abused as a child is finally having his day in court, decades after he says he first spoke out about the alleged offending.

“I’ve spent my whole life thinking he’s going to get away with this,” he testified yesterday afternoon.

That complainant, now in his 40s, said he first alerted his family to the alleged sexual assaults decades ago, and initially reported it to police several years later in 2002. It wasn’t until after his second complaint in 2024 that the older male was arrested in relation to the allegations.

The man, a retired teacher with interim name suppression, is facing 10 historic abuse charges in relation to two victims, including unlawful sexual connection, indecency with a child and threatening to kill.

He denies the offending.

On Tuesday, the first of the complainants testified that he had been abused by his former teacher as a child growing up in Auckland several decades ago.

Yesterday, the second complainant said in a police interview played to an Auckland District Court jury that the alleged abuse “f***ed” his life.

“When I initially made the complaint [to police] I thought that would be enough, I thought ‘yay I’ve done what’s right, I can save heaps of other people from going through it’.”

However, he said police sent him a letter after his 2002 complaint saying they would not investigate.

The complainant alleged the former teacher made him out to be “nuts” to his family and went out of his way to discredit him.

“He told me that if I told on him, I’d be the one in trouble,” he said in the 2024 police interview.

The complainant testified in court yesterday that he had “admired and trusted” the man he alleges went on to sexually abuse him.

He said he would stay at the man’s home every other weekend when he was between 10 and 13, and claims to have woken up to the ex-teacher sexually abusing him on one occasion.

“He’s just a dirty old c*** who abused me, I hate him.”

He also alleges the man touched him inappropriately in multiple ways and photographed him in compromising positions.

“It’s haunted me to this day, even now I don’t like being photographed.

“I’ve got no photographs in my home anymore, because I don’t do photos.”

The complainant said the alleged abuse had ruined his life.

“I don’t make friends easily, I never stay anywhere too long, I don’t trust people. I don’t trust the system anymore. It let me down.”

The man is scheduled to be cross-examined by the teacher’s defence team today.

The salad bar for cows: Lincoln University researchers test a new vision for healthier farming

New Zealand Herald September 02, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

What if the future of farming starts by letting cows choose their own lunch?

At Lincoln University, southwest of Christchurch, cattle are being offered their own version of a salad bar. Instead of grazing a single pasture species, they can choose from a buffet of grasses, herbs, flowers, shrubs and trees, selecting what they want to eat from different strips of their paddocks throughout the day.

The experiment is part of a much bigger idea being developed by Professor Pablo Gregorini, who believes farms could be designed not just to produce food, but to support the health of soils, plants, animals and people at the same time.

He calls the concept a “healthscape”.

The idea builds on more than 25 years of research into animal nutrition, grazing behaviour and agricultural systems around the world.

Gregorini’s work has increasingly focused on how soil, plants, animals and people are connected, a relationship he sums up with the phrase: “you are what you eat eats”.

The theory suggests the health and diversity of landscapes influence what livestock consume and, ultimately, the quality of the food that reaches people’s plates.

“We can move from a produce system to a healthscape,” Gregorini said.

“How we work with agriculture, we can be of help to the health crisis not only in New Zealand but all over the world.”

The idea began with a simple question: if people need variety in their diets, why shouldn’t livestock?

For decades, many farm animals have been raised on relatively simple diets, often based on one or two dominant pasture species – clover, lucerne and ryegrass mainly.

Gregorini wondered what would happen if cattle were given more choice.

To explain the concept, he reaches for an analogy many people can understand.

“If I feed you sushi for lunch, good. For dinner? Yeah. Tomorrow for breakfast? Maybe,” he said.

“But if I keep going for 365 days, eventually you get tired of it, you get cranky, and then you get potentially sick because of the constant flow of the same nutrients.

“Even if I offer you the perfect diet, one that fills all the requirements that you have, if I offer you the same thing over and over, although you are getting nourished, you will get tired of it.

“So, those cows were eating the same thing every day of the year. Is that fair for them?”

At Lincoln, researchers are testing whether animals can benefit from making their own dietary decisions.

The “salad bar” includes a range of plants chosen for different nutritional and functional properties.

Some are rich in minerals. Others contain compounds associated with digestive health or natural disease prevention. Some are native plants, while others are aromatic herbs, flowering species or browse crops more commonly found outside traditional pasture systems.

Rather than being directed towards a single feed source, the animals are able to choose what they want and when they want it.

“We enable the animal to express agency and to behave as an individual,” Gregorini said.

“They can graze or browse, and they can have alternatives to choose from.”

Researchers have observed that animals do not make random choices. Their preferences shift over time, suggesting they may seek different plants to meet changing nutritional needs.

The approach sits at the centre of Gregorini’s wider healthscape model.

In his vision, farms should be viewed as interconnected living systems. Healthier soils support more diverse plant communities. Diverse plants provide livestock with greater nutritional options. Livestock, in turn, may produce food with different nutritional characteristics.

The goal is not simply to maximise production, but to create positive connections between landscapes, animals and people.

“The health of soils, plants, animals and humans are connected,” Gregorini said.

The research is still evolving, but the team says the benefits are already becoming apparent.

Studies have found animals offered diverse diets can show improvements in growth rates and production.

Previous research by Gregorini’s team found beef cattle gained about 15% more weight and milk production increased by about 10% under the “healthscape” model compared with animals on more conventional feeding systems.

The researchers have also been investigating whether those dietary differences influence the composition of meat and milk.

Gregorini is careful not to overstate the findings.

He is not claiming the products can prevent or cure disease. Instead, the research is exploring whether farming systems can be designed to produce food with characteristics that may contribute to better health outcomes.

The work could also have environmental implications.

If individual animals are healthier and more productive, farms may be able to produce the same amount of food with fewer livestock.

“The greater the number of cows, the greater the environmental impact,” Gregorini said.

“We can focus on individual production, reduce the number of cows and ameliorate some of the environmental negative impacts of livestock production.”

While the idea may sound unconventional, Gregorini says farmers are increasingly interested once they see the practical results.

“At the beginning, we had some resistance,” he said.

“But when you start saying to the farmers, what if I tell you you’re going to produce more? And, by the way, it’s healthier? They say, ‘OK, you may have a point.’”

The researchers are now exploring how healthscape principles could be adapted to different farms and regions.

Gregorini stresses there is no universal formula.

“We are not saying copy and paste,” he said.

“We are treating the farmers and the farms and the landscape as individuals with their own mind, their own needs and requirements, and we offer a myriad of opportunities.”

For him, the salad bar is only the beginning.

The larger question is whether agriculture can be redesigned around health rather than production alone.

“Which glass of milk would you give to your kids?” he said.

For Gregorini, that question lies at the heart of the healthscape concept: not simply how much food a farm produces, but what kind of landscape it comes from, and what that means for the animals, environment and people connected to it.

She writes, hosts and produces the award-winning podcast A Moment In Crime, released monthly on nzherald. co. nz.

Lifejackets will now be required to be worn on all small vessels while underway under a new maritime safety law adopted by Parliament.

National MP Dr Shane Reti’s Maritime Transport (Lifejackets on Recreational Craft) Amendment Bill passed its third reading in Parliament last night, with unanimous support across the House.

The bill makes wearing a properly fitted lifejacket mandatory for all occupants on recreational boats six metres or less in length while the vessel is underway, introducing a blanket nationwide rule to replace the current patchwork of regional council bylaws.

It will be signed into law after receiving its royal assent.

“Passing this bill has been described as the biggest drowning-prevention opportunity in a generation,” said the outgoing National MP.

“Officials estimate that an average of 10 lives per year could be saved.

“Tasmania had a 60% reduction in their first year of policy introduction and we are looking for the same benefits.”

In 2024, nearly all craft-related drowning deaths in New Zealand involved people not wearing a lifejacket – 18 out of 20, or 90%.

Many regions – including Waikato, Northland and the Bay of Plenty – have implemented their own compulsory lifejacket bylaws for those travelling on vessels up to six metres while underway, removing skipper discretion in response to the statistics.

With regional data showing all watercraft-related fatalities in Auckland between 2021 and 2025 involved people not wearing a lifejacket, Auckland Council proposed its own bylaw earlier this year in an effort to close the gap.

“Removing variability with a nationally consistent policy will benefit water users and monitoring authorities,” Reti said.

“All existing exemptions such as surfers and sports events are retained.”

Reti said Maritime NZ would work to educate Kiwis about the new rules with the Safer Boating Forum, which includes Coastguard and Water Safety NZ alongside other stakeholders.

Proponents like Duncan Garner have argued that the lack of a “tough new water safety law” is contributing to a high annual drowning toll, noting that 82% of victims are men.

In advocating for such measures, Coastguard Water Safety NZ has pointed to data showing an average of 12 lives could be saved across New Zealand waters each year if lifejacket use was compulsory, not discretionary.

“You’re three times more likely to survive [in the water] if you’re wearing a lifejacket,” Water Safety NZ chief executive Glen Scanlon told the Herald in May.

“It’s that simple.”

Global dairy prices holding steady, despite increase in seasonal supply

New Zealand Herald September 02, 2026

Demand for protein is helping keep dairy prices up. RNZ / Alexander Robertson

By RNZ Digital reporters

Demand for proteins is helping milk prices hold steady.

The average price rose almost 0.1% at the Global Dairy Trade auction this week to US$3910 ($6639). It followed a 2.3% rise at the auction two weeks ago.

In a note, New Zealand Exchange head of dairy insights Cristina Alvarado said it was a “more resilient result than the increase in seasonal supply might have suggested”.

“Milk powder demand remained firm, while milk fat declines were more contained than at the previous event,” she said.

“With deliveries moving further into the seasonal stockpiling window ahead of Christmas, Chinese New Year and the beginning of Ramadan, buying activity has held despite the normal increase in volumes offered during this period.”

She said the clearest signal from the event was continued strength in protein demand.

“Protein demand is providing price support despite higher powder availability, while fats remain under pressure and cheese faces a much heavier supply burden.

“The resilience of powders will remain important as Northern Hemisphere milk production responds to the effects of recent heatwaves and drought.”

Whole milk powder prices fell 0.1% to US$3585 ($6088). It came as Fonterra increased its offering on the previous event by almost 8%, suggesting that additional supply was absorbed “relatively comfortably rather than creating significant downward pressure”.

Skim milk powder also rose 5.3%, reaching a new 12-month high – this was despite volumes rising almost 10% from the previous auction, though they were still back on this time last year.

Meanwhile, milk fats remained softer, but declines were more moderate than expected, Alvarado said.

Butter fell 0.8% while cheddar was the “clear weak point”, falling 6.6% to US$3503 ($5949), its lowest price on the GDT platform in five years.

Cattle farmers hoof it to Auckland’s first inner-city bull auction

New Zealand Herald September 02, 2026

A troublemaker escapes the lot. Photos / RNZ - Felix Walton

By Felix Walton of RNZ

It’s a bull rush.

A cattle auction at Epsom’s inner city Cornwall Park has attracted farmers from across the upper North Island.

The farm is known for its quiet and friendly animals, who’ve adapted to the buzz of urban life.

When she heard about the herd, Dargaville farmer Cynthia hoofed it.

“This sort of event is always very popular in any district, but this is a really different sort of experience coming to the city,” she said.

“And it’s the first annual, so I’ve got my souvenir bull catalogue to put in with all the others.”

Each of the 20 specially bred Simmental bulls is worth thousands of dollars.

Even with four stomachs, such a beefy price tag is hard to digest.

“Well, actually ... We were just looking at the scones and sausage rolls, because we think the bulls are going to be out of our budget,” Cynthia admitted.

But some brave bidders were ready to take the bull by the horns.

“I’ve looked through the catalogue and spotted some favourites,” Rebecca said.

“I’ll have to see once the bidding starts, I hope I don’t get carried away, stupidly.”

Repeat customer Ray was keeping his cards close to his chest.

“I do have a budget ... But that’s my business,” he laughed.

That attention was good news for farm manager Peter Maxwell.

It was his first time hosting an auction, and with beef prices at an all time high – the steaks are even higher.

“The beef market’s really strong, so it might be a good year to have a first go at an auction like this,” he said.

“These are breeders, these will go onto some possibly purebred herds or to some crossbred herds, that’s the big thing about Simmental cattle, they cross well with a lot of other breeds.”

For auctioneer Cam Heggie, this wasn’t his first rodeo.

He had sold cattle from Cornwall Park for several years, but said it was a novelty to host an auction on the farm itself.

“I’ve been fortunate enough to deal with Cornwall Park for a number of years, but there’s a lot of people who don’t even know there’s a Simmental stud in the middle of downtown Auckland.

“So to run an auction here, it’s actually pretty cool.”

He said the bulls, raised in a fast moo-ving urban environment, were among the calmest he had met.

“Unbelievable temperament, on not only the bulls but the cattle here at Cornwall Park in general,” he said.

“I could probably say, without fear of contradiction, these would be the quietest cattle I deal with day to day. Look at them in the paddock there, they just wander up to you, just incredible.”

At a rapid-fire auction, the bulls sold for an average of $5615, the highest for a whopping $8000.

Maxwell was pleased with the results.

“We haven’t sold a bull for that sort of money before, so that’s pretty cool.”

“That was a pretty amazing sale, to be all over in 30 minutes with a high average like that. A lot of work went into that so I’m pretty pleased about it.”

Proceeds from the bull sale will be reinvested into the park and farm operations.

Aftershocks from earthquakes near Milford Sound could last for days – seismologist

New Zealand Herald September 02, 2026

Felt reports for a quake in Milford Sound on Wednesday. Photo / GeoNet

By RNZ

A seismologist says small aftershocks following Wednesday night’s earthquakes near Milford Sound could potentially last for days.

A 5.5 magnitude earthquake struck at 6.16pm, followed by a 5.6 quake at 6.57pm.

Those two were followed by weaker quakes – 4.8 at 7.12pm, 4.6 at 7.39pm and 3.8 at 8.05pm.

The first quake hit 40km northeast of Milford Sound. The first two were listed on GeoNet as moderate in intensity, while the third and fourth were light and the fifth, weak.

Sam Taylor Offord, from Earth Sciences NZ, said there were frequent aftershocks on Wednesday evening, and people could expect the smaller shocks to continue for days – he added that there was always potential for a larger earthquake and the agency was monitoring the situation.

He said Wednesday night’s earthquakes were not big enough to cause landslides going into the fiord, to cause a tsunami.

However, Offord said people should still take precautions and move away from steep or unstable slopes when the ground is shaking.

Offord said the earthquakes struck about 15 to 20km from the plate boundary.

These were not alpine fault earthquakes, although the kind of movement was similar, he said.

‘I don’t have a death wish’: Meet the Aussie chef who swapped restaurants for the wild

Sydney Morning Herald September 03, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Cooking shows are boring, and supermarket shopping is too easy. So says Mario Kalpou, a Sydney chef who ditched restaurants to hunt his own food in the wild. His debut TV series, Man Eats Wild, saw him travel from the Amazon jungle to the ice floes of Greenland.

Still firmly of the belief that food “tastes way better, and the reward is much sweeter, once you’ve almost killed yourself catching it”, he’s back with a new action-adventure foodie travelogue, Deadliest Dinners Australia. Over eight episodes, Kalpou dodges sharks and crocodiles, hunts wild buffalo, abseils down cliffs to fish off rocks lashed by waves, and maroons himself for a week on a raft on the Great Barrier Reef. And when he’s dodged death and caught his prize, he pops on a singlet and cooks it right then and there, with a fancy French sauce.

“The whole point is me showing these elements in an exciting and adrenaline-fuelled manner, because I find food shows very boring,” says Kalpou, on the phone from the Greek island of Tinos. He’s there attending a family wedding with his Australian wife, Danielle, with whom he lives in Florida.

“I’m a chef, and even I can’t watch a cooking segment on TV for 20 minutes. You lose interest! But if you’ve got some crazy guy abseiling down a 600-foot cliff to catch a fish and then he cooks for you, well, that’s a bit more interesting.”

Having grown up between his mother’s home near Sydney’s Wentworth Hotel, where she worked as a waitress, and his grandparents’ pig farm in rural western Sydney, Kalpou’s appreciation for both ends of the food industry is ingrained. He went on to open the Zagat-awarded Old Library restaurant in Cronulla, before deciding he was done with commercial kitchens.

“I don’t miss drunk patrons and staying up ’til three in the morning every night. But I have a lot of respect for hospitality. For me, now, it’s all about reconnecting people to the outdoors, getting them to eat clean food, respecting nature and getting healthy. I think that’s a really big missing part of today’s culture. I’m hoping this show can get people to start thinking more adventurously.”

After a stint in New Zealand operating an extreme adventure lodge, he left for the US nine years ago, where he now divides his time between Miami and his Montana ranch. “It’s a perfect mix for me – I’m out on the ocean, and then I’ve got the mountains.”

In the new series, Kalpou also garners knowledge from traditional owners.

“Everywhere I go in the world, I meet local indigenous people. They are the original harvesters of the land. They have knowledge that is far beyond anything that I can bring to the table … The Aboriginal community in Tiwi was no different. They taught me a lot and I had a great time with them. Understanding how they’ve been doing it for thousands of years was one of my highlights of making the show.”

He’s disappointed that some of the most dangerous aspects of the shoot weren’t caught on camera, though. Specifically, when he was charged by a wild buffalo in the outback, and the camera operator stopped filming and ran. Another time, he narrowly missed being stung by a box jellyfish.

“Thankfully, my spear caught the tip of the tentacles before my shin did,” he says. “That would’ve killed me. I had sharks attacking my raft at one point. I was caught in a storm out at sea. Once, when I went spearing for stingrays, I said, ‘Why don’t we just throw the drone up, just in case?’ And sure enough, there was a massive crocodile right where we were going to go in. So there were a few close calls.”

Unsurprisingly, the late Steve Irwin was an early influence.

“For me, it’s very important that there’s an abundance of game out there,” Kalpou explains. “We only take what we need for the plate. I had a lot of respect for that guy, and it was definitely a very, very sad moment for everyone when we lost Steve … Obviously, you have to be as careful as you can. We are dealing with a lot of uncertainty and with wild animals, nothing’s guaranteed.”

Kalpou is often stopped by celebrity fans in America, from UFC mixed martial arts fighters Luke Rockhold and Chuck Liddell to (once) Matt Damon. And that success suggests the trope of the rugged and fearless outback Aussie still holds appeal.

“It doesn’t matter where we are in the world, anyone will tell you, ‘Those Australians are crazy!’ So we’ve got to keep that reputation going,” he says. “A lot of Americans have that idea of Australia being deadly, which it is. We have some of the most dangerous animals on the planet. But among those dangerous animals also live some of the freshest ingredients in the world. Our oceans have got some of the tastiest protein, and we have an abundance of it, so I think this show is going to be really well received.”

He’s not suggesting that everyone risk their lives for their evening meal. Rather, that Deadliest Dinners Australia encourages a closer look at what’s on our plates.

“I understand that not everyone can jump on a raft and catch their own fish, or go out and hunt … And no one should be doing anything that’s not within their parameters,” he says. “I’m a professional. I’ve been doing this for 25 years, and I don’t have a death wish. If anything, I’m telling people, ‘Hey, this is a beautiful line-caught fish. If you can access it in the supermarket, this is what you should be buying.’

“We’re getting a lot of processed foods, and there’s a lot of nasty stuff coming out of the food industry on a mass scale. So watch me do the crazy stuff, but you, at home, should be able to start thinking more about where your food comes from.”

Deadliest Dinners Australia is streaming from September 9 on Binge.

Jonathan LaPaglia has one word for fans boycotting Australian Survivor: ‘Good’

Sydney Morning Herald September 03, 2026

A year on from his controversial sacking, the reality host is returning with a new show – and new appreciation for his loyal audience.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The last time I spoke with Jonathan LaPaglia, we were on set in Samoa for what neither of us knew would be his final season of Australian Survivor. It was a brief and sometimes tight-lipped interview, snuck between filming commitments on a sweaty day which followed a tricky late-night tribal council.

Had I known what was coming, I tell him at the start of this new interview two years later, this time over the phone, I would have asked different questions. “Well, had I known, I probably would have given you different answers,” he says, laughing.

LaPaglia certainly didn’t hold back this time.

A year on from his controversial sacking, the longtime host is returning to reality TV with a new show and a new appreciation for his surprisingly loyal audience.

“I really had no idea how much [fans] appreciated what I was doing,” he says, reflecting on the outrage that many Survivor fans and past players have expressed over the past 12 months at his “blindside” from the network. “I was just head down, grinding away – and I wasn’t doing it to get praise or approval … [The response] has been heartwarming and humbling. And it still continues now.”

His discontent with former employer Network 10 continues, too. When I ask for his response to the many Australian Survivor fans who say they’re boycotting the show without him as host, he had a cheeky one-word reply: “Good.”

The network, he says, “told me ratings were declining, and they were looking for a way to boost that. But that hasn’t worked out, has it? They’ve lost 40 per cent of their audience. Honestly, I can’t believe they’re going again with ratings like that. Those ratings are really catastrophic. And if it continues like this, I don’t see how they can sustain it.”

That 40 per cent drop refers to the overnight ratings for this year’s finale. It’s slightly less than that, but he’s not far off.

On free-to-air and 10Play that night, 462,000 people tuned in to see new host David Genat crown Caleb Beeby in April; that’s compared to a total of 764,000 the year before when Myles Kuah triumphed. Notably, this year’s final episode clashed with the finale of Australian Idol (which pulled 1.08 million viewers) but that doesn’t wholly explain the smaller audience.

JLP’s last season, a shorter international special called Australia v The World, pulled 653,000 viewers for its final instalment at the end of 2025 despite being up against The Block with a mammoth audience of 1.62 million.

In response, Network 10 said that much of the show’s audience comes from catch-up after those figures are collected. And if you look at the whole season, livestream numbers were up 6 per cent from the season Myles Kuah won in 2025. The latest season premiere, for instance, grew its audience 58 per cent in the seven days after it aired. But a drop of 300,000 viewers between the 2025 and 2026 finale is undeniably significant either way – especially considering the latter was triumphantly billed as a live finale and reunion.

“It makes me sad in a way because we all worked really hard on that show,” LaPaglia says. “For 10 years, we worked hard trying to build success … It’s kind of sad to see it crumble like that. It’s not what it was. And there’s a whole bunch of reasons for that.”

Speaking over the phone from his home in Los Angeles, LaPaglia seems unfazed by the prospect of appearing impolite or ungracious. He feels Network 10 and the production company Endemol Shine Australia have made “terrible decisions” for Australian Survivor – from this year’s “clunky” theme to what he perceives as heavy-handed production and, of course, the decision to let him go.

Though he admits to not watching the full 2026 season, not having access to it in the US, LaPaglia is also happy to comment on his successor’s performance: “The stuff with David felt weird, you know?”

LaPaglia theorises Genat is being “fed everything in his earpiece … it disconnects you from the players – and I think that’s what the audience is sensing”.

4:06

'I'm not looking to change Jonathan's legacy': David Genat talks Australian Survivor

The reality show's new host tackles the controversy around replacing Jonathan LaPaglia.

Wearing an earpiece to communicate with producers is standard practice in TV production, and in Australian Survivor scripts are often used as jumping off points for broader conversations – especially in unpredictable situations such as challenges or tribal councils. But LaPaglia, a trained actor, says he prided himself on memorising as much as possible before filming to make things feel organic.

“If the producer is trying to control every word that comes out of your mouth, you’re not in the moment any more,” LaPaglia says. He specifically praises Jeff Probst, the host and executive producer of Survivor in the US, who famously operates without an earpiece at all – occasionally to the show’s detriment.

A spokesperson for Endemol Shine Australia, however, defended Genat saying, “Australian Survivor is produced today exactly as it always has been, including how the host communicates with the cast. Nothing about that process has changed between hosts. Any suggestion otherwise is untrue.”

It’s tempting to read LaPaglia’s comments as sour grapes – and that might be partly true – but he’s also clearly motivated by a genuine passion for the show. Two of the three interviews LaPaglia has done in the past year have been with respected fan podcasts, diving deep into the mechanics of the game and how it could be improved. And that’s a passion the show’s former executive producer also appreciated.

Shortly after LaPaglia’s shock exit, former EP David Forster (who had left the show around the same time and was not speaking on behalf of Network 10 or Endemol Shine) told me the pair had “epic fights” and “creative differences” over the years but “Jonathan was a brilliant host. And he was super, super, super dedicated to making the show the best it could be.” Forster does not share the former host’s criticisms of the network or production company.

LaPaglia is also liberated, of course, by the fact he has a new gig to focus on.

The presenter is returning to reality TV as the narrator of Apocalypse, a new series co-commissioned by Binge and Channel 4 in the UK, which drops five Australians and nine Brits into an abandoned town for 28 days with no food, running water or power – and no rules. It’s Survivor-adjacent. But a closer comparison would be Alone. The series is actually produced by some of the team behind Alone Australia, as well as the much flashier Netflix sensation Squid Game: The Challenge.

“This show doesn’t have [Survivor’s] game element,” LaPaglia says. “It’s more an experiment about survival and society.”

It has a far spookier aesthetic, too, at least partially informed by its unique setting. The eight-part series is filmed in Muscatatuck, Indiana, a once fully functional town the size of Sydney’s CBD that was created in the 1920s for psychiatric patients but has since been abandoned. The site has been used for the past two decades to train civilian first responders and military personnel in urban warfare. As it’s depicted in the show, it could just as easily be a set for The Last of Us or The Walking Dead.

“When I first saw the trailer, it really reminded me of The Blair Witch Project,” LaPaglia says. “It forced me to ask more questions than I was getting answers, and to me, that’s good, right? That’s good TV.”

1:00

Apocalypse - official trailer

This new Binge reality series sees 14 Australians and Brits survive with no food, no power and no running water in an abandoned city.

There are a few surprises, but LaPaglia confirms there are no zombie jump scares. All the same, the show reveals reasons for contestants to be nervous around each other. Unlike Alone, these people are not survivalists. They’re everyday people with everyday jobs – from taxi drivers to cattle farmers to content creators – who occasionally have very different ideas on how to get things done.

Before the first episode is over, one contestant has already unilaterally decided to start rationing food and threatened to burn everyone’s shelter to the ground if they disagree.

“You’re not only trying to survive the environment, but you’re also trying to survive each other,” LaPaglia says. “It’s a pressure-cooker situation. I think even the players are surprised sometimes about how they behave.”

Conflict like that makes for compelling reality TV. But Apocalypse doesn’t just benefit from other people’s misfortune. As with other survival-based shows – from Alone to Man v Wild to Outlast – it enables audiences to imagine how they would fare in a similar situation.

“We all live in modern societies with all the conveniences that we take for granted – water, food, power, heat, air-conditioning, plus all the distractions that we have in phones,” LaPaglia says. “I think people fantasise about what it would be like to remove all of those things.” He’s done it himself, as a “big fan” of Alone.

“These kinds of stories allow you to safely explore your fears,” LaPaglia says, explaining the enduring appeal. “Every period in history has some kind of potential global threat, right? The Cold War or the nuclear threat or climate change or the pandemic. And now we have AI, right? Is that going to wipe out society?

“I think there’s a there’s a real fascination with that: what that means, what that looks like and who’s going to be left.”

However harsh the circumstances of the show, it was a nice change of pace for LaPaglia.

“This is a very different gig [to Survivor],” he says. “All I have to do is narrate this one! It’s so much easier. I’m not out in the field, in the dirt, in the elements for months on end. I get to go into a nice air-conditioned booth once a week and read a script. I don’t have to memorise anything. What’s not to like, right?”

He then adds, unprompted: “The producers have been great on this show. Very welcoming, very collaborative.”

But, after a decade on one of the most beloved reality series in the world, there’s still an element of fear in embarking on something new. How do you follow up that kind of success?

“There’s always that in the back of your head,” LaPaglia says. “But at some point you just gotta step off the edge and take the leap.”

He’s also been approached for a proposed new reality show on Stan*, which he can’t give more detail on and, of course, there are those tabloid headlines suggesting Nine wants him as host if they can secure the rights to Survivor. LaPaglia says he hasn’t had any conversations with Nine – or any other broadcaster – about the show.

But is there a world in which he would ever come back to Australian Survivor?

“You mean if another network picked it up?” The nervous laugh that follows sounds like a no to Network 10, then...

“If another network picked it up,” he says earnestly, “yes, I would consider it.”

Apocalypse is streaming on Binge and Foxtel on Demand from September 16.

*Stan is owned by Nine, which also owns this masthead.

O Lord, this is still the best six hours of Australian television ever made

Sydney Morning Herald September 03, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Brides of Christ is officially a middle-aged woman this month, the landmark miniseries having screened on the ABC over six scintillating and controversial weeks in 1991. Have mercy on me, O Lord, but I still think it might just be the best six hours of Australian television ever made.

When it premiered 35 years ago on September 4, it all felt rather radical: Nuns and Catholic schoolgirls trying to be the women they want to be in a changing Australia, while the church and society are trying to keep them on a leash (except for a pre-phone-chucking Russell Crowe, who needs some sexual tutelage before flying out to the jungles of Vietnam).

Brides of Christ heading into middle age, however, comes with a remarkable discovery: we can age with it.

I first watched it as rerun at about age 13, and spent the coming years terrified about sex – my BOC interpretation was that sex looks awful, being a nun would suck and why (35-year-old spoiler alert!) couldn’t Sister Paul make it with Father Jack?

In my 20s, my viewing was angry at the Catholic Church and all the ways it tethered the women trying to live within it. In my 30s, it was all about the technical brilliance of the series – the economy of the writing, beauty of the cinematography and truth in the performances.

Now in my 40s, watching Brides of Christ is a profound experience: one where I realise every single character is drawn with compassion. Where once Brenda Fricker’s Sister Agnes was a cross taskmaster, I see her as a woman whose security and self-worth comes through playing by the rules and wanting the same for those around her. Where Kym Wilson’s Rosemary was once the mean girl I feared at school, I see her vulnerability and desperation to find a place in the world where she feels like she belongs.

The miniseries was the brainchild of producer Penny Chapman, inspired by her school days in the Catholic school system at St Bede’s at Braidwood and St Scholastica’s at Glebe. It tells the stories of three generations of women being educated or existing within a fictional order of nuns.

Chapman told ABC Local Radio she pitched the show to the ABC, having experienced nuns as “very independent thinkers” during her own education and wanting to explore why “feminists like Germaine Greer and Susan Ryan credit the nuns with a great deal of their formation” despite the restrictions placed on women by the Catholic Church.

“I wanted to make a series about women and authority,” Chapman said. “A show about how a particular group of women deal with authority and the politics of that.”

The show is set firmly in the mid-to-late-1960s, but the only thing “swinging” in this world on screen are the rosaries adorning the nun’s habits. It’s a pre-Whitlam Australia: young men are still being sent to war via the birthday ballot, the White Australia Policy hadn’t been completely dismantled and the 1967 Indigenous referendum was yet to happen.

It’s also a time of great upheaval within the Catholic Church. The Second Vatican Council (or Vatican II to most) was debating ways on bringing the church into the modern world. It’s also the decade where women finally got a bit of control over their reproductive rights, with the birth control pill introducing more sexual freedom, even though the Catholic Church would officially reject it in 1968, reaffirming its use as a mortal sin.

This is the societal backdrop in which Brides of Christ asks us to follow the stories of Diane (the university graduate who ends her engagement for the convent), Frances (a young Naomi Watts dealing with the shame and confusion of divorced parents), Ambrose (the mother superior who begins to question everything), Rosemary (the rebel with the raging hormones), Paul (the all-heart innocent nun who falls in love with a man) and Catherine (the former Diane, now finding her place in a church denying birth control untenable) – and the many nuns, students and women (and occasionally men) in the Church community.

These stories were expertly woven by writers John Alsop and Sue Smith, who crafted each hour’s episode to include the personal emotional journey of the character whose name is on the episode and the wider community implications of the issue within.

The writing is so good and the performances so truthful, it’s only on reflection you realise the personal is always political. It’s a truly great drama: tickling your funny bones one moment with cheeky nuns making jokes about each other, leaving you in floods of tears moments later when a middle-aged nun has a breakdown over the new post-Vatican II uniform requirements.

While it made young actors Josephine Byrnes and Lisa Hensley into household names, Brides of Christ is a rollcall of incredible Australian talent, and talent that would go on to huge international success – Watts and Crowe have featured roles showcasing some thoroughly relatable teen angst. If you look carefully, you’ll find a young Alex Lloyd leading the rock band at the school dance!

The miniseries was made for just over $6 million, which, converted to today’s money is about $14 million – a similar budget to what a six-part limited series could be made for today. A co-production with the UK’s Channel 4 and RTE Ireland, it quickly became the ABC’s most viewed drama ever, and went on to reruns on the ABC frequently.

In 1992, it swept the Logies, winning the “most popular” and “outstanding” awards for a miniseries, which means it was really popular, and also really good. By the time it won its fifth award that night, the whole of Australia could hum its evocative and enticing theme tune written by Mario Millo.

Seemingly, Brides of Christ could seem like an extremely niche subject matter – Catholic women in the 1960s, and their lives within the confines of the school and convent. Somehow, it’s this that gives the show its wide appeal: by focusing on the minutiae of these women’s lives, we see that humanity, and that humanity shows us that ultimately we’re all striving for the same things: security, community and a little bit of happiness and joy.

Brides of Christ’s huge mainstream success and wide appeal says something about the audience that is still relevant today: women want to see their stories told truthfully on screen. Women are half the population, and when the series was being made, women were being massively under serviced. Nine out of the top 10 films of 1991 were men’s stories (the one that wasn’t was a Disney cartoon about a young bookish woman being held hostage by a beast).

This is a high-end drama series unapologetically centring women’s stories. These women exist in relation to each other, not as an afterthought around a man or men. Their stories are taken seriously. In Brides of Christ, women are more than appendages – they’re intelligent, big-hearted and have aspirations that come up against the church status quo. At the same time, for some of the characters, the church is a safe space of tradition and security. The complexities of the church mirror the complexities of living within the patriarchy.

It’s also the Catholic Church of women: priests are little more than featured extras, the institutional sexual abuse we’ve come to know of since isn’t delved into. There’s a sexual safety to the nuns of this order, even if there isn’t always an emotional safety to their actions.

And that’s the thing with Brides of Christ, and why it has, for 35 years resonated so strongly with the women of Australia: every one of us wants to live a life of her own choosing, and feel secure in the community in which she lives – regardless of the limitations our gender may place on us.

Brides of Christ is six hours of vastly differing women in age, class and intellect, all striving to do just that.

The 30 best movies to stream on SBS On Demand right now

Sydney Morning Herald September 03, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great movies that span genres, filmmakers and languages. This week: SBS on Demand. For 150 other movie choices, check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and Disney+.

What we remember and what we will never know underpins this intimately audacious debut drama from Scottish filmmaker Charlotte Wells, with a young British father (Paul Mescal) taking his 11-year-old daughter (Frankie Corio) on a holiday to Turkey.

A romantic fantasy intended as a balm for World War II’s losses, this wonderfully constructed tale follows a British airman (David Niven) who dodges the hereafter. His second-chance appreciation of life becomes joyful.

A legal thriller – in a rarely experienced Swiss setting – rendered as an investigation of how malleable truth and family have to be, this riveting drama delivers a powerhouse performance from a pre-Project Hail Mary Sandra Hüller.

With an all-time performance from Jeff Bridges as Los Angeles slacker “The Dude”, this noir-ringed black comedy from the Coen brothers remains a winningly idiosyncratic affair, complete with a scene-stealing John Turturro.

David Lean’s first epic is a sober examination of duty and heroism during World War II, as imprisoned American and British officers (William Holden and Sir Alec Guinness) clash over a bridge they built for their brutal Japanese captors.

Thai director Apichatpong Weerasethakul is a revered figure in world cinema and this is a signature work – a gracefully fluid exploration of national trauma and private memory that turns a military hospital into a spiritual way-station.

All too relevant, Bernardo Bertolucci’s drama of warped political belonging follows a 1930s Italian civil servant (Jean-Louis Trintignant) who takes part in a fascist murder plot against his former professor. A film of cruel beauty and erotic malaise.

The great Sam Neill was at ease in any genre, and this mordant Australian farce, where he plays a Melbourne chef in over his head with his girlfriend and associated gangsters, is a showcase of his comedic skills.

When an exiled photographer (Rachel Weisz) returns to her insular Orthodox Jewish community and the best friend (Rachel McAdams) she left behind, the roiling emotions between them become overwhelming. The leads are sublime together.

Anchored by a graceful Forest Whitaker as the titular hitman, Jim Jarmusch’s take on the wronged gangster flick intertwines hip-hop beats and Japanese philosophy. Sometimes violent, often wry, always unique.

With David Fincher directing, this portrait of marital discord has a forensic fierceness as a cheating husband (Ben Affleck) becomes embroiled in suspicion when his wife (Rosamund Pike) disappears. The storytelling delivers brutal implications.

An enduring masterpiece of French cinema, Jean Renoir’s humanist classic explores the bond during World War I between two captured French aviators and their German overseer. Individual connection can’t trump duty’s tragic demands.

The South Korean master Park Chan-wook delivers a stinging mix of erotic thriller and period crime drama in this twisty, immaculately staged tale of obsessive 1930s love between a trapped heiress and her knowing servant.

Taylor Sheridan’s best writing, this modern-day western from director David Mackenzie is a withering attack on inequality couched as a thriller pitting bank-robbing siblings (Chris Pine and Ben Foster) against a wily lawman (Jeff Bridges).

An irresistible mix of cartoonish mayhem and Chinese martial arts cinema, Stephen Chow’s action comedy unfolds in an under-attack Shanghai tenement where the impoverished residents harbour unexpected skills. An innovative, invigorating pleasure.

In this magisterial German drama, you can see a conscience defiantly return to the Stasi officer (Ulrich Mühe) who is bugging a playwright and his actress girlfriend in a communist East Germany defined by oppression.

The enduring peak of Spike Lee and Denzel Washington’s many collaborations is a fiercely contested portrait of the revolutionary African-American activist that eschews biopic cliches. A vast, compelling story, shot with eloquent precision.

One of Clint Eastwood’s finest works behind the camera, this mournful Boston thriller intertwines a trio of men – played by Sean Penn, Tim Robbins, and Kevin Bacon – who cannot escape their shared childhood damage.

With Cary Grant and Ingrid Bergman as lovers and spies torn apart by her mission to infiltrate Nazi exiles, this tense thriller is an expert distillation of Alfred Hitchcock’s technical prowess and emotional cynicism.

Bong Joon Ho’s charred black comic thriller took its deceptive critique of wealth’s unavoidable distortion all the way to Academy Awards dominance, deploying architecture and amorality to chart a family of grifters fastening on to their rich hosts.

The everyday attains the profound in this late-career classic from Wim Wenders, which tracks the solitary days of a Tokyo sanitation worker, Hirayama (Kōji Yakusho), who experiences his work and life with graceful acceptance.

Images, hearts, and entire futures are grasped and set free in this quietly staggering French romance where a 19th century portrait painter (Noémie Merlant) connects with her watchful subject (Adèle Haenel).

“Kill for us or we’ll kill you,” the vulnerable 19-year-old Malik (Tahar Rahim) is told by Corsican gangsters on his first day in a French jail, and from there, filmmaker Jacques Audiard turns survival into a detailed crime epic.

Quite simply one of the greatest Australian movies ever made. Warwick Thornton’s debut feature depicts with wrenching realism and intimate detail the union between two Indigenous teens who flee a remote community for Alice Springs.

The most influential action film ever made, Akira Kurosawa’s 16th-century saga follows a group of warriors hired to protect a farming village from bandits. If you like actors with presence, prepare yourself for the legendary Toshiro Mifune.

Bleakly illuminating, this Polish drama from the gone-too-soon Krzysztof Kieślowski contrasts the taking of a life by an individual and the state. The film doesn’t offer consolation – it’s the right decision.

Paul Thomas Anderson captures America’s industrial transformation with the tale of a driven oilman (an unparalleled Daniel Day-Lewis). Frame after frame evokes a furious wonder that can’t be stilled by success or family.

Written with an ear for moral failings by Graham Greene, Carol Reed’s thriller unfolds in the ruins of post-World War II Vienna, where a dogged author (Joseph Cotten) searches for a missing friend (Orson Welles) with a troubling reputation.

Yasujiro Ozu’s timeless Japanese classic is closely observed and wrenchingly restrained. When an ageing couple visit their children in the city, they’re mostly treated as a burden. But instead of recrimination there’s acceptance: this is life’s price.

As an alien in human form prowling Scotland to harvest male admirers, Scarlett Johansson underpins an otherworldly character study. Shot like a documentary in the key of inexplicable, this is a deeply unsettling experience.

All information correct at August 2026. *Stan is owned by Nine, the owner of this masthead.

I inadvertently misled parliament over a British nuclear scandal. Now I’m calling for justice

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 21:30:35 GMT

Thousands of service personnel took part in dangerous cold war-era nuclear tests. The government owes them the truth – and compensation

In December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament. Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was “unable to locate any information” suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.

I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them. This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.

More than 20,000 armed forces personnel took part in dozens of nuclear tests and nearly 600 radiation experiments, the majority between 1952 and 1967. This was for the entirety of the cold war. The science was deemed necessary. How effective were our own bombs and, just as importantly, how well could our military function if the Soviet Union used theirs against us? Test after test was conducted in the Australian desert, at Christmas Island in the Pacific, and we also sent service personnel into the atomic clouds of allies and enemies. Yet their medical records for the period are missing.

Other nuclear nations, such as the US, France and the Soviet Union, did the same. Yet they acknowledged that it happened and created dedicated compensation schemes for nuclear test veterans who subsequently developed serious illnesses. Britain stands apart here. In Britain, the burden was placed on veterans to prove their case. But how do you claim what happened decades earlier when potentially vital records are missing or inaccessible?

In 2007, about 1,000 nuclear test veterans and families took the MoD to court seeking compensation. Pilots had been instructed to fly through mushroom clouds. Service personnel sailed and crawled through fallout. Others witnessed nuclear explosions, in some cases just two miles from ground zero. Surely our service personnel deserved better?

This is where the scandal turns ugly. To deal with the veterans’ litigation, the MoD instructed the Atomic Weapons Establishment (AWE) to collate relevant documentation into a searchable database called Merlin. More than 28,000 documents were eventually assembled, covering radiation, precautions, health monitoring and what was known about the possible biological effects of the tests. Yet the veterans’ lawyers had no practical access to this vast archive. Thanks to the extraordinary investigative journalism of Susie Boniface, historical documents began emerging referring to blood and urine testing.

When I saw the evidence, I raised it in November 2022 as chair of the defence committee. The MoD finally acknowledged that the AWE held copies of blood-test results and urine-radioactivity measurements for “a small number of individuals”. That took me straight back to my parliamentary answer four years earlier.

I challenged the then defence secretary, Ben Wallace. If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture? He agreed that withholding relevant medical information would be “deeply wrong” and undertook to investigate.

The dam was beginning to burst. Searches of Merlin for “blood” and “urine” subsequently identified 151 documents. Then another extraordinary twist. A software change meant the AWE could no longer provide a historical audit trail showing who had accessed Merlin.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

In 2024 (after the general election), the government finally ordered a discovery exercise into what blood and urine testing had taken place. Its findings, published this July, are damning. Evidence indicates that medical examinations or blood testing were required for “the majority, if not all” of Britain’s nuclear-testing period, across all three armed services. Bizarrely, the review says it found no evidence of intentional concealment.

But after seven decades of incomplete answers and ministers kept in the dark, this cannot be where the story ends. Had veterans and their doctors known the full picture decades ago, cancers and other illnesses could have been diagnosed earlier. Lives could have been saved.

Merlin is now being transferred to the National Archives. But declassifying 28,000 documents into the public domain will take time and is not the same as giving veterans answers. Many are now in their 80s and 90s.

Given the numbers of veterans involved and the decades this has been allowed to drag on, this is arguably one of Britain’s biggest scandals – alongside infected blood, Windrush and the Post Office. It demands an apology to the nation from the prime minister, an independent tribunal to establish the truth, and a compensation scheme for veterans and widows similar to that provided in the US.

These men served their country. Their country failed them. Seventy years on, veterans should not still be fighting their own government for the truth.

Tobias Ellwood is a former defence minister and the author of Ten Steps to Prevent World War Three

Nuclear bomb test veterans were victims of one of ‘greatest scandals in Britain’, says ex-defence minister

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 21:30:35 GMT

Exclusive: Tobias Ellwood says he gave MPs inaccurate information in 2018 provided by his department, the MoD

I inadvertently misled parliament over a British nuclear scandal. Now I’m demanding justice

A former defence minister has admitted misleading parliament over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans.

Tobias Ellwood has said he unwittingly gave MPs incorrect information in 2018 when he told them he had been unable to locate information on veterans’ blood tests after being given incorrect information by officials at the Ministry of Defence (MoD).

Veterans have been fighting for years to see the records as many look to prove that years of serious illnesses such as cancer were linked to their experiences testing nuclear weapons. Ellwood’s admission will increase pressure on the MoD to explain whether its officials have helped prevent those veterans get justice.

In a piece for the Guardian, Ellwood says: “In December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament.

“Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was ‘unable to locate any information’ suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.

“I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them.”

He added: “This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.”

An MoD spokesperson said: “This government commissioned and completed an extensive records discovery exercise, examining tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme.

“The findings have now been published in full, following regular engagement between ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process.”

Between 1952 and 1967, about 22,000 British military personnel took part in 45 large-scale nuclear weapons tests in Australia and the South Pacific. Some pilots flew through mushroom clouds, some troops crawled through fallout and many witnessed the first test wearing little more than short-sleeved shirts and shorts.

Large numbers later suffered blood disorders and cancers, which they believed were caused by exposure to radioactive fallout. Most were denied pensions because of their ill health.

Unlike other nuclear-armed countries such as France, the US and the Soviet Union, the UK has never compensated those involved in testing atomic bombs.

The case has been compared with the infected blood scandal, which saw more than 30,000 people contract HIV and Hepatitis C in the the 1970s and early 1990s after being given contaminated blood and blood products.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has previously said he was misled by officials when he claimed as health secretary in 2009 that there was no evidence that people were knowingly given contaminated blood. His claims echo those being made today by Ellwood.

Burnham has also been a vocal supporter of the nuclear test veterans in recent years.

As Greater Manchester mayor in 2022, Burnham said: “If the state was conducting medical tests upon servicemen and not informing them when they found serious irregularity, that is at least misconduct in public office, and more serious, perhaps gross negligence manslaughter, in respect of people who died as a result.

“Crimes have been committed.”

The prime minister is now coming under pressure to begin an inquiry and allocate government money for compensation to the victims.

One of the major problems with securing compensation so far has been the lack of medical evidence linking veterans’ health problems to their experiences helping with nuclear tests.

The government long maintained that it did not hold any such medical records – a claim that was proved incorrect in 2022 when the journalist Susie Boniface revealed the existence of a database of 28,000 documents known as Merlin.

That database had been put together in response to a 2007 lawsuit by 1,000 British test veterans and their families, but the information was classified.

Ellwood says he did not find out about the existence of this database until 2022, when details began to emerge in the press.

He writes in his piece: “If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture?”
