Stolen Babies review – the scale of this cruelty is almost impossible to fathom

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 21:30:35 GMT

For decades, thousands of unmarried mothers in the UK were forced to give up their newborns after being denied pain relief in labour so they would ‘not be a bad girl again’. This harrowing documentary hears their stories

The scale of the suffering at first threatens to make you numb to it. The 90-minute documentary Stolen Babies is as unsparing as it is unsentimental and opens with a bald statement of verified fact: “Between 1949 and 1976 over 250,000 unmarried mothers in the UK were forced into handing their newborn babies over for adoption.” State apparatus facilitated this every step of the way, supported by religious institutions. These institutions ran, or were involved with running, the mother and baby homes to which the girls and young women were banished (“They do not quickly acknowledge themselves as sinners,” notes one report on its inmates), along with self-proclaimed moral welfare societies and the NHS.

The statistics are appalling. The details are worse. Some of the women whose stories are told in the film became pregnant by boyfriends. Some were victims of rape. Joan Chambers was 14 when a teacher took her for a walk in the woods. “I trusted him, I really did … All I remember was the pain. I honestly didn’t know what was happening.”

Ann Keen was 17 when she went on a date with a salesman from the factory she was working at. “In today’s term,” she says hesitantly, “it was without consent. You couldn’t say that in the 60s.” Doctors and nurses refused to speak to Keen while she was in labour, and they denied her pain relief – including when she was stitched up after the birth – so that she would “remember it and not be a bad girl again”. Her baby was taken away eight days later. “And you’ll never see him again,” a midwife gleefully told her, before putting the teenager in a bath and starting to squeeze her breasts: “I’m getting rid of the milk. You won’t be needing this.”

Chambers gave evidence at her teacher’s trial when she was nearly eight months pregnant. “Children are so apt to make up taradiddles and wicked invention,” the judge advised the jury. “You will not allow sympathy for the girl to cloud your judgment.” The teacher was found not guilty. During the birth she was “absolutely torn to shreds”. Her baby was taken from her three weeks later and she was told to go and strip the bedding from his cot, ready for the next one.

The dehumanisation, the cruelty is unfathomable and the film leaves the viewer to sit and wrestle with the accruing conundrums. To say that it is the result of different attitudes is only to push the bafflement back a stage: how could they, we, anyone privilege the importance of marriage over the right of a mother to keep her child; how could class – and it was overwhelmingly young working-class women’s babies being given to middle-class couples – be such a blinding factor; how could religious belief have such a chokehold on a society that rage-fuelled punishment could be visited on women with barely a murmur of reproach; how could babies be treated like commodities?

But so it was, and social historian Dr Michael Lambert has the evidence, which would be used alongside the women’s testimonies when the Sunday Post journalist Marion Scott broke the story of the scandal after a long investigation. Painstakingly gathered from thousands of council and state records of the adoptions, of reports from mother and baby homes up and down the land, it is, he says, “evidence of a system designed to supply infants”. It’s also tangible proof of what the women’s stories have told us: that at every level, written through the national psyche like poisonous letters through a stick of rock, was the idea that women are lesser beings and that “fallen” women are the very least of them all.

Marion McMillan, whose mixed race son stayed with her for nine months because most families wanted white babies (“No freckles” was one couple’s further stipulation), has spent 20 years supporting mothers like her and campaigning for government apologies. Nicola Sturgeon supplied one from McMillan’s native Scotland in 2023, and Keir Starmer followed suit this year. The women speak of it as a release from the shame that has pursued them down the decades. Again, the suffering visited upon them all seems incalculable.

Adoption law changed after 1976 and put an end – or the beginning of an end – to the grey and hidden market in babies from young, unmarried, poorer women to affluent older couples. Contraception cutting off the supply seems to have been a more immediate factor than changing attitudes, but minds always take longer than bodies to respond to change. Whether you feel the writing through the rock reads truly differently today – looking at rape statistics; state neglect and underfunding of women’s services; authorities’ complicity in ignoring gangs of groomers and predators in recent decades – is up to you.

Stolen Babies aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer now

Trump administration sides with OpenAI in lawsuit against New York Times

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 20:39:54 GMT

The Times and many companies are accusing OpenAI of misusing their material to train AI systems without compensation

The Trump administration is supporting OpenAI in ⁠a lawsuit against the New York Times, arguing in favor of the use of copyrighted writing to train artificial intelligence.

The Times accuses OpenAI and its largest financial backer, Microsoft, of using millions of newspaper articles without permission to train OpenAI’s popular chatbot. Other newspapers have joined in the suit, first filed in 2023.

In a brief filed in Manhattan federal court on Tuesday, the US government weighed in for the first time on lawsuits over the tense battle over AI and copyright. A brief has advisory rather than legal weight but could bolster tech ⁠companies as they fight the claims.

“The United States has a strong interest in continuing to develop a robust and competitive artificial intelligence industry that sets the standard for the practice and procedure of AI use globally … As such, it is critical for the United States to ‘retain global leadership in artificial intelligence’,” the brief said.

Copyright owners, including authors, publishers, music labels and news outlets, have filed dozens of lawsuits over AI training against tech companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms. They say the companies ⁠misuse their material to train AI systems and do so without compensation.

For AI chatbots to generate responses, machine learning systems are first fed billions of lines of text. The bots produce their output by statistical analysis of what the next word should be by matching a user’s query to parts of the database.

Spokespeople for the Times and OpenAI did not immediately respond ‌to requests for comment on the filing on Wednesday.

“AI dominance is critical to promote national security, prosperity, and economic mobility for all Americans,” US associate attorney general Stanley Woodward Jr said in a statement posted to X. “This Administration will never let our Nation be at a disadvantage relative to our foreign adversaries based on a plainly incorrect understanding of copyright law.”

The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, separately told G20 officials ‌at a meeting in North Carolina on Wednesday that their countries should embrace fair use and allow AI companies to train their models on creators’ work while finding ​a way to “protect artists”.

All of the pending cases will probably ​revolve around whether AI systems make ​fair use of copyrighted material by ​using it to create new, transformative content. The first two judges to consider the ​question issued diverging rulings ‌last year.

JD Vance has said he is “doing as much of God’s work as possible” and that he is OK “if that leads to the end times”, which he says “are coming”.

The US vice-president made the comments during a Monday podcast interview with Bryce Crawford, a 22-year-old evangelical host with over a million YouTube followers and videos featuring sensationalist headlines including “Preaching the gospel in Chicago’s deadliest neighborhood” and “Debating a ‘gay’ pastor”.

Speaking about the Christian prophetic notion that the world as humanity knows it will end one day, Vance said: “Do I think we are in the end times? I don’t know.

“While I’m fascinated by it, I think that focusing on it too much can be very bad,” he said, adding that if his work “leads to the end times, OK, and if that leads to … us building a better world that thrives and survives for a very long time after I’m gone, that’s great, too”.

Vance, who published a spiritual memoir earlier this summer about his conversion to Catholicism, said: “I think you got to just kinda try and have an attitude of: the end times may be coming, in fact they are coming, it’s just a question of whether they’re coming thousands of years down the road, or a few months down the road.”

He said: “I think there are things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the antichrist was walking among us.”

Vance pointed to artificial intelligence, using the example of an acquaintance who uses AI as a marriage counselor, which he described as “kind of satanic”. He said: “When you completely divorce the human from the social element that God made us for … that’s very bad.”

In response to a question about whether he had ever been in a room that was “spiritually dark”, Vance said he had “been in meetings with world leaders where various issues are being discussed, and somebody will say something or somebody will make an observation, and I’ll feel some darkness about it”.

“It sets off every spiritual alarm bell in my body,” he added.

Vance also defended Donald Trump’s controversial depiction of himself as Jesus in an AI-generated photo, subsequently deleted, that the president posted earlier this year, which Crawford said “made me upset”.

“The president didn’t mean any offense. Obviously, he loves Christians … Did Donald Trump mean to post a meme of himself as God? No. The president has a good sense of humor. He did not mean to mock or mimic God. That’s just not who he is,” Vance said, adding that Trump is “a backslapper” and “a bit of a ball buster”.

Following outrage from Christian supporters, Trump deleted the photo and insisted that the photo was “supposed to be me as a doctor making people feel better”.

Chelsea ensured there will be three Women’s Super League teams in the league phase of the Champions League as Keira Walsh’s second-half strike against Real Sociedad extended their three-goal margin from the first leg of the third-round qualifier.

The 5-2 win against the Spanish side in Chelsea’s first game at Wimbledon’s Cherry Red Records stadium gave Sonia Bompastor’s side a commanding lead in the tie, after a rusty start had forced them to come from a goal down. It wasn’t a particularly pretty performance, though, and that continued into the second leg against La Real, who will now drop into the Europa League.

Bompastor, who returned to the dugout after serving a one-match ban in the reverse game, made four changes for the trip to San Sebastián, probably with one eye on the WSL opener on Saturday against Aston Villa. The scorer of Chelsea’s second last week, Veerle Buurman, was named on the bench, alongside Katie McCabe, Sjoeke Nüsken and Alyssa Thompson. Among those to come in was the 20-year-old midfielder Lexi Potter, who scored in her first league start for Chelsea, a 2-1 win against Brighton, in March.

There were only two changes for the home team. The change that mattered most, though, was the one that had taken place in the ­dugout. In between these two critical ­Champions League qualifying games, Arturo Ruiz, the Real Sociedad ­manager, exited and was unveiled as the new Brighton manager following the shock departure of Dario Vidosic. If Vidosic’s exit had been a surprise, Brighton poaching Ruiz was a bigger one. Gorka Álvarez, who left Real Sociedad in 2025 following three seasons managing the reserves and a year as an assistant to SD Eibar’s women’s team, was hurriedly brought in to lead them in their Liga F opener against Logroño on Saturday, a 2-0 loss, and the second leg against Chelsea.

It was a mountain of a task ­facing the 40-year-old and, in many respects, a bit of a free hit, with few expecting Real Sociedad to come close to overturning a three-goal ­deficit against European heavyweights.

However, setting the tone for his tenure and building confidence was important. La Real did well against the visitors, holding Bompastor’s side at bay until Walsh swept in from a corner in the 54th minute to kill any outlandish hopes there may have been of a comeback.

Until then, the London side ­struggled to create clear chances with La Real mirroring their well-organised display in the first half of the first leg.

Ellie Carpenter, playing further forward, ahead of Lucy Bronze on the right, was Chelsea’s best outlet but they couldn’t capitalise on her balls into the middle. Walsh’s side-footed effort in the first half was weak and easy for the goalkeeper Julia Arrula. Aggie Beever-Jones had a good chance to break the deadlock moments before Walsh’s goal but the forward’s strike was too central and Arrula made an easy save.

Maltese tycoon found not guilty of involvement in Daphne Caruana Galizia murder

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 19:26:32 GMT

Yorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrage

One of Malta’s richest men has been found not guilty of involvement in the murder of the anti-corruption journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

The verdict, which is expected to be appealed against by the prosecution, will come as a blow not only to the victim’s family, but to the politicians and campaigners who regard the case as a landmark action in the fight to protect press freedom in Europe.

Nearly nine years after Caruana Galizia’s death in a car bombing in October 2017, a jury of six women and three men found Yorgen Fenech, 44, not guilty of both counts with which he had been charged: complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, and association with the intention of committing a crime.

Delivered at 7.30pm, the verdict was decisive. To gasps from the gallery and cheers from Fenech’s relatives, the forewoman announced jurors had voted to dismiss both counts by an eight-to-one majority.

As Caruana Galizia’s family listened in shock, with some relatives in tears, the judge, Edwina Grima, immediately ordered Fenech’s release from custody. If convicted, he would have faced a life sentence. He left court through the front entrance, without responding to requests for comment.

“Everybody is much more at risk now, because this signals you can kill journalists with impunity,” Caruana Galizia’s sister, Corinne Vella, said. “We knew an acquittal was a huge possibility. But it’s like when someone dies, it still shocks you.”

In a message on Facebook, the journalist’s eldest son decried a “terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from. They had a great responsibility to deliver justice. And washed their hands of it”.

The leader of the opposition Nationalist party, Alex Borg, requested the urgent reopening of parliament, which is currently in recess, to discuss the verdict. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” said Borg, speaking to a crowd of demonstrators that had assembled on Wednesday night outside parliament. He described the verdict as a black spot on the Labour government, and said the press should be free to do its work “independently and without undue pressure”.

Fenech, an influential businessman and property developer whose family owns two Hilton hotels and has a share in a power station in Malta, had been accused by prosecutors of paying €150,000 (£129,000) via a middleman, Melvin Theuma, to have the journalist killed.

The murder of Caruana Galizia, who targeted Fenech and leading political figures in her reporting, triggered the most consequential political scandal in Malta’s postwar history, becoming a rallying point for anti-corruption and press freedom activism.

The fallout resulted in Joseph Muscat, the then prime minister of the EU’s smallest member state, being forced out of office along with two of his ministers and his chief of staff.

While Muscat left office, the party he led remains in power. In a statement, the government noted the verdict and appealed for prudence in public comments at a delicate moment, insisting: “The government remains committed to seeing justice served by its institutions.”

The two-month trial laid bare the extent of Fenech’s network of political contacts, and raised questions about attempts to sabotage and interfere with the police investigation. Key witnesses, and the defendant himself, claimed the prime minister’s chief of staff had repeatedly leaked sensitive information to Fenech.

Summing up the case against him, prosecutor Anthony Vella said Fenech believed he could “buy justice”, telling the jury: “You are being asked to decide whether a man who had extensive contacts in politics and among the heads of public entities had enough power to pay for Daphne to be killed.”

The defence argued that the chain of command went higher, with suggestions from Fenech and his lawyers that the person who had ordered the killing was Muscat’s former chief of staff Keith Schembri. They said police had not done enough to investigate allegations about his involvement.

“All roads lead to Keith, and all bridges to Keith were burned,” the defence lawyer Charles Mercieca said in his summing up.

In his testimony, Fenech told the jury: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.” He said he had merely acted as a messenger between Schembri and Theuma, and that the taxi-driver had blackmailed him.

Schembri, who gave evidence at the trial, denied all wrongdoing, saying he had no involvement in leaks and no knowledge of the murder.

Fenech’s defence lawyer, Giannella de Marco, said Schembri and others should have been investigated. She said the prosecution’s chief witness had not been believed.

“The jurors did not believe Melvin Theuma. It was an eight-one verdict, which means unanimous … don’t you think jurors saw who the real masterminds were?” she said.

The vote was effectively unanimous because juries in Malta rarely convict 9-0, as this would allow the public to know for certain which way individual members voted.

Repubblika, a Maltese campaign group, called for a “national reckoning” in which the corruption investigated by Caruana Galizia, who was 59 when she died and one of Malta’s best-known journalists, is prosecuted.

“Those politically responsible for the culture of impunity of the Muscat years must not be rehabilitated into public life. The state must sincerely accept its responsibility and apologise to Daphne’s family,” a spokesperson said.

Occupy Justice, meanwhile, described the verdict as “deeply painful and disappointing”, saying Malta remained “without full accountability for the person or people who ordered her murder”.

An independent public inquiry, for which the family fought, concluded in 2021 that the state had to shoulder responsibility for the killing because it “created an atmosphere of impunity, generated from the highest levels”. It made a number of recommendations, many of which have yet to be implemented.

In a statement, the Daphne Foundation said: “Nine years after Daphne’s brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed. Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne’s life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost.”

Tom Gibson, the deputy advocacy director of the Committee to Protect Journalists, was in the courtroom for the verdict. In a statement, he said: “This is a heartbreaking verdict for the family after years of waiting for justice. We will continue to stand by them while they seek accountability for all of those involved in the murder.”

Experts are examining a gun found by tourists to determine whether it might have been used to kill a British family in the French Alps 14 years ago.

In what remains an unsolved murder case, Saad al-Hilli, 50, his wife, Ikbal, 47, and her mother, Suhaila al-Allaf, 74, were shot dead on a road near Annecy, a remote Alpine village in eastern France in September 2012.

The couple’s two young daughters, then four and seven, survived but a passing cyclist, 45-year-old Sylvain Mollier, was also killed.

The French prosecutor Marie-Céline Lawrysz confirmed that a pistol, thought to be a Luger, was uncovered on 20 August by two tourists swimming in Lake Annecy. The weapon is currently being analysed by ballistics experts in France in connection with the al-Hilli cold case.

During the initial investigation, pieces from the butt of the weapon used in the killings, a vintage Luger P06-29 pistol, were found on the ground near the British-registered BMW estate car that the family had been driving at the time of the attack. The gun was identified as a model used by the Swiss army in the 1930s, but its owner has never been traced.

In a statement, Lawrysz said a semi-automatic pistol had been found by the tourists, reported to be British, at a depth of about five feet, a few dozen metres away from the shore of Lake Annecy.

She said: “They kept the weapon for 24 hours and conducted online research to identify its type.

“They subsequently drew a link between the discovered weapon and the one believed to have been used in the Chevaline [near Annecy] killing on September 5, 2012.

“On August 21 2026, they handed the weapon over to gendarmes from the local Saint-Jorioz brigade.”

Detectives have so far ruled out the possibility of a contract killing, saying a professional killer would not have used such a vintage weapon as the Luger.

The discovery of the pistol is the latest in a long line of leads that investigators have followed in an effort to unravel the mystery that has surrounded the four deaths.

Suspects previously arrested in connection with the case include an Iraqi prisoner known as Mr S who was claimed to have said he had been offered “a large sum of money” to kill Iraqis living in the UK.

Mr al-Hilli’s brother Zaid was also arrested on suspicion of murder in 2013, but was later told he would face no further action after police found there was insufficient evidence to charge him with a crime.

In 2022, another suspect was questioned but released without charge. Two years ago, DNA analysis was ordered by detectives in France’s cold case unit on clothes belonging to the victims, as well as on the pieces of the gun and cigarette butts found at the scene. No arrests were made following the tests.

Premier League money has lost all meaning amid chaotic spectacle of excess

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 19:00:32 GMT

The transfer window has broken all rational rules and limits, leaving us to marvel and, ultimately, pick up the bill

There was a research study a few years back into a key period in the life of the TV show Location, Location, Location. You know the one. Half an hour of mid-morning drift. Hosted by two people whose common quality is they both look as if the minced essence of Wellington boots, the Volvo XC40 and the phrase “picky bits” has been reconstituted into human shapes, then sent out to judge people for buying houses.

The big reveal was always the bit where they came back a year later and saw how much the value had shifted. Because all conversations about houses are, in the end, an excuse to talk about money. Oh wow, it’s gone up by £20,000. You are good. Oh no, you’re now bankrupt and your flat looks like a hostage cell with fairy lights. Unlucky. You are bad.

What the study found was that prices basically always increased. Ripping out the stairs, living in a tent in the garden, arguing about what to do with the two-and-a-halfth bedroom – all of this was irrelevant. These were the boom times of the early 2000s, UK housing recast as a global money trap, an endlessly whirling laundromat, a bricks and mortar central bank bond.

These people could have bought their run-down three-bed, left it empty and done absolutely nothing for two years. The price would have still gone up. That drama about exactly which shade of Anaconda Breath Morgue And Cakebread Mega-Gloss to use in the underfloor wine cave? Just doesn’t matter. Buy the soil. Shut the door. Let money do its thing.

And yes, this is a way of talking about the 2026 summer transfer window, and the way in which everyone has basically now been Chelsea-ed. Think back four years to the start of the age of Clearlake, the first post-Roman spree. At that time it seemed impossible there could be a profitable outcome. Chelsea were out there buying the vintage copper-plate statement bidet. Chelsea were digging out a third sub-basement. Who will redeem this expense? Who will provide a similarly deranged response to such overinvestment?

Well, it turns out the market will do this for you. If you’d predicted then that Chelsea would miss out on the Champions League and go through five permanent managers, but still make a profit from selling Enzo Fernández, would anyone have believed it?

Or that Mykhailo Mudryk could run around briefly like a deranged hamster, get banned for failing a drugs test and still become a potential growth asset? This is pre-subprime crash energy. Yes, you can install a solar-powered mega-wetroom that fires sourdough breadsticks directly into your eyes. Whatever. Ownership is all. Money will take care of you.

There are still levels to this. The one Chelsea thing to shift in the window is that the curtain has now been drawn on those initial eight months, the period where Todd Boehly became the world’s worst director of football, a director of football who basically didn’t know what football was.

That period has now been safely capped off. Only two players remain. Rough out the numbers and Chelsea spent something like £200m in fees, wages, leaks and cuts, with only Malo Gusto and Wesley Fofana to show for it. No real damage. Money comes, money goes. We roll on.

This is the lesson of the latest summer transfer window. Right now it doesn’t really matter what you do in the Premier League. Just being in it is the thing. With one caveat, which is that nobody actually knows what’s happening here. We can marvel at a record window. We can see the biggest spenders are Manchester City on £457.5m, the lowest Crystal Palace on about £50m, the highest net Liverpool on £216.8m. We can pore over Aston Villa buying the bones of a new squad for £56.7m net gain.

But we can’t know what it means, at least not financially. This is part of the design of money on this scale. As the then Federal Reserve chair Alan Greenspan put it in a famous speech on the mysteries of big money: “How do we know when irrational exuberance has unduly escalated asset values, which then become subject to unexpected and prolonged contractions?”

Nobody knew what this meant then. Nobody knows what it means now. “Irrational exuberance” is a good phrase, one Greenspan later said came to him in the bath. It was designed to convey the essential point: opacity, vagueness, invisible flows. If not for those actually riding the tide, because someone is always making money. Someone out there actively wants the Premier League’s financial chaos, and is benefiting from it gloriously.

Otherwise, reading the runes is just a matter of guesswork. Money moves between networked entities. Everyone inside wins. Everyone outside pays for it. But still, this feels new, if only in its extremity.

This was captured by the weirdness of Sky Sports’ transfer deadline programme on Tuesday. At one point a man appeared strumming a guitar, smiling as if he had just filleted a litter of kittens in his basement, and sang a Bradley Barcola Liverpool song to the tune of Don’t Dream It’s Over, like this is all just normal and fine.

Later there was a golden period at about 5.30pm where every deal just seemed wrong and impossible, a fever dream after an over-ripe seafood risotto. Aston Villa have paid £47m for an 18-year-old winger. Gabriel Jesus is going to Barcelona. Jack Grealish is having a medical at Everton, an event that seems to prove the non-linear nature of time, a medical that is always happening, never not happening, a constant time-space event.

Meanwhile two private jets are on the tarmac in Lyon as three clubs try to sign Malick Fofana. “We STILL don’t know what Malick Fofana is thinking,” the man with the microphone concluded, mournfully, and this seemed profoundly true and on point. We don’t. Does Malick Fofana even know this? If so, how can he? Nobody else has a clue what’s going on.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

It is worth trying to list the best deals. Harry Wilson on a free can only be good. Djed Spence to Inter is great. Forza, Djed. Barcola to Liverpool for £123m is lots of money, but he’s really young and knows how to score once he’s settled.

Newcastle seem to have had a good window, racking up a list of signings that scream inside knowledge and good data, and chime with Matthias Jaissle’s mercurial vibe. Manchester City’s signings have to be good. There’s so many of them, and they’re all excellent players. That midfield is surely just too big to fail.

Arsenal will also be fine, despite not signing a 1950s-style hotshot goal ace with dynamite in his boots and the brain of a hungry magpie. Yes, they’ve lost two, maybe three attackers. But these are Jesus and probably Gabriel Martinelli, meat in the room, plus Leandro Trossard, replaced by basically the same guy. Arsenal won the league with Kai Havertz, Martin Ødegaard, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze short of their ceiling. If you can’t score enough to win with that lot then it’s really not the players.

Manchester United’s window looks quite good, but also scattergun. Carlos Baleba may be great, or may wander around like a lost child in Lidl before being loaned to Monaco. Tottenham have mined the club’s DNA, gone back to their spiritual roots, and signed players who will be really good for four games, then disappear and get tattoos.

Meanwhile Everton have swapped Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. What does it mean? Can you even visualise this as an event? Beto and Iliman Ndiaye have gone, taking away a third of last season’s league goals. Welcome, Everton fans, to the fully immersive Thierno Barry multiverse.

Otherwise the main takeaway is the meaninglessness of big football money. Most notably the size of the most basic fees. Little wonder there is a sense of alienation from familiar notions of team building, blocks in place, footballers as recognisable avatars of graft and cultural chemistry. These are stocks, talent units, a flow of resources.

Remember the Peter Odemwingie deadline day fiasco, where Odemwingie sat fuming in his car while the world was sucked into this human drama? That whole thing was about the unbridgeable leap from £2m to £3m. Coventry have just signed Caleb Yirenkyi from Nordsjælland for £23m. Does “Caleb Yirenkyi” really exist? Are you sure?

Who pays in the end for this circulation of funds? You, for starters. There is no such thing as football money. It’s all TV rights, state propaganda funds and hard private investment from the kind of people who really don’t give without taking back in the end.

On one level books are being balanced, accounting rules satisfied, clubs swapping assets at fees driven in part by regulatory requirements. More obscurely Boehly once talked about a rush of cash being diverted football’s way as a sub-avalanche from quantitative easing in the US, because money just has to go somewhere. No, me neither.

All that seems certain is money is being pushed around the board. And that it feels wildly abstract. The window was thrilling, its possibilities endless, a shot of blood for the new season. Beyond this, big football and big finance are playing their own game, in a way that goes beyond the human scale and into a world of pure money. The message below the headlines is clear. This thing belongs to them. Your job, human consumer unit, is simply to look at it and have feelings.

The loan of the Bayeux tapestry was “the best possible symbol” of the “entente amicale” between France and the UK, King Charles said, as he visited the famous embroidered masterpiece at the British Museum in London.

Though the tapestry recounts a conflict, “here it is today, nearly 1,000 years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations,” he said.

The “70 metres of memory and artistry” were a reminder “that our two nations have been bound together for almost a millennium”, added Charles, speaking at the new exhibition and accompanied by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.

In a speech partly delivered in French, he said: “We have defended our values together in times of peril; we continue to do so today across the world.”

He continued: “May this tapestry – and the treasures that will travel in return – stand as symbols not only of our shared past, but our shared future: a future woven, as it should be, by Britain and France together.”

Macron, also speaking in French and English, said that the return of the tapestry “had required a little patience” , since he first spoke of it in 2018.

“Since the first British request dates back to 1931, I choose to regard eight years as something of a speed record,” he said.

He added that, with the tapestry in Britain, his hopes were that the two countries could “forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery”.

The tapestry – the woven record of the Norman conquest – has returned to the UK for the first time in almost 1,000 years, and is on loan until September 2027 as part of a special trilateral agreement between the UK, France and the museum.

Charles’s reference to entente amicale followed his use of the phrase to rebrand the famous “entente cordiale” between the two nations in his banquet speech at Windsor Castle when he hosted the Macrons in July last year.

During Wednesday’s visit, he expressed his “deepest appreciation” to Macron and the French people “for the trust you have placed in the United Kingdom by agreeing to this unprecedented loan”.

He said: “It once depicted warriors crossing the Channel; yet today it forms part of a cultural exchange that will see some of the British Museum’s own precious artefacts travel to France in return, in a spirit of friendship.”

Thanking all those who made the loan possible, he added: “Anyone studying the tapestry’s scenes in detail will notice that, even in the 11th century, historic events rarely happened without extensive discussion, careful planning and a great deal of organisation beforehand.”

The party, which also included Queen Camilla, France’s first lady, Brigitte Macron, and Burnham’s wife, Marie-France van Heel, stopped at key moments along the 11th-century artwork to hear from curators about historic events such as the coronation of Harold Godwinson and the much-disputed depiction of his death by an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

At his first prime minister’s questions earlier on Wednesday, Burnham said: “The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation, the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low.”

The Labour leader also said the Bayeux Around Britain programme, which will see the digital exhibition displayed in museums, galleries and castles in all four nations, would “give communities across the UK the opportunity to learn about one of the defining stories of our past”.

In exchange, Britain will loan the Sutton Hoo treasures – an assemblage of gold and other historic objects dating from the 7th century AD – and a selection of Lewis ‌chess pieces and other masterpieces owned by the trustees of the British Museum to museums in France.

Burnham tries to calm bond market fears as sell-off threatens crucial first budget

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 18:28:57 GMT

Prime minister promises his government will make decisions ‘grounded in fiscal responsibility’

Andy Burnham moved to calm volatile bond markets on Wednesday as surging borrowing costs threatened to wreck plans for his government’s crucial first budget next month.

After a days-long sell-off of government bonds – and with the chancellor, John Healey, facing the prospect of sharply reduced spending power, Burnham used his first appearance at prime minister’s questions to promise decisions would be “grounded in fiscal responsibility”.

That was widely seen as an attempt to soothe investors after his statement to parliament on Tuesday, in which he made bold promises of more public control of utilities, further interventions on the cost of living and a recommitment to a 3% increase in defence spending.

While those offers were broadly welcomed by Labour MPs, Burnham was criticised by others for inflaming the sell-off. His former economic adviser, Jim O’Neill, said it was the “last thing” the markets needed.

Investors across world markets have been dumping government bonds amid fears about rising inflation, runaway deficits and competing demand for capital from tech companies on a debt-fuelled AI spending spree. The sell-off has driven up yields, or interest rates, including in the UK. At one point on Wednesday, the cost of 10-year borrowing for the government hit its highest level since 2008, at 5.29%, before easing slightly.

That is expected to be costly for Healey when the Office for Budget Responsibility draws up its budget forecasts. The independent watchdog bases its projection for bond yields on a snapshot of market interest rates taken several weeks before each budget and that is expected to be about now for Healey’s 28 October statement.

The chancellor has repeatedly stressed that fiscal discipline is the “bedrock” of government policy. He will give a speech on Monday setting out his plans for economic growth – less than six months after senior City and business figures gathered to hear his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, lay out her approach.

In his first PMQs clash with Kemi Badenoch, Burnham blamed the Conservative leader’s party for leaving the UK vulnerable to market turmoil.

Criticising Burnham’s three-hour statement in the Commons the day before, Badenoch said: “He did not say no to a single spending request … And personally, I think it’s delightful that he wants to make everyone happy. But a prime minister needs to be a leader, not a people pleaser.”

Burnham said his budget would “stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents”.

Analysts believe higher interest rates on public debt could wipe out up to half of the £24bn headroom Rachel Reeves built up against Labour’s fiscal rules.

Government insiders told the Guardian they believed it would be very difficult for Healey to deliver a budget that had less than double-digit headroom, given the signal that would send to bond markets. However, that would leave him with almost no leeway for additional spending. No 10 sources declined to be drawn on what Burnham’s preferred level of headroom would be.

Healey will also have to show how the Treasury intends to fill a funding gap in defence spending and pay for Burnham’s cost of living measures, including the VAT cut on electricity bills.

Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest is now one in every £12 the government is spending, so even relatively small changes can add up quite quickly.”

Alongside the narrowing margin for error against the rules, Miller identified two other budget headaches for Healey – the likely hit to growth forecasts from falling immigration and the demand for more spending on defence.

She said: “It’s not that any one of these things on their own are the kind of ‘hit the panic button’ moment, but when you add them all together, they do add real pressure on the government.”

Ruth Curtice, the director of the Resolution Foundation, said febrile markets meant the government would face additional scrutiny over the sustainability of the public finances.

She added: “The risk of not facing up to the challenges has gone up, but also maybe the reward from showing that you’re serious about addressing them might have gone up too.”

The thinktank boss backed a call by Lord O’Neill for the new government to scrap the triple lock pension as a way of showing it was serious about balancing the books: “Jim O’Neill was on to something, in that part of the test for markets is, are they prepared to do politically unpopular things, in the name of trying to sort some of these fiscal problems out?”

O’Neill had been mooted as an economic adviser to Burnham but has instead gone public with criticism of the fledgling government.

A Treasury source insisted that unlike other major economies, including the US, the UK had a plan – inherited from Reeves – for reducing the deficit and bringing down debt. “To the extent that investors start looking at fiscal plans, we should start to distinguish ourselves in a positive way,” they said.

Global markets have been spooked by higher oil costs after a resumption of the Middle East conflict, resulting in higher expectations for future inflation.

Investors now believe the Bank of England will step in and raise interest rates three times, to 4.5% over the next year, to tackle inflation. That would push up mortgage costs just as Burnham hopes to cut the cost of living.

Burnham will host Emmanuel Macron for talks in No 10 on Thursday, as he begins to build his own relationships with European allies before the next stage of the UK’s reset with the EU.

The prime minister is expected to use the talks to continue pushing for greater cooperation with Europe to support British businesses and drive growth, with the French president a key figure in the government’s pursuit of a closer trading relationship.

Downing Street sources suggested that while the EU reset would not officially be on the agenda – because the responsibility for any deal lies with Brussels – it was likely to come up in the margins of the bilateral discussions.

Burnham indicated in the Commons on Tuesday that the next reset summit, which was delayed by the EU after Keir Starmer was ousted as prime minister, could be held in November.

Ink review – Danny Boyle turns the birth of the Sun into a lurid tabloid frenzy

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 18:24:34 GMT

Venice film festivalJack O’Connell is terrific as editor Larry Lamb in James Graham’s tale of Rupert Murdoch, Page 3 and the newspaper that transformed Fleet Street

Danny Boyle presents us with a lurid, violent and thumpingly unsubtle movie full of Dutch angles, cartoony shocks and gargoyle closeups. It’s a chapter in the prehistory of modern media, adapted by James Graham from his 2017 stage play, filled with shame and fear and self-hate. It is in fact the story of the Sun newspaper, and how Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) bought the ailing minor title in the late 60s and hired a tough Yorkshire newspaperman, Larry Lamb, to turn it into a raucous and gleefully vulgar circulation powerhouse.

Ink summons up the energy and frenzy of tabloid papers of the era, but also – and not entirely intentionally – how strangely depressing they were. Audiences used to the super-rich anomie of the Roy family from TV’s Succession might find all this very unsexy. This is a world of officer-class Fleet Street execs having expense-account meals at Rules and the Savoy Grill in pinstripe suits, smoking and drinking and impassively writing salary offers on paper napkins and silently passing them across to each other. Meanwhile, the other ranks of journalists and print unions are covered in sweat and ink.

Murdoch and Lamb had something to prove: both wanted to take a slap at the establishment club that had until that moment kept them out. Jack O’Connell is excellent casting as Lamb; muscular and pugnacious as a working-class reporter made good. Pearce is less of a panto monster than you might expect; in fact, he is increasingly squeamish and fastidious at the rude ideas that Lamb keeps coming up with for the paper – even if the Page 3 girls were not immediately introduced. It’s a coolly composed performance, though the traditional question of what makes Murdoch tick is incuriously passed over; again, this suffers in comparison with Brian Cox’s Logan Roy in Succession. Claire Foy plays the fictional-composite figure of Jules, a kind of young Marjorie Proops women’s-page editor powerless to stop the coming tide of sexism.

Yet this is a film with a story-within-a-story to tell, about a truly horrifying true-crime nightmare (in this way, oddly reminiscent of Akira Kurosawa’s 1963 film High and Low), an event which perhaps deserves a film of its own. In 1969, Muriel McKay (played here by Lucy Russell), the wife of Murdoch executive Alick McKay (Jonathan Hyde), was kidnapped by people who thought she was Murdoch’s wife Anna; it was a chaotic and incompetent abduction that resulted in the death of Muriel McKay, whose body was never found.

The film is perhaps unsure exactly how much prominence to give this horrible affair in the midst of the bleary, knowing and lenient black comedy that governs everything else. Was the McKay kidnapping a terrible karmic judgment on the Murdoch group and the Sun itself, that did so much to promote materialism and celebrity obsession? (The kidnappers were reputedly inspired by Murdoch’s appearance on TV.) Maybe. Boyle’s movie imagines Lamb unrepentantly running sensational stories about the kidnapping – as he never would have dared if the victim was actually Anna Murdoch – on the grounds that a reader might have important information to give the police. And then, after the tragic outcome becomes clear, he rejects guilt and doubles down on Sun-sationalism and introduces Page 3 girls.

So was the McKay kidnapping the primal scene of media degradation, the seed that led to Fox News, Trumpism and the social media manosphere? Again, maybe; but perhaps the kidnapping should occupy a more central dramatic position if the film is not to appear cynical and detached in the way that the Sun was accused of being. Either way, it’s a resoundingly tough and confident performance from O’Connell.

Ink screened at the Venice film festival; it is in cinemas on 11 December in the US, 7 January in Australia and 8 January in the UK

Israel’s defence minister has said his country is seeking Donald Trump’s support to approve plans to expel Palestinians from the Gaza Strip in what has widely been condemned as a potential war crime.

Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration” during a conference hosted by the Israeli news site Ynet and the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth. He said the Israeli government was “organised and prepared to get them out by sea, by air, by every way possible”.

Trump discussed a US takeover of the Gaza Strip in early 2025 that would have involved removing Palestinians from the territory, but has since pulled back from the idea. A 20-point peace plan the White House drew up last year did not call for Palestinians’ deportation, an act that would be widely seen as ethnic cleansing.

Katz, however, said on Wednesday that he believed US support could tip regional opinion in favour of the forced resettlement of Palestinians from Gaza. He said Trump’s approval was crucial to convince neighbouring countries to accept Palestinian refugees.

“Every country that is willing to take them in wants American backing,” he said. “Trump has not cancelled this at the moment. He has frozen it.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request from the Guardian for comment on whether Trump was continuing to hold discussions on Israel’s proposals to forcibly depopulate the Gaza Strip.

Katz pointed in particular to Egypt, which he said had lobbied Washington to oppose the forced removal of the Palestinian population. “It has not been cancelled,” he said. “It is being discussed all the time, including now, and I think there is no other solution in the end that is in everyone’s interest.”

The remarks come during a competitive election season in Israel in which the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his rightwing allies have appealed to voters by calling for more aggressive measures against Palestinians.

Some have been openly inflammatory and cruel. The far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, posted footage on X from a women’s prison where he said he was responsible for the dire conditions in the facility.

When one prisoner told him they were not receiving medical care, showering or receiving clean clothing, Ben-Gvir said: “The good conditions in the prisons are over. This is the current situation, and I am directly responsible for everything. I am pleased with these conditions.”

Netanyahu visited an Israeli military post close to the yellow line in the Gaza Strip on Wednesday. Israel has said it would not pull back from that line until Hamas disarmed, despite calls for a phased withdrawal to facilitate a recent ceasefire with the group.

“We control the territory and are staying on this line,” Netanyahu said. “We are doing everything to achieve our goal – disarming Hamas and demilitarising Gaza. Gaza will no longer pose a threat to Israel.”

Lando Norris launches LN4 Fusion team to develop young drivers in F1 and motorsport

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 18:06:32 GMT

F1 champion first to back junior team in single-seater era

Norris also creates legacy programme to support talent

Lando Norris has co-founded a new junior, single-seater racing team. Named LN4 Fusion it will compete in multiple championships including the feeder series for Formula One, F3 and F2, as the current F1 world champion commits to helping young drivers make it to the top level in motorsport.

Norris’s involvement, including a personal financial undertaking alongside an investment group, represents the first time an F1 world champion has directly backed a team in the modern junior single-seater era. As part of the project he has also established the LN4 Legacy programme, a driver development initiative designed to identify and support talent coming through the ranks from karting upwards and then provide assistance financially as well as in coaching, performance and career support.

The McLaren driver launched the project at an event in Monza, which will host the Italian Grand Prix this weekend. It constitutes a serious and comprehensive effort to address some of the difficulties facing junior drivers coming through the ranks, which Norris has previously identified as a fundamental problem for the sport.

“I know that getting to Formula One takes so much more than just talent. You need the right people around you, the right support and the right opportunities at the right time,” he said.

“That’s what these two projects are all about. LN4 Fusion is about building a race team that can compete with the best in junior motorsport, with great people and a great environment for drivers to develop. The LN4 Legacy programme is about helping talented young drivers get opportunities they might not otherwise have.

“They naturally fit together. I want to help create opportunities for the next generation both on and off the track and hopefully make a real difference to young drivers coming through the sport.”

The intent for the LN4 Fusion team will be to compete across a range of championships as of next year with already confirmed programmes in F3 for 2027, as well as the Italian F4 Championship and the FIA Formula Regional European Championship. As part of the process the team has acquired key assets from the German team AIX Racing, which has an F3 entry until the end of the 2027 season and has applied for participation in the F2 Championship.

Norris will play an active role in the organisation and his role was welcomed by the F1 chief executive, Stefano Domenicali. “Seeing Lando Norris involved in this new project is an incredible statement on how much the pyramid of Formula 3 and Formula 2 is crucial to the future of Formula One,” he said. “Through Lando’s investment and experience we can build a future, with new drivers, engineers, mechanics, and a tradition that will be followed by motorsport lovers.”

The seriousness of Norris’s ambition was emphasised with the appointment of René Rosin as team principal. Rosin was formerly the principal and managing director of the Prema team, which has enjoyed more than 40 years of competition in the junior series. They have won multiple titles and are one of the go-to teams for developing young talent. Prema brought on many drivers who went on to F1 including, among others on the current grid, the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc as well as Norris’s McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri. The team also nurtured Jacques Villeneuve who went on to take the F1 title.

Part of the LN4 Fusion team will be formed from the experience and personnel at the Fusion Motorsport team, which has enjoyed huge success for 25 years in UK karting, with multiple national and more recently international titles. The head of Fusion Motorsport karting, Dan Hazlewood, will be team principal of the LN4 Fusion UK operation, including overseeing the planned entry into the British F4 championship and in bringing talent through from karting.

Rosin emphasised the importance of having Norris as a key part of the new venture and its expectations of success.

Deadline-day shambles leaves Everton and David Moyes fighting the odds again

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 18:02:02 GMT

From accepting a bid for Armstrong to collapse of Balogun deal, TFG has shown an amateurish and unambitious approach

To be placed in the same bracket as owners whose lack of ambition, lack of resources and/or incompetence has contributed to the longest trophy drought in Everton’s history, particularly 20 months into a reign that has accompanied the move to a glittering new stadium and the clearing of onerous debt, should be cause for considerable discomfort and embarrassment at The Friedkin Group (TFG) on Wednesday. The slight on Everton’s owner is neither unkind nor unfair. At least Farhad Moshiri had a go before the taps were turned off.

TFG may have restored financial stability to Everton after the near-ruinous chaos of Moshiri’s final years and his attempts to sell to 777 Partners but its reputation as “winners” – as the club’s chief executive, Angus Kinnear, labelled his American employers – has been shredded in the space of four days. The description always appeared generous given its approach to the summer transfer window, part two of Everton’s strategic rebuild according to Kinnear. But from accepting Nottingham Forest’s £35m bid for Harrison Armstrong on Saturday morning to Folarin Balogun walking away from a £40m move from Monaco on Tuesday night, and more in between, TFG has positioned itself as just another Everton owner unable or unwilling to realise the club’s potential and to give an expectant fanbase grounds for optimism.

Evertonians hoped for an overdue departure when TFG acquired the club in December 2024 and proceeded to refinance damaging loans and the long-term repayment costs of Hill Dickinson Stadium. The shambles of deadline day, however, was all too familiar and has caused serious damage to its standing among supporters.

David Moyes kept his counsel throughout pre-season as Everton spent £16.5m on Hayden Hackney, rising to £25m for last season’s Championship player of the year, £18m on each of Merlin Röhl and Tyrique George, who he had on loan last season, £7m on Christian Nørgaard and swapped Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. The most Everton paid up front for a player all summer would prove to be £18m.

When Moyes did eventually speak in public it was to stress, repeatedly, the need for Everton to sign more players, more quality and to keep their best talents. At the end of last season he had 22 outfield players at his disposal. At the start of deadline day he had 20 outfield players. By the end of transfer deadline day he had 18.

That total includes one striker, Thierno Barry, no back-up for either full-back and, strictly speaking given that Ainsley Maitland-Niles did not start out in the position, no natural right-back. Everton sold their most creative asset, Iliman Ndiaye, to Manchester City in a below-market price £65m deal despite the Senegal international having three years on his contract. They sold Beto, their only striking alternative to Barry, before securing a replacement and were left desperately scrambling around for one when Balogun’s medical went awry.

Manchester United said no to a loan offer for Joshua Zirkzee that arrived a few hours before the deadline. Tammy Abraham said no to leaving Aston Villa. Finally Balogun, having arrived later than scheduled for his medical and seen Everton renegotiate the terms of his fee with Monaco, compounded the chaos by also saying no despite signing a deal sheet shortly before 11pm. Barry looked out of his depth for much of his debut season in the Premier League. Now he is the precious commodity that Everton cannot afford to lose.

Kinnear, perhaps in response to Moyes raising concerns over Everton’s business for the first time, gave several local interviews two weeks ago that painted a rosy picture of the club’s finances, transfer strategy and ambition. Subsequent events have cost him credibility on every count. The chief executive also got his manager’s back up by claiming TFG regarded not qualifying for Europe last season as “a failure” and that the squad is better placed to sustain a European challenge while striving to end Everton’s 31-year wait for a trophy.

Moyes’s team face-planted during last season’s run-in, failing to win any of their last seven games when Europe was in reach. He has been challenged to go further with fewer resources. An added annoyance for Moyes and supporters is that Everton have started this season brightly, only to be surrounded by problems entirely of the hierarchy’s making.

It was Kinnear who implemented a new “senior leadership team” at Everton and the move away from a director of football model. The team consists of the technical director, Nick Cox, director of scouting and recruitment, James Smith, director of football strategy and analytics, Chris Howarth and head of player trading, Nick Hammond. Moyes is also part of the leadership team, although he has appeared to be on a different page this summer. There has been sensible, cost-effective recruitment for Hackney, Röhl and Johnson but the end to the window invites criticism of the leadership team’s effectiveness and expertise. It resembles a case of too many chiefs and no clear direction, especially given some of the targets Everton went for in the final days.

The collapse of the Balogun deal has caused turmoil at Everton but a player getting cold feet over a move or a medical jeopardising a deal can happen. It is events under Everton’s control, and decisions they have taken, that are of greater concern. TFG’s decision to accept Forest’s offer for Armstrong, the first academy prospect to graduate through the ranks and establish himself since Anthony Gordon six years ago, was the first indication that Everton were struggling to meet the new squad cost ratios. So much for a new financial era at Hill Dickinson.

TFG merits some credit for listening to supporters over the proposed sale of Armstrong and pulling the plug. To then consider selling Ndiaye to Tottenham for £60m and spending £35m on Richarlison, however, was another alarming sign.

Everton have been looking for a right-back since Moyes returned to the club in January 2025, and needed one before then. Moyes wanted Guéla Doué from Strasbourg but the 23-year-old was deemed too expensive. Doué joined Bayer Leverkusen on deadline day for £25.7m. At least five alternatives were explored before Everton, their £9m deal for Fulham’s Kenny Tete having fallen through, signed Maitland-Niles as the £4.3m answer to one glaring problem.

A bigger weakness lay up front. No Premier League club of serious intent would enter a second season with their striking options limited to Beto and Barry. An upgrade was essential. Instead, Everton downgraded. So much for the leadership team’s vision and the owner’s ambition.

Everton are the lowest net spenders in the Premier League over the past five years and, more by accident than design, ended this summer making a net profit of £25m on transfers. TFG committed £78m on signings in a summer where, by the calculations of the football finance expert Kieran Maguire, the average spend per Premier League club was £181m. Everton’s outlay does not include the significant cost of re-signing Jack Grealish on loan.

TFG’s frugal spending and efficiency drive – redundancies were made behind the scenes at Everton this summer – has fuelled talk of Dan Friedkin and co looking to sell the club. However, the owners have allocated £40m to cover the compensation payable to Burnley should Everton fail in their appeal against the outcome of a profitability and sustainability breach case, and are investing almost £14m in infrastructure projects at Hill Dickinson, Goodison Park and Finch Farm training ground.

What is certain is the anger TFG would face if they attended Sunday’s home game against Manchester United. Dan Friedkin has yet to attend a match at Hill Dickinson, where some season ticket prices were increased by up to 10% this season.

The Everton fans’ forum and Everton fan advisory board issued statements on Wednesday criticising the club’s amateurish, unambitious approach to the transfer window. The 1878s, the group of volunteers responsible for the impressive tifos and banners at the stadium, has withdrawn its support for the foreseeable future. “We do not feel that our fanbase’s ambitions and the club’s ambitions align right now – what happened yesterday has proved that even more,” the group said.

It looks a long road back to acceptance for TFG, Kinnear and Everton’s senior leadership team.

The Guardian view on Kemi Badenoch and the economy: a plan stuck in the Tory comfort zone

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 17:29:43 GMT

The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election

To outlast a prime minister always counts as some kind of achievement for an opposition leader, although Kemi Badenoch cannot claim credit for Sir Keir Starmer’s downfall. Sir Keir’s wounds were mostly self-inflicted. To the extent that opposition pressure was involved, it was electoral threats from Reform UK and the Green party that stoked Labour party frustration to a regicidal pitch. The Tory leader’s role was largely as a spectator.

Mrs Badenoch still hopes to use regime change to her advantage. She thinks the economy, and fiscal discipline in particular, will be her most fruitful line of attack. In their first confrontation at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, the Conservative leader called Mr Burnham a “spendthrift” and “people pleaser” who will dodge the tough decisions required to prove Britain’s creditworthiness on international markets. She expects him to yield to Labour MPs’ demands for budget increases, which will then have to be financed with tax rises.

In that scenario, Mrs Badenoch imagines a vacancy for a rehabilitated small-state Conservative party offering hard-headed budget management, less profligate than Labour; more sober and respectable than Reform UK. That message would unite what remains of her depleted party. She can’t compete with Nigel Farage on the terrain of anti-immigrant rhetoric (although that doesn’t stop her aping his stances). She shows no interest in finding political accommodation for socially liberal, pro-European one-nation Tories who now have more in common with the Liberal Democrats than the modern Conservative party.

This leaves the Tories with a narrow focus on tax cuts, reining in welfare spending and deregulation as a spur to enterprise. Mr Farage supports those things too, but Mrs Badenoch believes that Reform UK’s maverick style and the whiff of impropriety around its financial dealings make it an unreliable vehicle for a classically Thatcherite agenda that belongs, by rights, to Lady Thatcher’s own party.

The claim to be the true keeper of the Thatcherite flame has become a ritual for Tory leaders. The mantle has passed through so many hands, it is threadbare as a political definition in 2026. It was worn most preposterously by Liz Truss, who posted photos of herself on social media recreating iconic images of the Iron Lady in her pomp. She then detonated her government with a “mini-budget” that was a crass pastiche of the economic ideas she claimed to venerate – a wild foray into fiscal irresponsibility masquerading as free-market radicalism.

One of the Treasury ministers who enthusiastically endorsed Ms Truss’s plan, Andrew Griffith, was this week appointed Mrs Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor. He replaces Mel Stride, a lower-octane performer who was deemed not to have made sufficient impact in the role. It is a revealing choice that undermines the Tory leader’s plan to make economic competence the centrepiece of her pitch to lead the nation. When considering a potential chancellor, she clearly values the ability to grab attention over economic judgment.

This is consistent with a pattern of failure to engage with the full spectrum of failures over many years that accounts for the scale of Tory defeat at the last election. What Mrs Badenoch imagines to be a political strategy looks more like retreat to an ideological comfort zone in the hope that a second prime minister will self-destruct while she watches from the sidelines.

The Guardian view on Israeli settlements: Britain can no longer look away

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 17:29:38 GMT

International law, European action and UK public opinion point the same way. Britain should stop helping to sustain Israeli settlements economically

In the Commons this week, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, appeared to have accepted the principle of a trade ban between the UK and Israeli settlements, which Britain says are illegal under international law. This is long overdue. The test now is whether his promised “comprehensive reset” deserves the name. Stopping settlement-produced goods at the border is not enough. Britain should prohibit its companies from sustaining settlement activity – by financing, constructing, insuring, advertising – in territory whose occupation it regards as unlawful. The ban must have teeth.

The UK can no longer ignore the violence and pressure exerted on Palestinians in the West Bank by Israel’s government, military and settlers. There have been more than 1,400 settler attacks so far this year, according to the UN, against a record 1,800 registered in 2025. An election campaign has only made matters worse. Last month, Israel issued tenders for 1,234 homes in the 3,401-unit E1 development east of Jerusalem. The country’s ministers gave the green light for the controversial settlement – long condemned for effectively bisecting the West Bank – expressly to “erase” the idea of a Palestinian state, the creation of which the UK officially supports.

Israeli ministers have reacted with fury, threatening retaliation if Britain imposes sanctions over settlement expansion. This is disappointing, but hardly surprising. Benjamin Netanyahu has accused countries imposing sanctions of “moral bankruptcy”. Yet Britain would be following several comparable European states that increasingly regard such bans as a consequence of international law. Spain has banned settlement imports; Norway is legislating against trade and services linked to settlements; nine EU governments have demanded action from Brussels.

Since 1967, Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jewish people among 3.3 million Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem. There are now calls to suspend the EU’s trade agreement with Israel. Britain has such a deal and, under Sir Keir Starmer, Labour wanted to “distinguish and protect trade with people and businesses across the state of Israel”. This gave critics reason to warn that targeting settlements could end up as a “de facto” boycott of Israel. But that gets the argument backwards: Israel cannot make the settlements part of its economy and then argue that other nations must treat them as part of the country.

Mr Miliband has political room to manoeuvre. Polling suggests that even Reform UK and Conservative voters are more likely to support than oppose a settlement trade ban. In parliament there was agreement stretching from the Greens to Labour to Tory MPs that something has to be done.

Settlement expansion accelerated after Mr Netanyahu’s far-right coalition took power in 2022 and then again after Hamas’s murderous attack sparked the Gaza war in 2023. The legal case is clear: other nations are acting and the political space is opening up – all while creeping annexation becomes a reality. Israel is extending civilian control over occupied territory as settlements expand. Gaza, where more than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed, has understandably commanded the world’s attention. No one disputes that Israel exists in a violent and unstable neighbourhood, though its actions aggravate, rather than alleviate, that instability. But the West Bank and Jerusalem cannot be ignored. Security cannot justify an ideological land grab.

Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 17:14:31 GMT

Fair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s status

It’s too soon to say the bond markets have turned on Andy Burnham. Tuesday’s spike in gilt yields, taking the UK’s 30-year borrowing costs to their highest level since 1998, was part of an international sell-off of government debt.

The main contributors are well known. The Iran war, by increasing the cost of energy, has overturned the comforting start-of-the-year thesis of falling global inflation and interest rates. A plunging Japanese yen has kicked away another assumed source of financial stability. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, hasn’t calmed nerves with his solo, and so far futile, attempt to bring down US yields. Meanwhile, the early stage of the AI revolution is an exercise in issuing squillions of debt before long-term returns on capital can possibly be assessed meaningfully.

From the point of view of the mythical bond vigilante, in these circumstances it’s only logical to demand a higher return to lend to profligate governments with high debt ratios, which is most of them.

In a narrow sense, then, UK gilts were just moving with the market at a moment of rising financial risks in all directions. It’s just that the UK was already uncomfortably placed at the cold edge of the pack with the highest borrowing rates in the G7, a status largely reflecting a dismal 20-year record in keeping a lid on inflation and, especially now, a dependency on energy imports that stood at 43% in 2025.

It is also true, unfortunately, that six weeks into the job Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, have said nothing to make bond investors rethink the UK’s status. Investors have heard the dutiful commitment to Rachel Reeves’s fiscal rules, but Burnham’s Commons speech on Tuesday carried little sense of urgency about the UK’s financial predicament, or appreciation of how 10-year gilt yields at 5.2% will cause damage if sustained for long.

More “public control” of utilities – the theme Burnham constantly returns to – may be desirable and play well on the backbenches. But, even when the ambiguous meaning is made clearer, how does it translate into, say, substantially lower costs of building infrastructure? Should it really be a top economic priority?

“Markets are sceptical that ‘devolution’ and ‘control’ are levers for lower government-led inflation,” said the Panmure Liberum economist Simon French. “Burnham/Healey’s unenviable task is to prove they are the right levers. If they fail then a very painful period of financial repression/demand side-led disinflation will be necessary.”

There is an uncomfortable sense that the bond market expects next month’s budget to be a bigger event than Burnham and Healey will produce. The tone of Burnham’s Commons speech was “the last thing investors wanted to hear”, said the former Goldman Sachs economist Jim O’Neill – quite a verdict from a friendly critic who was being lined up for a role in government until recently.

But one can see his point. He told the BBC that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to get real about dealing with the triple lock on the state pension and “excessive” welfare spending. There has been little rolling of the pitch, as they say in Westminster, in either of those directions to date.

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 17:07:21 GMT

The government’s tougher stance towards the Kremlin is drawing attacks from both the far right and far left

Even before the German government laid the blame this week on Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport, the topic of German ties to Moscow was high on the political agenda.

But the timing of the unsurprising yet explosive Leipzig announcement – days before a key regional vote – has exposed the extent to which German politics is polarised on the issue.

Leading the polls nationally and in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, which votes this weekend, is the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The party has repeatedly called for a closer bond with the Kremlin, and crucially, for its cheap oil and gas to flow to Germany once again, despite Moscow’s unrelenting onslaught on Ukraine.

Germany is already on tenterhooks. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, had warned that Berlin faced a growing threat of hybrid warfare, and on Wednesday morning, the day after the Leipzig announcement, police were investigating a second sabotage assault on the electricity grid within just 24 hours.

An explosion at Augsburg railway station in the early hours of Wednesday morning also initially looked like it might fall into the same category, illustrating the extent to which the country remains nervous and on high ‌alert for attacks on its vital infrastructure.

Investigations into all these incidents and others from the near past, many of which are said to be linked, are ongoing, even as authorities warned against drawing premature conclusions.

Moscow has denied involvement, and accused Berlin of trying to divert attention from its own domestic problems, including the rise of the far right, and the state’s failure to protect its own infrastructure.

The resulting uncertainty, chaos and angst appear to be nothing less than grist to the mill of the AfD. Its foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, accused the government of sorting acts of sabotage “according to political expediency”.

While it had “escalated the situation against Russia within days”, he said, the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukrainian operatives are suspected of being responsible for sabotaging a key route for Russian gas to Germany, had so far remained without consequence. (Two Ukrainian nationals named by Germany as suspects have been arrested over the attack, with one last year extradited from Italy and the other currently in Croatia.)

“This is not a consistent security policy, but rather a double standard in foreign policy,” Frohnmaier claimed, adding he was convinced the government would use the Leipzig incident “as justification for even more support for Ukraine and an even deeper involvement of Germany in this war”.

The AfD, which has called for talks with Moscow, ending sanctions against Russia, and slashing support for Ukraine, has urged the government to lay bare its proof of Russia’s involvement, saying so far the evidence is lacking.

Wary of escalating a conflict with Moscow, the government of Friedrich Merz waited days before making its painstakingly worded declaration. In a more frank admission than the German government has ever made, foreign minister Johann Wadephul stated: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.”

The details released on Wednesday of two Russian suspects identified as having been involved in the Leipzig incident are unlikely to assuage the AfD’s complaints or, it would seem, the far-left party Die Linke.

Its leading MP, Dietmar Bartsch, said on Wednesday that the suspicions of Russian involvement did not justify the government’s decision to shut down the Russian consulate in Bonn as well as a sprawling Russian cultural centre in Berlin and would not make Germany safer. On the contrary, they increased the risk of a “major war” drawing closer, he said.

With the AfD on around 42% in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt and possibly poised to form the first far-right-led administration since the second world war, Merz’s Christlich Demokratische Union (CDU), on around 22%, is under intense pressure.

However, when contacted again by the Guardian, a Reform spokesperson said this had been an administrative error and that they were still not accredited for the conference. Isaac broke the story that Farage had accepted an undeclared £5m gift from Christopher Harborne. Her reporting also revealed that a host of transactions involving Reform UK’s most senior figures and donations to the party caused bankers to report potential money-laundering concerns to the National Crime Agency.

The story has caused issues for Farage all summer and he has drastically reduced his time in front of the press. He also resigned as an MP over the furore, prompting a byelection which the other main parties boycotted, leaving Count Binface as his main opponent. Farage won, and was sworn back into parliament on Monday.

Geoghegan runs the Democracy for Sale newsletter on Substack and has written for the Guardian and the New York Times. He received the news he had been banned from the conference shortly after publishing a piece revealing negative comments the pro-Reform journalist Isabel Oakeshott allegedly made about Harborne. Geoghegan said: “Reform clearly wants press coverage but it doesn’t want the scrutiny and accountability that comes with it. Farage and co like to present themselves as the anti-establishment insurgents, but banning independent journalists like me from party conference isn’t anti-establishment. Crick said: “I can understand why the Reform high command might not want me talking to ordinary party members.” He published an unflattering biography of Farage in 2022, including details of a letter a teacher once sent to the head of Dulwich college when Farage was proposed as a prefect, complaining about his “publicly professed racist and neo-fascist views”.
