On the party’s apparent reinstatements and then U-turn, Crick said: “What cock-up merchants!”

A party spokesperson said: “Reform UK accepted 950 of about 1,000 media applications from a variety of outlets, including the entire Guardian lobby team.

Andy Burnham must face down unions over donation cap

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 17:04:19 GMT

It is no use promising to reform politics and return power to the people without addressing the power of the big beasts, writes Paul Sawbridge. Plus letters from Marcus Hallside and Martin Knott

So much for a new way of doing politics. Even before parliament had convened under his premiership, Andy Burnham had already stumbled at the first hurdle (Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donors, 26 August).

Despite widespread support for hard caps to political donations, and despite years of affirming support for such measures, a whisper of opposition from the union lobby has produced a screeching U-turn.

It is no use promising to return power to the people via devolution, employee ownership and so on, and then refusing to address the power of the big beasts of the politics of yesteryear. Come on, Andy! If you are to make any impact on reversing the appalling effects of Thatcherite neoliberalism, you are going to need to show more bottle than this. You should immediately support Stella Creasy’s amendment – and throw in a commitment to a national commission on electoral reform. Paul SawbridgeEaling, London

The GMB union’s opposition to a cap on political donations raises a question that goes beyond the immediate dispute: when does legitimate defence of an organisation’s interests become defence of a political system that gives that organisation disproportionate influence? Trade unions have a legitimate role in politics. But political finance should ultimately be governed by the democratic interests of citizens, not those of organisations. The same principle must apply to wealthy individuals and corporations.

There is a troubling historical precedent. In the 2010 Labour leadership election, the GMB was one of the unions that backed Ed Miliband against his brother, David. David led decisively among Labour MPs and party members, but Ed won overwhelmingly in the union section and ultimately became leader by just 50.65% to 49.35%. The unions did not single-handedly determine that result, but their mobilisation was crucial. It is therefore reasonable to ask whether the GMB has reflected on the consequences of using its organisational power to influence Labour’s political direction.

Ed Miliband’s leadership was followed by Labour’s defeat in 2015, the return of Conservative government and years of austerity. His defeat also formed part of the political sequence that culminated in the Brexit referendum. To say the unions “caused” these outcomes would be simplistic. But to pretend that their intervention had no consequences would be equally misleading.

The GMB argues that a cap on donations could damage Labour’s ability to raise funds from affiliated organisations. That is institutional self-interest. But it should not be confused with the national interest. Britain needs political finance rules that reduce the influence of money and organised interests, whoever they are. Marcus HallsideRadlett, Hertfordshire

I am in favour of both empowering unions and capping donations. The objectives of union donors are widely different to those of the mega-rich donors. While the latter seek self-enrichment, the unions’ only aim is to enable a society where workers’ rights are upheld and a fair wage is earned, and to increase employment rates. This fits perfectly with the aims of the Labour party: to support everyday working people and provide for those who cannot work. So I say: cap at around £1m to enable unions to donate and to curb the excessive influence of the mega-rich. Martin KnottEdinburgh

An autism or ADHD diagnosis without access to treatment is a hollow outcome

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 17:03:24 GMT

Helen Macdonald responds to a report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsman

The parliamentary and health service ombudsman’s findings are stark and sadly familiar (Autism and ADHD care complaints more than triple in five years in England, 26 August). A more than 200% rise in complaints, years-long waits, patients paying thousands of pounds for private care when the NHS fails them, and a system so complex that people are routinely denied rights they are legally entitled to – these are exactly the issues that the British Association for Behavioural and Cognitive Psychotherapies (BABCP) has been documenting and raising for years.

What the ombudsman’s report does not fully address is what happens once people are assessed and diagnosed. Too many people with ADHD and autism receive a diagnosis only to find that there is no evidence-based treatment pathway attached to it. Cognitive behavioural therapy is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence for the anxiety and depression that commonly accompany neurodevelopmental conditions, and in specific contexts for adults with ADHD itself. Yet workforce shortages mean that even where the clinical will exists, the capacity often does not. A diagnosis without access to appropriate treatment is a hollow outcome.

A final report by the clinical psychologist Prof Peter Fonagy is expected soon and will inform a new national approach. It must go beyond assessment waiting times and address the full pathway, from recognition to diagnosis, treatment and ongoing support. Closing the regulatory gap that the ombudsman identifies is important. Equally important is ensuring that the services people eventually reach are staffed by clinicians with the specialist training to deliver the care that neurodivergent people need. Helen MacdonaldSenior clinical adviser, BABCP

As the mother of a child with anaphylactic allergies, I am sympathetic to the terror that Lucy Pasha-Robinson describes (Food allergies when flying are no joke. That’s why nuts should be banned on planes, 27 August). Indeed, last summer I spent six hours compulsively cleaning on a demonstrably filthy flight. Flight crew handed out wipes to passengers “to clean your tray tables”, then proceeded to serve packets of cashews (my child’s anaphylactic nut) with drinks. My nerves were shredded by the time we arrived in Chicago.

However, I am firmly against the banning of nuts from the skies. Food bans do not improve compliance, and they create a false sense of security in patients.

Because my son’s most severe anaphylactic allergy is not nuts but lentils (which, like peanuts, can be airborne and serious from the tiniest quantities), we have had to learn to live with risk. Time and again, I note his allergies on intake forms, only to be blithely reassured that “we are a nut-free setting”, as if that constituted a proper allergy-protection policy. Instead, I am the helicopter parent boarding flights early with gloves and wipes, deep cleaning our entire row before we sit down.

My son knows not to accept food from others and to touch nothing on board until I give the all-clear; we pack meals, pillows and blankets for every flight; brief every flight crew on his allergies and the location of our EpiPens; and, from the age of three, practised administering Epi at least once a month. We will never travel fear-free, but we feel the fear and travel anyway. Alison SmithWorcester Park, London

Autumn is a wonderful season, but it’s even better in the bleak midwinter (Letters, 31 August). Andrew CarrollCastletimon, County Wicklow, Ireland

I used to resist the temptation to read any letter about nominative determinism. Now I just give in. Peter CaveIlkeston, Derbyshire

Is it not time to stop this correspondence?Roger BrakeShaftesbury, Dorset

Quidditch, Muggles, magic: new Harry Potter trailer gives full look at TV show

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 16:23:37 GMT

HBO’s extended trailer reveals more details of JK Rowling’s wizarding world coming to screens this Christmas

The second official trailer has been released for HBO’s forthcoming TV adaptation of Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone.

Starring newcomer Dominic McLaughlin in the lead role, the new trailer gives an extended look at life at Hogwarts and the challenges that Potter and the gang face in their first year at the school.

The newly released footage provides glimpses of well-known moments from the book and shows Potter using the invisibility cloak, playing quidditch and being confronted by Professor Snape.

The trailer follows an initial teaser unveiled this March, which gave a first look at the new eight-episode series based on JK Rowling’s first Potter book.

As well as McLaughlin as Potter, the series also features the British newcomers Alastair Stout and Arabella Stanton as Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger. The young actors were chosen after a lengthy casting search among British child actors aged nine to 11.

The series also features actors Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall, Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid and John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, the Hogwarts headmaster.

Luke Thallon will play Quirinus Quirrell, while Paul Whitehouse will appear as Argus Filch, Lox Pratt as Draco Malfoy, Johnny Flynn as his father, Lucius, Bel Powley as Petunia Dursley, Daniel Rigby as Vernon Dursley and Katherine Parkinson as Molly Weasley.

The series began its big-budget production in Hertfordshire, England, last July. The show is led by two Succession alums, writer Francesca Gardiner and director Mark Mylod, who will also direct some episodes.

Last month, Nicholas Hoult stepped back from a previously announced role in the show’s second season amid backlash from those opposed to Rowling’s views on trans rights. Kit Harington, the Game of Thrones actor, was announced as Hoult’s replacement to play Gilderoy Lockhart, Hogwarts’ defense against the dark arts teacher.

Previously, Lithgow called Rowling’s stance on trans rights “ironic and inexplicable”.

“It upsets me when people are vehemently opposed to me having anything to do with this,” he said. “But in Potter canon you see no trace of transphobic sensitivity. [Rowling] has written this meditation of kindness and acceptance. And Dumbledore is a beautiful role.”

Last month, Powley also commented on the issue. “I strongly disagree with JK Rowling’s views on gender,” she said to the Telegraph. “I think that the trans community deserve safety and dignity and respect and total acceptance.”

Rowling is involved in the HBO series in an advisory capacity as an executive producer.

The show will premiere at Christmas with each subsequent book adapted for further seasons.

Andy Burnham faces an impossible job. At least he’s got a secret weapon – Kemi Badenoch

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 16:17:32 GMT

Labour is up against a Tory party with a leader who can’t stop getting lost in her own sense of brilliance. And then there’s Andrew Griffith

Call it the gentlest of all reality checks. A quantum realignment in expectations. The faintest reminder to both Andy Burnham and Labour backbenchers that international bond markets are impervious to Manchester charm and positivity. Despite a summer of feelgood announcements from the government, there is no escaping the fact that the country is still up shit creek. It’s going to be a tough ride ahead. Nothing will come pain-free.

Still, a new prime minister has to learn to take the wins – however small – as they come along. In the wider scheme of things, a good prime minister’s questions means next to nothing: it’s nothing more than politics as performance. Yet it can set the tone and buy a prime minister some goodwill from MPs and the media. Plus, it’s a weekly event so you may as well be good at it.

Burnham can be very pleased with his first outing, even if it didn’t go totally as billed. We had been promised a more consensual politics. An end to point scoring. That lasted all of five minutes. After that, it was business as usual. Partly because that’s the way PMQs has always been set up, but mainly because Andy just couldn’t help himself.

It would have taken a will of iron to resist. Not least because Kemi Badenoch made it so easy for him. Not for the first time, Labour’s secret weapon is the Tory leader. She just can’t help herself from speaking without thinking, getting lost in her own sense of brilliance and failing to spot the traps she is setting for herself. Still, at least no one can call Kemi boring. Though it is quite hard to see why so many Tories seem to drink her Kool-Aid.

You could tell that Burnham was very nervous at the start. Understandably so. Twitchy. Not totally in command. PMQs is always an ordeal and never more so for a leader on whom so many Labour hopes have been pinned. Some of them Burnham has even pinned on himself.

“It’s good to be back at the dispatch box,” he began, before listing some of the Labour government’s achievements. Like the number of small boat crossings being at their lowest for years. The Tories barely looked up. It was almost as if they had never been that bothered about illegal immigration, and they certainly weren’t about to give Labour any credit. Opposition parties hate it when something goes well. There’s nothing that suits them better than a country in crisis. They never seem to realise that one day they might be called upon to sort it out.

Kemi’s opening gambit was flirtatious. Going out of her way to congratulate Andy on his stamina. Burnham merely nodded. A lot of people had said that to him. Then Kemi decided she had had enough sweet-talk. That was Burnham’s problem. Always promising the earth. Never daring to say no to anyone. Too desperate to be loved to be a good leader. So could he mention anything he had ever cut?

First the smile, then the reply. “Tax,” Burnham said. This was effectively game over for PMQs. Kemi had imagined a Keir Starmer-like evasion. A prime minister caught out. She had never dreamed of this. Andy spelled it out. He had removed VAT on electricity bills. He had cut business rates for pubs and hospitality venues. He didn’t choose to point out these cuts had been paid for by cutting a budget for digital ID that had never existed. Best to keep it simple.

Next Kemi turned to the bond markets. She seemed to think they had it in for Labour. Burnham kept it pleasant and polite. It was like this. The international bond markets didn’t have a special grudge against him. This wasn’t personal. They hadn’t been waiting for Tuesday’s statement, itching to put interest rates up.

This was a global problem. Other countries were also facing rising borrowing costs. And if Kemi really wanted to know where the blame lay, she could take a look at her own party’s 14 years of stagnant growth. It was the Tories who had trashed the economy. He was merely trying to pick up the pieces. He could also have blamed the Iran war and the spike in oil prices. A war for which Kemi had been initially enthusiastic. Her judgment is seldom the best.

Now Kemi sounded almost hurt. As if a promise had been broken. Burnham had said there would be no more point scoring, and here he was openly point scoring. I know, I know, said Andy unapologetically. He just couldn’t help himself. It was just too tempting. It made him feel good about himself to hear the laughs and support of his own backbenchers. PMQs wasn’t all about him. It was a team sport.

So while he was about it, Burnham had plenty more points to score. Kemi has yet to realise just how vulnerable she has made herself by appointing Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor. The man who co-authored Liz Truss’s mini-budget and was one of its most outspoken defenders.

For Labour this is an open goal and they are going to be kicking the ball into the net as often as possible. Kemi may be a woman who doesn’t believe in history. Who thinks each day is a surprising new beginning. But the country is still a long way from forgiving the Tory party for the lasting damage caused by 49 days of Tory chaos. So the self-harm is going to continue for a while.

After failing to rule out further tax rises and spending commitments, Burnham went back to his happy place. Good vibes, hope and positivity. All of which are enough to make this a comfortable first PMQs. But he will be more than aware that this is a half-hour bubble and that life will only get tougher outside it.

Though Andy appears to be a sucker for work. He spent the rest of the session offering meetings to virtually every MP. Soon his whole life will be one long meeting. Or a meeting to find out why a meeting was not necessary. Meetings to rule out further meetings. Still, I am sure he will enjoy his meeting with Samantha Niblett, whose stated mission has been to have a summer of sex. And to tell as many people as possible about it.

Not everything went Burnham’s way. A disgruntled Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the defence select committee, was extremely grumpy about the 3% promise. Or possibly not being asked to be a minister. Still, Andy looked happy enough when the speaker called time. The first PMQs was over and he was 1-0 up. Not that anyone was keeping the score. Much.

I thought I was too broken for sex. Here’s how I found pleasure again

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 16:00:28 GMT

I was forced to examine the idea of sexual pleasure after a tumor was removed from my spinal cord

Ten years ago, my right elbow started to hurt. The internet suggested I had tennis elbow, so I stopped playing tennis. Once the outer elbow pain moved inward, I changed my self-diagnosis to golfer’s elbow. I stopped lifting weights, competitive dragon-boating and bouldering.

For good measure, I consulted an occupational therapist about my nightly bullet-vibrator routine after reading that golfer’s elbow is common among construction workers who operate heavy-duty vibrating machinery. He listened closely and said he’d note VRI on my patient chart. I asked what VRI meant, eager to end my diagnostic journey. “Vibrator-related injury,” he responded. We busted out laughing.

After three years, weak hands and shaky legs had joined the elbow pain. None of the diagnoses I researched or received (a pinched ulnar nerve, tendinitis and thoracic outlet syndrome) fully explained my symptoms. Eventually, an MRI found a tumor growing inside my spinal cord. One surgeon estimated that without treatment, my body would undergo complete, permanent paralysis from the neck down within a year.

The surgery itself carried the same risk.

Against medical advice to schedule surgery immediately, I postponed it for five weeks. Even that was barely enough time for all my worry, denial, resentment, anger and end-of-life arrangements. Most importantly, this tumor confirmed that the pain I had suffered for years had never been my fault. I wanted to relish the hobbies and pleasures I’d abandoned in case I never experienced them again. Moreover, I’d already booked a snowboarding trip to Chamonix-Mont-Blanc, and my immigrant sensibilities would not let that money waste.

Dating also became urgent. Within moments of matching with Nicolas on an app, we were on the phone sharing belly laughs and hard truths. I told him about my diagnosis and flight to New York City that evening to prepare for surgery the following week. Hours later, we had our first date over a pot of tea inside my Seattle apartment. Nicolas neatened my favorite cardigan with an electric fabric shaver while I packed. We talked non-stop until my ride to the airport arrived. Our kiss goodbye lingered like we’d never say hello again.

When an unexpected job interview brought me right back to Seattle three days later, Nicolas asked me to be his girlfriend.

Surgery successfully removed my tumor. Days turned into three weeks in the hospital’s inpatient rehabilitation unit. By day, I was a patient, relearning how to walk and use my hands. By night, I pretended I was just a person on the phone with her boyfriend. Nicolas and I wove dreams about sailing together, sleeping underneath stars at sea. He promised I’d be able to walk again, and when we aged, I’d be sitting on his lap in his wheelchair.

Everything hurt. Many nights, I wailed with regret that Nicolas and I had not had sex before my body changed. Did I lose the chance to enjoy his touch? Was my body now too broken to please him? Would numbness make it too difficult – not worth the effort – for him to please me? My sisters called him Santa, short for Saint Nick. And who but a saint could desire me as my desirability faded?

There’s a lot of talk about sex these days, namely how little of it we’re having. I too had deprioritized sex and dating, mostly because boyfriends are embarrassing and men ain’t shit. But lately I have found myself re-examining my sex life after surgery. How has medical trauma and disability changed my relationship to sex and pleasure?

In the wake of my diagnosis, I experienced first-hand how loved ones and even doctors can dismiss the difference between being alive and feeling alive. Medically, not dying is the goal. It is a task so big that we are often too grateful, exhausted, unprepared or ill-supported to think about what’s next. If we’re lucky enough to survive, pleasure is simply a trivial extra.

I had enjoyed a healthy, active sex life before surgery and thought working back towards that would prove cancer and disability hadn’t changed me. That I was more than just a patient.

But the reality was that my spinal cord injury and surgery had an impact. Dr Lisa Ruppert, a physiatrist and spinal cord injury specialist who treats cancer patients and survivors at the Memorial Sloan Kettering cancer center, helped me understand the sensory disorders that immediately followed surgery: temperature dysregulation, heightened and dulled sensitivity to touch, bladder and bowel incontinence and sexual dysfunction. I told her my concerns about having sex again, which is common for people living with spinal cord injuries.

We started with some basics. Ruppert suggested strategies to trigger arousal: keep the lights on for visual stimulation, stay on top of the sheets to mitigate sensory overload and discover whether and where my erogenous zones had shifted.

“For someone with spinal cord involvement, we have to think about what’s still working and what’s not,” said Ruppert when I spoke to her recently. “You and I had a lot of conversations about how it’s going to feel, what still feels good, what doesn’t. That also depends on a patient’s willingness to explore their own body.”

Able-bodied people don’t often think about how their bodies work. Not until my spinal cord injury did I ever consider the mechanics of sexual pleasure.

Sexual arousal is more complicated than just touch and response, said Ruppert. There are two pathways: reflexogenic and psychogenic. Reflexogenic arousal is triggered by “touch stimulus” to the genitals. That information travels to the spinal cord and causes vaginal lubrication or penile erection. Psychogenic arousal, on the other hand, does not necessarily require physical contact. It’s stimulated by sexual thoughts, fantasies, emotions and other inputs – like what you might see, hear and smell.

I remember passing Ruppert’s instructions on to Nicolas, whose knowledge of my body became as significant as my patient chart. I loved our sensory games, but started treating them like rehab. Dates with Nicolas slotted into my calendar alongside weekly physical therapy, occupational therapy, aqua therapy and talk therapy sessions. After we broke up, I resigned myself to a medicalized, dissociative relationship with my body, believing sex just wasn’t for me any more.

“Sex after surgery was a project,” I admitted during an interview with Rachel Smith, a licensed marriage and family therapist who specializes in sex therapy. Most of Smith’s clients find her when their sex lives are disrupted by critical life transitions. I have a master’s degree and career in public health, and it wasn’t until I was researching this piece that I learned sex therapy could have been part of my post-operative care.

“But what if pleasure became an exploration?” Smith offered. “Something to be discovered versus something to work on.”

I noted my use of the word “project”, which held associations of achievement, work and productivity, a stubborn tenet of millennial hustle culture. I also often described my experience within the US healthcare system as a project – its maze-like inefficiencies, high cost and bureaucracy typically require patients to become both the project and the project manager.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

My goal of rehabilitating my body so it could function as it did before disability was narrow and unfair. Sex only mattered if it helped my body work. “I see this in a lot of my clients, especially Bipoc children of immigrants,” said Gabriela Fullon, a licensed mental health counselor. “Enjoyment must be deserved. It is only something you are allowed to have if you work your ass off for it.”

These capitalistic norms particularly do not permit pleasure for disabled people. “The idea is that our lives should be focused on treatment, cure and management of disability – above all else,” said Sami Schalk, PhD, a disability and gender studies scholar and author of Black Disability Politics. “That pleasure only comes into our lives when it is therapeutic. That pleasure must somehow move you towards able-bodiness or able-mindedness in some way. But can’t we just make art for the sake of making art? … Can’t we fuck to fuck?”

In theory, absolutely. But in practice, did I?

I’m not sure I’ve completely forgiven my body for growing something that hurt me. I punished my body into repair, which is not the same as healing. I spent years believing the more embodied, sensual version of myself had to die as the price for survival.

I am not alone.

Pleasure is not recognized as important within the US healthcare system, which prioritizes reproductive sexual function. This makes accessing sexual healthcare especially challenging for disabled people, cancer patients and survivors, postpartum parents and others whose bodies start behaving in unexpected and inconvenient ways.

“There is no standard sexual health curriculum in medical schools,” said Sonjia Kenya, PhD, sexologist and professor at the University of Miami school of medicine. This means that physicians like Ruppert or providers like Smith, Fullon and Kenya are not default care options. Their open, informed and non-judgmental approach to sex are only available to patients who know enough to seek them out. In a 2013 survey of OB-GYNs, only 29% reported asking patients about sexual satisfaction. If they don’t ask, who does?

“The system is supportive of men’s sexual functioning,” Kenya said, reminding me that more than 80% of women do not experience orgasm through penetration alone. Conversely, “insurance won’t even cover menstrual supplies”.

Even the most competent healthcare providers are constrained by an immoral (my word), fragmented (Kenya’s word) healthcare system. Patient access to services, including sex therapy, largely depends on insurance reimbursement and billing: “Is it general medicine? Is it psychology? Do you need a diagnosis before you can get treatment?” said Kenya.

These providers want change. Ruppert helps medical residents to practice talking with patients about sex. Kenya said more physicians should expand their referral networks to include providers who can better address sexual health needs. But in the meantime, patients must self-advocate.

If you don’t know how to address concerns about sexual pleasure, Kenya suggests that if or when a provider asks whether you are sexually active: “You can say: ‘I do not enjoy sex.’ That should encourage the provider to go a little deeper and ask the next question, or refer you to someone else.”

Support for our sexual health also exists outside a doctor’s office. As Schalk reminded me, those “institutions are not focused on our pleasure. They are focused on activities of daily living and survival in order for you to be a productive citizen.”

So we must reckon with our relationship to sex ourselves. As a starting place, Fullon suggested some simple curiosity, saying: “What about pleasure feels scary? Why? How do you feel about that? Do you want it to shift?” Instead of asking myself how to have sex again, I began asking myself why. Why was sex important to me? Who and what is sexual pleasure for?

I sought out books and podcasts about disability, and community with other disabled women of color who affirmed that my post-operative struggles with sex and feelings of undesirability were normal. I began to question harmful narratives, like why women are taught to tolerate painful sex and that our pain is necessary for someone else’s pleasure. They are so normal that when women experience these things, we feel we are the ones doing something wrong.

My experience with disability actually required me to understand my pain, not ignore it. My spinal cord injury is invisible to others now; I no longer need a wheelchair or a cane. But this intimate, informed relationship with my body has made me more confident in communicating what I need.

For example, I shared details about my spinal cord injury with the last guy I dated. During sex, I worried that my needs would offend him, and I felt comfortable enough to share those anxieties. “There is nothing about how your body responds to me that makes me question whether we’re having a good time,” he said. Prioritizing intimacy over intercourse made sex more pleasurable.

Audre Lorde presented her groundbreaking essay Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power, in 1978, the year she received her first cancer diagnosis. That Lorde’s cancer coincided with her scholarship on the erotic challenged me to rethink pleasure for pleasure’s sake. “[The erotic] is an internal sense of satisfaction to which, once we have experienced it, we know we can aspire,” she wrote. “For having experienced the fullness of this depth of feeling and recognizing its power, in honor and self-respect we can require no less of ourselves.”

The erotic teaches us that we deserve, and must fight for, deep joy and satisfaction in every part of our lives. Pleasure is political, and provides the vitality I need as a disabled woman of color to believe I can do more than survive.

I don’t accept a culture that ignores women’s sexual pleasure or believes disabled people shouldn’t have it at all. A pleasure-filled life can be lived with or without sex, with or without a partner, and alongside disability and pain. Schalk suggests keeping a pleasure journal as a way to “comfort and care for our bodies, even in the midst of hard moments”. I took her advice.

This summer, I did not find the fling I hoped for, but no matter. I went outside, blasting Beyoncé down the freeway – as she sings in Church Girl, “I’m gon’ let go of this body, I’m gonna love on me.” I practiced the choreography from Janet Jackson’s Pleasure Principle music video in the park. There I heard Schalk’s words echo in my mind: “Pleasure is what brings us back to ourselves.”

Jodi-Ann Burey is a writer, speaker and author of Authentic: The Myth of Bringing Your Full Self to Work

Maro Itoje ready to ‘come back better’ for England after taking mini sabbatical

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 16:00:28 GMT

Itoje rested for Nations Championship games in July

Captain has had a rare full pre-season with Saracens

Maro Itoje says it felt “very weird” watching England play from afar this summer but he believes more top players should consider taking a break to prolong their careers. The British & Irish Lions captain was rested for his country’s three Nations Championship games in July and is now feeling the benefits of “taking a breath” after an intense year on and off the field.

In addition to the burden of leadership for club and country, Itoje also lost his mother last year and, with the 2027 World Cup looming, the national coach, Steve Borthwick, offered his captain the chance of a mini-sabbatical. He has emerged fit, healthy and mentally rested for the season ahead having enjoyed his first full club pre-season at Saracens since 2014.

“I don’t regret it at all,” Itoje said at the Prem media launch at Twickenham. “In some respects it was a little bit weird being away from the team, especially whilst games were going on. But at the same time I felt like it was the right thing to do. Mentally it was a busy year, both personally and professionally, so it was nice to have a bit of time to take a breath.”

Coincidentally, Itoje bumped into the England squad at Heathrow airport on the day they were returning from the South African leg of their tour but otherwise he did his best to keep his distance, even choosing not to watch the games live to avoid getting too emotionally involved. “When you watch a game live, you’re in every nook and cranny, every tackle. But that also probably has a hidden emotional kind of weight. I felt it would have defeated the purpose of what I was trying to achieve.”

Itoje, who turns 32 next month, would certainly recommend a break to other leading players as and when the chance arises, with South Africa and New Zealand having long since pursued a policy of allowing their top stars to sign contracts in Japan. “It is very much case by case but I think that, for players who have the blessing to be at the top of the game for a period of time, a proactive approach like this one works.

“I was taken aback initially because it just never entered my mind. It was never something that I thought was an option … I kind of had it in my mind that ‘this is the way the cookie crumbles’ and you just have to power through. [But] the more I thought about it, the more I kind of agreed with it. If I was not going to do it then I’m not sure when the next window would have been.”

The next challenge is to hit the ground running when the Prem season kicks off this month before a busy November. England are scheduled to play four Tests on successive weekends, starting with a game against Australia on 8 November, and a refreshed Itoje will be keen to make an immediate impact.

“I hope the break is giving me what’s necessary for me to come back better. Since I’ve been involved with England, I’ve pretty much been involved in every campaign. Saracens for a large period of that time were the top team in Europe, so we’re going deep into Europe and deep in the Premiership. And that has also helped with Lions tours and selections.

“I’ve been very fortunate to have had what I’ve had but the cost of that, I guess, is that you don’t tend to have a break. Apart from missing training today, I’ve had a full pre-season [with Saracens] to work on myself and my body and be around the team, and I think that’s been a good thing.”

Itoje will soon have added responsibilities on his plate with his wife, Mimi, who is pregnant with the couple’s first child – but on the England front he says he was encouraged by what he saw towards the end of England’s summer Tests under the leadership of his Saracens teammate Jamie George. “I was delighted with the last two results,” he said.

“Obviously the Fiji game was a big win and in the Argentina game they showed a lot of character away from home. The challenge and opportunity for us now is to build on that to go forward.”

Russian airspace becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, Zelenskyy says

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 15:52:05 GMT

Ukraine president says aviation industry needs to take account of growing number of Ukrainian drones in Russia

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has declared that Russia’s airspace is becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, as Vladimir Putin promised to increase strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities in the run-up to winter.

The Ukrainian president said there was no intention to directly threaten civilian flights, but the growing number of attack drones being flown into Russia by Ukraine would have to be “taken into account” by the aviation industry.

“We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelenskyy said in a statement.

Ukraine’s foreign secretary, Andrii Sybiha, said Kyiv had notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that “Russian airspace is not safe for civilian aviation” because of increased military activity.

A rapid escalation of Ukrainian military capability in the past few months has allowed Ukraine’s forces to strike at targets around Moscow, St Petersburg and other locations deep inside Russia.

Reliable figures for the number of drone flights are hard to obtain but Ukraine is already capable of launching a few hundred a day, and military sources say the country is chasing a target of 1,000 drones in an effort to hurt Russia’s economy.

Justin Bronk, an aviation analyst at the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, said he believed Ukraine could force “periodic closures of Russian airports on a semi-regular basis” by relying on an element of surprise.

It could do so by flying small waves of drones at short notice, though trying to close an airport permanently would be difficult, he said, because a sustained attack would become predictable and easier for air-defence systems to halt.

Ukraine’s commercial airspace has been closed since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 because Russia has been able to strike targets throughout the country, making airports unsafe for civilians.

This year, Ukraine began bombing oil refineries and warehouses near Moscow and St Petersburg, as well as hitting military and industrial sites at ranges in excess of 2,000km (1,250 miles) from its border.

Concerns linger about the safety of civilian aviation in the war zone. A Malaysian Airlines plane flying over eastern Ukraine in July 2014 was shot down by Russian separatists operating a surface-to-air missile launcher. All 298 people onboard were killed.

Putin described Zelenskyy’s remarks as “state terrorism”, saying: “Negotiations are not conducted with terrorists.”

Giving one of his most detailed updates on the war, the Russian leader told a news conference that Moscow was preparing to increase its bombing of Ukrainian energy facilities this winter, aiming to knock out heating and electricity supplies.

“The Russian armed forces have been ordered to prepare and carry out mass strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. They are striking us, and they will get a response,” Putin told reporters after a two-day summit in Kyrgyzstan. “I’m not saying we’ll collapse the economy there, but it’s a serious challenge for them.”

Asked whether Russia would strike British military facilities in the UK that produced weapons for Ukraine, Putin sidestepped the question, saying: “That’s a military secret.”

Russia earlier accused the UK of “escalation” and threatened “consequences” after reports that British-made drones were used by Ukraine in long-range strikes deep inside its territory.

Putin sought to stress that Russian forces retained the initiative on the battlefield in Ukraine, despite Moscow’s slowing progress. He appeared to push back against western intelligence reports suggesting he was being given an overly optimistic picture of the war, saying he relied on numerous sources of information that together provided him with an “objective assessment” of the battlefield.

Russia’s sluggish advance on the battlefield has fuelled speculation that the Kremlin could resort to another round of mobilisation, the first since Putin called up about 300,000 reservists in September 2022.

Zelenskyy and western officials have said Moscow could be preparing such a move, though its diplomats do not consider it a certainty. Putin dismissed the prospect as “nonsense”.

Also on Wednesday, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said a drone attack on Leipzig airport marked a new escalation by Russia, and that itfitted a broader pattern of “repeated incursions in our airspace, drones that paralyse our airports, interference with our critical infrastructure”.

The German government said on Tuesday that Russia was responsible for a drone laden with explosives which was discovered at Leipzig airport last month near a Ukrainian plane used to transport weapons.

Von der Leyen said: “Europeans are faced with the hard truth that this is the new normal. We have to step up, and that means being ready to respond to Russia’s recklessness faster and better.”

The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, told reporters Russia had grown “increasingly reckless” and there had been an increase “in malign activities targeting our territory directly”.

The EU is drawing up further sanctions against Russia targeting about 1,600 companies and individuals. Poland’s foreign minister, Radek Sikorski, said the bloc should pass these sanctions in response to the Leipzig attack and others. “Hybrid war is not just nuisance on the internet,” he said, speaking on the sidelines of a meeting with his European counterparts.

“Hybrid war means assassination squads, it means arsonists, it means blowing up moving trains, like in Poland, it means breaches of airspace with drones and cruise missiles. We need to convince Putin that such actions are not for free.”

The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the Leipzig attacks had the “hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism”, adding that Brussels had summoned Russia’s ambassador to the bloc.

What did I learn in the kitchen this week? The longer it takes to cook, the less you want to eat it

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 15:46:26 GMT

After grilling, skinning, chopping and stirring, stirring, stirring, my feelings towards my favourite Balkan relish, ajvar, changed. Those Macedonian nans must be made of girders

If you ever meet someone from North Macedonia and find yourself short of conversation, then one word will get things going nicely. That word is ajvar. Pronounce it “Ivor”, as in The Engine – not quite right but it’ll do. Depending on who you ask, ajvar is a condiment, spread, sauce or relish. It’s made – also depending on who you ask – with red peppers and aubergine. You can eat it with meat, cheese, fish, vegetables, on toast or, using a large spoon, straight from the jar.

I was accompanying a 13-year-old called Ilijana as she played the British chess grandmaster Nigel Short. This was on the waterfront in Split, Croatia. Long story. All you need to know is that my contribution to the contest was zero. All I could do was try to bond with her somehow, by finding some area of common ground. So I said the magic word: ajvar! This was the conversational equivalent of a chess move – something with a knight perhaps? – which she didn’t see coming. It worked a treat. Suddenly she was all smiles, telling me how her grandma’s ajvar was the best in the world.

Ajvar is a Balkan thing, but it is especially common in North Macedonia due, I assume, to an abundance of red peppers there, ripening nicely even as we spoke. Ilijana was one of a couple of dozen young players taking on Mr Short. As he made his way around the other boards I quizzed her about ratios of peppers to aubergines, the right oil to use, the cooking process and so on. She seemed happier discussing this than trying to answer my daft questions about the rudiments of chess tactics. My dad used to say that in chess you need to be thinking five moves ahead, whereas he was always five moves behind. Same. But on matters concerning ajvar, I was now right up to speed.

By the time I got back from Croatia, I was champing at the bit to make some of my own. My junior chess friend suggested 5kg of peppers was about right for a batch. Further research made it clear that only pointy peppers would do. The bloke in the world foods shop in Swansea registered no surprise, or indeed interest, at the quantity I was after. With a kilo of aubergines added to the box, I was in business.

First came the charcoal grilling of the vegetables. My neighbours have one of those fancy Egg barbecues which they very kindly got going for me. Aware of the fire risk, I was relieved the rain was steady. It took me about two hours to blacken all the skins. I found the first 10 minutes of the process quite enjoyable. The last hour and 50 minutes, less so. My fingers were singed and all the tong-wielding had my right arm begging for mercy. Those Macedonian nans must be made of girders.

Then everything had to be skinned, which took longer than I might have hoped. Then drained overnight. Then chopped up, and cooked down, while slowly adding sunflower oil and salt and stirring, stirring, stirring for three hours or more. During this period, as the molten lava spat blobs of fire at me, my feelings for ajvar went from strong love to something approximating dislike. The longer you cook something, the less you end up wanting to eat it. I cooled it and put it in sterilised jars, marvelling at how a box of peppers I could barely carry had ended up filling only four jars. Exhausted, I went to bed, but all I could see on the inside of my eyelids was a cauldron of seething red stuff.

Day three, without relish, I tried my relish. It was quite good, but food and drink from your travels never tastes quite the same at home. I hope to rediscover my love for ajvar soon. I’ve a fair amount to get through.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

A newborn baby girl died from multiple stab wounds before she was found on top of a washing machine in an outhouse in Sheffield, a court has heard.

Two men and two women appeared in court on Wednesday charged with the murder of the newborn, named only as Baby S. She was found with 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings when police were called to a property in the Wincobank area of the city on Sunday.

Andrea Skopova, 20, and Peter Horvath Jr, 19, have been charged with the baby’s murder, as have Horvath Jnr’s parents, Peter Horvath Sr, 38, and Nina Horvathova, 37.

The four, all from Slovakia, are additionally charged with causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.

Police were called to a property in Holywell Heights on Sunday morning after reports of concern for the safety of an infant. The prosecutor Luke Hopkinson told the court that Baby S was found wrapped in a towel in a blue bag in an outbuilding at an address in Holywell Heights.

A 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons due to her age, has been charged with perverting the course of justice. The girl sobbed in the dock as representations were made about whether she should be released on bail.

The district judge Tim Spruce decided she should be remanded in youth custody until Thursday, when she will appear at crown court with the other defendants. The four adults were all remanded in custody following the short hearing on Wednesday.

Two women, 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remain on bail.

DCI Tom Woodward, of South Yorkshire police, said: “This is a significant step in our investigation into the tragic circumstances that resulted in the death of this baby girl. I would like to thank our communities, who I know will have been deeply impacted by this traumatic incident, for supporting us as we work through this intricate investigation.

“We would ask the public to avoid speculating and posting information online about this case while the legal process takes it course. Protecting the integrity of the criminal justice process is crucial to us securing justice for this little girl.”

Bouquets of flowers had been left by a police cordon near the property in Holywell Heights on Wednesday.

Uber drivers launch European class action over ‘soulless’ and ‘scary’ AI algorithm

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 15:37:26 GMT

Landmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earnings

Uber drivers have launched a landmark legal action against the ride-hailing company claiming they live in “constant fear” of a “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs.

Drivers from the UK, the Netherlands and other countries have joined the compensation claim that could run into billions of dollars. It alleges an AI-powered pay-setting system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings.

The claim has been filed at Amsterdam’s district court, where the $150bn (£111bn) San Francisco tech company has its European HQ. It is the first collective legal move of its kind, according to the European Trade Union Confederation.

The case centres on an opaque “black box” algorithm fed on information about drivers, which sets a personalised rate for each ride. Drivers fear it pushes down fares to the minimum they are willing to accept.

Drivers have told the Guardian the algorithm has offered the same job to different people at different pay rates and offers them less for a return journey after a long trip because it calculates they will not want to come home empty.

“It is like someone watching you all the time and knowing about your weakness – the boss is the algorithm,” said Mohammed Shirwa, a 41-year-old Uber driver in Rotterdam. “All the time the algorithm is learning about you and what you are willing to accept. So the prices go low but you are stuck. It knows you need the job.”

Kola Oba, who calls the algorithm “soulless”, was taking a break in Tottenham, north London, with another driver when they were offered the same job.

The other driver was offered £27 and Oba was offered £23. The pair suspected it was because Oba, 48, had taken several cheap jobs and the AI assumed he would accept a lower price. Uber has previously said such discrepancies were down to other features of its system including GPS, surge pricing, promotions and testing.

“It’s scary – they have all my information and they are using it against my own wellbeing,” Oba said. “It defines how much I earn, how long I have to work, my time with my family, my resting time.”

AI models take an increasing role in assigning work to humans by using their rapidly increasing power to learn about a business’s needs and staff behaviour and then acting as a “synthetic manager”.

The Dutch data protection authority fined ⁠Uber €825m (£708m) last month for deactivating driver ⁠accounts through automated systems without ​adequate notice. Uber said it would appeal. The company is also planning to roll out driverless cars in European cities from London to Zagreb, initially with human supervisions.

The legal case is being led by the Worker Info Exchange, a campaign group whose founder, James Farrar, secured a UK supreme court ruling that Uber drivers should have worker rights.

Relating to about 241,000 drivers across the EU and the UK, the claim alleges that Uber has unlawfully used automated decision-making, including profiling, in dynamically setting pay and allocating work.

The lawsuit, which also claims the company unlawfully used driver data to train its AI models, is seeking damages for affected drivers and an injunction to halt the conduct which it claims breaches GDPR data regulations.

The drivers claim Uber has operated dynamic pay-setting in the UK since 2023, pushing down their annual incomes by about £5,000. The system was introduced in the Netherlands this year.

Uber’s chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi, said in 2023: “I think that what we can do better is targeting of different trips to different drivers based on their preferences or based on behavioural patterns that they’re showing us.”

Uber said it did not adjust the price offered for a trip based on an individual driver’s behaviour and that a history of accepting or rejecting trips was not used to personalise pay offers. Instead, it said, dynamic pricing allowed it to increase pay on less attractive trips, boosting a driver’s earning potential.

“While we haven’t seen the claim yet, we categorically reject the allegations,” an Uber spokesperson said. “The Uber app uses real-time information about the trip such as journey, duration and destination to calculate fares.

“Drivers see their earnings and where a trip is going before they decide whether to accept it. The vast majority of total fares continue to go where they belong: into drivers’ pockets, and the percentage that Uber keeps from fares has remained relatively flat.”

A 2025 study by academics at the University of Oxford, which Uber said relied on incomplete and selective data, found there had been substantial cuts in driver earnings after the “dynamic” algorithm was introduced.

Farrar said: “It’s bad enough that Uber’s dynamic pay algorithms have squeezed driver pay for years now but the intrusive and underhanded way in which Uber uses its technology to monitor and influence drivers’ behaviour is an affront to their dignity as workers and as human beings.”

Anton Ekker, a Dutch lawyer leading the case, said: “A computer algorithm should not independently make decisions that strip individuals of their livelihood. Like so many other online platforms, it should be held accountable for the large-scale exploitation of vulnerabilities of European citizens.”

Premier League transfer talking points: three things we learned from the data

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 15:29:31 GMT

After record spending in the transfer market, England’s top clubs have widened the gap to their European counterparts

Premier League clubs have invested more than £3.4bn in players this summer, an increase of 11.9% on last year. There are three aspects of this enormous spending worthy of closer scrutiny.

Premier League clubs are spending less on players in the peak 24-27 age band even though those players are increasingly the core of their selections.

As recently as 2021-22, 40% of minutes were taken by players at least 28 years old at the start of the season. That proportion has dropped each year, reaching 26.6% in 2025-26. The reliance on veterans has declined. The bulk of their lost minutes went to players aged between 24 and 27, which is now the dominant age band.

The spend on that key demographic has fallen by 23% since last summer though. Without Manchester City signing the 25-year-old Enzo Fernández for a British transfer record-equalling £125m shortly before the window closed, the drop would have been even greater.

Younger players account for some of the shortfall but a surprisingly high slice of it has gone towards older footballers. The Premier League has invested £323.3m in players aged at least 28, only around £50m shy of the outlay on this age range in the previous three summers combined (£370.5m). Their proportion of the total has not been as high for four years.

How much this increased spending on veterans affects the playing time figures depends in part on the selection decisions of Mikel Arteta. Arsenal signed two 28-year-olds for a combined £126m: Bruno Guimarães (£75m) and Ezri Konsa (£51m). Transfermarkt considers them to be the most expensive central midfielder and centre-back respectively aged over 27 in history.

The three most expensive Premier League signings of the summer before Fernández – Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson and Bradley Barcola – were 23 when their deals were completed. With only slightly less spent collectively on footballers who are 22, clubs have gone hard for players on the verge of entering their peak years rather than those in them.

Perhaps the most notable aspect of transfer spending this summer is how much of it has remained within English football. Fourteen of the 19 signings that cost Premier League clubs at least £50m were made from within the division or from relegated West Ham. Where 30.2% of spending remained in the Premier League in summer 2022, the figure hit 39.3% this year.

after newsletter promotion

With the combined outlay growing by almost £1.5bn in that period, what appears a relatively small percentage shift becomes a significant figure in the accounts. The squad cost ratio rules are unlikely to stem this flow either, because clubs will be happy to sell for inflated fees that can almost only come from within the division.

Barcola was the oldest of the five costliest signings from overseas, with Matias Fernandez-Pardo and Jérémy Jacquet (aged 21), Johan Manzambi (aged 20) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (aged 18) completing the set. The Premier League is able to retain its top stars, its clubs exchanging them among themselves, while having the funds to hoover up the most exciting young talent from elsewhere.

Squad-building trends may be evolving in the Premier League, but the money is here and a significant portion of it is not going anywhere else. English football is starting to become an enclosed ecosystem.

Very few clubs across Europe come close to competing financially. The Premier League features a match this weekend between the top two teams in Europe for net spend and it isn’t Arsenal v Chelsea. Liverpool’s trip to Ipswich takes the honour.

The promoted sides have invested enormous sums to try to be competitive. They have all played League One football within the previous eight seasons, yet Real Madrid are the only club from another country with a higher net spend than Hull or Coventry.

The cream of the Premier League crop can probably only move within England. The transfer fee for Rogers (£117m) or Anderson (£116m) was above the net spend of 75 of the 76 top-flight clubs in France, Germany, Italy and Spain. Milan narrowly spent more than the cost of Sandro Tonali (£92.5m) net, but no other side beyond Madrid from mainland Europe did. Most non-English sides would have to have a clearout of talent to raise funds for a single elite player from the Premier League, which isn’t practical.

This financial dominance can be seen in continental competitions. Five English clubs have featured in the past eight Champions League finals, as many teams as the rest of Europe has provided in that time. The Premier League has supplied three of the past four Europa League finalists and three of the past four Conference League winners. This is unlikely to change when relegation favourites in England can outspend all but the very richest clubs overseas.

I was once ashamed to admit I’d been strangled nonconsensually during sex. Now I’m speaking up to save women’s lives

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 15:00:28 GMT

Young men are being taught that acts with the potential to kill are erotic. The Albanese government must urgently regulate big tech and criminalise pornography depicting strangulation

Last week, a 16-year-old girl was found unresponsive in a home on Sydney’s northern beaches. She was airlifted to hospital and died two days later. New South Wales police are investigating her death as the result of a sexual strangulation act. Sources told the ABC the deceased may have experienced a seizure following asphyxiation, and that officers were told the sex was consensual.

While that investigation has yet to run its course, speaking generally, strangulation during sex is not a new phenomenon or conversation. Just a few years ago it was relatively taboo to criticise this normalisation of violence in sex – it was often framed as “anti-kink” to raise concern about this dangerous act that is increasingly depicted in mainstream pornography.

In 2024, Australian research affirmed the prevalence of sexual strangulation. The Archives of Sexual Behaviour published data revealing that 57% of Australians aged 18 to 35 had been strangled at least once during sex, and 51% said they had strangled a sexual partner.

Not only are reports of this act increasing, so are the reports of health impacts. Denele Crozier, the CEO of Women’s Health NSW, stated that since 2023 there had been a 123% increase in women presenting with concerns of a possible brain injury linked to strangulation.

I was previously ashamed to share my own experiences of being strangled during sex nonconsensually. Despite being an outspoken, progressive woman, I froze up and dissociated. Afterwards, I remember questioning whether my response was one of being in shock and afraid for my safety, or if I felt “prudish” if I spoke up and as if I’d be ruining the mood. For a long time, I was embarrassed to admit that while I intellectually knew something wasn’t right, I still failed to call it out in a moment of uncertainty.

That is exactly the concern I have for so many women who may be experiencing sexual strangulation. Affirmative consent is incredibly hard to achieve in these contexts; sexual strangulation is now commonplace and we are not equipped with the sophisticated sex education to match.

In 2022, consent advocate Chanel Contos wrote about this: “Another US study found that 58% of female college students have been choked during sex, further suggesting that this ‘kink’ is becoming increasingly common in younger age demographics. This study found that while many women enjoyed choking, others did it largely to please their sexual partner. This is the real kicker. The problem here is not only that women are being choked during sex without giving consent, but that a lot of the time they are ‘consenting’ not because they derive their own sexual pleasure from it, but because they think it turns the guy on.”

Violence against women and girls has been normalised to such an extent that pornography is convincing us it is normal to be strangled during intimacy, and that we are supposed to like it. I appreciate that messages from leaders like “talk to your kids” are made in good faith, but conversation cannot combat the nature and influence of sex content depicting violence as a standard part of sexual intercourse. We are teaching young men that perpetrating violent acts that have the potential to kill are erotic, and we are teaching women to endure having their lives threatened under the guise of pleasure.

There are people who engage with control of breath as part of particular kinks, but even in acknowledging these consensual engagements, it is important to reiterate that there is no safe way to engage in strangulation.

In response to this expanding dialogue, the social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, has shown her support for Australia to adopt legislation that was introduced to the UK in 2025, making it a criminal offence to possess or publish pornography depicting suffocation or strangulation. I want to add my voice to the many calling for the Albanese government to legislate this imminently.

The government is also, rightly, considering a second significant piece of reform proposed by Contos and her organisation Teach Us Consent. Contos has been campaigning for the government’s digital duty of care legislative drafting to adopt their “Fix Our Feeds” pitch, regulating big tech companies to ensure algorithms are an opt-in feature. This would introduce a consent-based model that allows users to have more control over the information these platforms are serving us, reducing the extremist material that so many are exposed to.

Our government has established that they are willing to take on the regulation of big tech. Australia was the first country in the world to legislate a social media ban for under-16s. We know we have the capability; now it’s time to introduce something that would actually be effective – and give power back to individual users.

These would be two significant steps from the government, after last week’s national cabinet meeting where the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, discussed violence against women and children with state and territory leaders. The subsequent announcements of frameworks and reviews were weak. We need politicians to meet the moment. The safety of women and girls depends on tangible action, now.

Hannah Ferguson is the chief executive officer of Cheek Media Co and is running as an independent candidate in the federal seat of Grayndler

The Eyes Wide Shut conspiracy theory: did someone cut a crucial 20 minutes from Kubrick’s final movie?

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 14:58:00 GMT

For years some have claimed a key part of the thriller was excised after the director’s sudden death – and that it provided clues to the real-life behaviour of rich predators. Now, his daughter has spoken out

Name: The Eyes Wide Shut conspiracy

Age: The erotic psychological thriller Eyes Wide Shut starring Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman (married at the time, though that isn’t so important now) was released in 1999.

Stanley Kubrick, no? yes. It was the great film-maker’s final movie. He died of a heart attack just days after screening his final cut to Warner Bros. His sudden death is what started it all.

Started all of what? The conspiracies.

Oooh, go on. OK, so there are rumours that the studio cut 20 minutes of the film after his death, including an alternative ending.

Why would they do that? It was too dark apparently, even by Kubrick’s standards. The theory goes that in Kubrick’s original, Cruise and Kidman’s characters sacrificed their own daughter to a child sexual abuse ring.

Perhaps it was a premonition of the Pizzagate theory? Make that Jeffrey Epstein.

Seriously? That’s what they say.

That’s what who say? There was an episode of Joe Rogan’s podcast a couple of years ago in which the screenwriter Roger Avary said the film had been cut.

Was Avary involved in the making of the film? No, but on Rogan’s podcast he claimed that “as a student of Kubrick” he noticed parts of the film Kubrick wouldn’t have done himself (scenes the director would have trimmed, a “missing” narration, among other things). So it looked to Avary as if EWS had been cut after Kubrick’s death.

And those comments helped fuel the rumours that Kubrick may have known about Epstein’s crimes, or possibly some other cult involving the global elite? Precisely. It doesn’t help that Kubrick was no stranger to conspiracy theories. It’s claimed that he staged the first moon landing then alluded to it surreptitiously in The Shining.

Of course. Back to EWS though. What do people who actually worked on the film say? Nigel Galt, the movie’s editor, said in an interview last year that nothing was cut. And now Vivian Kubrick, Stanley’s daughter, has weighed in. She worked with him on several films.

And Vivian says? It’s a long X post, including: “I never heard of a missing 20 minutes at the time, I have never subsequently seen or been shown any evidence that such a section existed, and I know of no surviving material that establishes that it did.”

That doesn’t completely rule out the possibility, though, does it? She goes on to say: “If indeed 20 minutes had been removed, I definitely would have found out about it eventually.” And she tags @joerogan and adds a whole bunch of hashtags including #EpsteinFiles, #GhislaineMaxwell, #SexTrafficking and #ConspiracyTheory, just to be clear who she’s talking to.

Do say: “Hmmm, should I believe family and the editor, or a load of people on Reddit?”

Don’t say: “What do you think, Joe Rogan?”

Messy, clever and can barely conceal its rage: is Furious the most outstanding TV show of the year?

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 14:17:56 GMT

The story of a serial killer taking revenge on the rich predatory men who abused her just earned a fantastic finale. With career-defining acting, daring Epstein parallels and super dark comedy, it’s a total must-watch

You could easily watch the first few minutes of Furious without knowing that it would turn out to be so special. It opens with a scene of pure horror: it’s Halloween night and a real monster is hiding among the pretend ones. A woman we come to know as Catherine Grace (an astonishingly good Lola Petticrew) is inside a man’s house, wearing a creepy kitten mask. The man is in bad shape, crawling on the floor, gasping for air and begging for his life. Catherine is alternately chirpy and tender with him, but eventually, she loses her patience with his pleading. She takes a syringe filled with fentanyl out of a pencil case decorated with sparkly stickers and jewels and finishes the job.

So far, so creepy crime drama, but Furious is already hiding in plain sight, because the monster is not who we think it is. What looks as if it will be a cat-and-mouse story, in which a tenacious FBI agent hunts a twisted serial killer, quickly rips up any expectations. We learn that Catherine was trafficked into sex work as a teenager, and is now making her way through a kill list of predatory and powerful men. Her life has been shaped by a conspiracy of abuse, violence, neglect and indifference. She has decided to take matters into her own broken hands.

The case finds its way to the desk of Alice Black (Emmy Rossum, in the role of her life), a tough former NYPD homicide detective turned recent FBI recruit. Her boss, Nora Washington (an equally excellent Quincy Tyler Bernstine), is the head of the sex crimes and crimes against children unit. She drinks to cope with the horrors she has to witness on a daily basis and is in possession of the darkest sense of humour on TV. She sees the potential, and pain, in Alice, and puts her to work. But as the series progresses, we see what it demands of them both to pursue justice, when they are repeatedly told to step back and stand down.

It is hard to think of a recent drama that has placed quite so much trust in the intelligence of its audience. Every character here is flawed. It has moral ambiguity baked into its core. Alice left the NYPD after being beaten by her cop ex-boyfriend Marshall Connelly (a truly sinister Jake Lacy). She has been ostracised by most of their former colleagues, who either do not believe her or, more likely, do not care. She is suffering from a complex response to trauma, and Furious does not shy away from depicting those complexities. It is a raw and unusually vivid portrait of women and PTSD.

When Alice begins to investigate Catherine and her crimes, Furious becomes a big, bold examination of justice, and what that might look like for women who have no access to it. It can barely conceal its rage, and by the final episode, few would expect it to. Catherine, and countless other young girls like her, have had their lives stolen and destroyed by men who believed themselves to be invincible. “I didn’t get to decide a fucking thing about my life,” she shouts, in one of the series’ most devastating scenes.

There is an obvious timeliness to this story, which may be one of the reasons why it is capable of landing such a blow. The Epstein parallels are not subtle, nor are they intended to be. The rich buy people off to cover up their terrible deeds. They operate in plain sight, daring people to catch them. There is an important photograph of trafficked teenage girls with older, wealthy men. One can only imagine if this show will pop up on the Mountbatten-Windsor streaming queue.

But what Furious provides is a fantasy of power, reclaimed and repurposed for the women who have had it taken away from them, if they ever had it at all. One cop describes Catherine as “five feet tall with her fuckin’ socks on”; that she can overpower her victims is something of a fantasy in itself. The finale has a near-impossible task in that it needs to maintain the bleak spirit of the story, while offering some sort of relief, or reward, for the women we have come to care so much about. It pulls it off by allowing for some magical thinking, while never veering too far from the grim reality of the situation. Some men pay for what they have done, whether formally or off the books. Some are given medals for their criminal behaviour. As messy as it is, the resolution is satisfying enough. Justice was never going to be clean.

Furious is a clever show. It works as a straightforward thriller, gripping and tense, using a murder mystery and a manhunt to expose an institutional conspiracy. It is also an emotionally astute act of catharsis, and this fantasy of revenge can feel, at times, like a much-needed balm. It has been renewed for a second season already. No wonder. It is one of the year’s most outstanding shows, and, after all, there are plenty more monsters out there.

Furious is on Disney+ in the UK and Australia and Hulu in the US

Farewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something more

The Guardian Wed, 02 Sep 2026 14:02:26 GMT

‘U-turn’ doesn’t do justice to the myriad ways he found to break a pledge. Now the former PM is resigning as an MP, why did I have such high hopes?

Keir Starmer exits the British political stage as he entered it: doing the exact opposite of the thing he said he was going to do. It’s only 10 weeks since he pledged to remain as MP for Holborn and St Pancras until the next election, despite stepping down as prime minister. That’s plainly the decent course of action: a dedicated Labour man wouldn’t want to force a byelection. Even if it’s a slam dunk for the party, it inevitably draws focus and resources from more important matters. Someone who takes the business of representing constituents even a 10th as seriously as all MPs say they do would feel that the honour of those votes should be repaid.

It’s a pretty boring life for an ex-PM turned backbencher. You have to keep your counsel as a large amount of blame is tacitly shovelled your way, while keeping your opinions to yourself. But that second requirement was the one thing Starmer was really good at. Once it transpired that the opinions he said out loud were open to endless revision and denial, I was never able to figure out what the real ones were.

The Tories are crying U-turn at this resignation, and technically it is – but the category needs more subdivisions to properly describe all the different ways Starmer found to break a pledge. There were the grand statements with which he came armed when he was initially seeking the Labour leadership: economic justice, social justice, climate justice, migrants’ rights, putting human rights at the heart of foreign policy. It would be tedious and a little depressing to track the moment at which each aim was jettisoned. Suffice it to say, these did not describe the politician he was. In fact, to be a Starmerite Version 2020 – Corbyn in a tie, basically – was enough to get you kicked out of the Labour party by 2024, and to vote in favour of policies he had once championed (ending the two-child benefit limit, for instance) was enough to have the whip suspended. “U-turn” doesn’t really cover a deception so kaleidoscopic.

There were specific reversals on policy, of course, forced by backbench rebellion (on welfare) or the first disastrous local election results (winter fuel allowance). But those didn’t feel like Starmer’s decisions so much as his having been backed into a corner. Then there were statements he made that he later claimed not to have meant. In October 2023 he told Nick Ferrari that Israel had a right to defend itself – even, when pressed, if that meant cutting off power and water to Gaza – then a few days later said: “I was saying Israel had the right to self-defence and when I said ‘that right’, it was that right to self-defence. I was not saying that Israel had the right to cut off water, food, fuel or medicines.” Not really a volte-face, more of a squirm.

Starmer, in short, was bad at politics in so many ways, and in ways that oughtn’t to coexist within the same politician. He wasn’t a communicator, but nor was he a meticulous or far-sighted planner. He had no backbone, and yet was incredibly rigid. He was extremely tribal in his determination to extinguish the left of his party, and yet he didn’t seem to have his own loyal tribe. None of that really matters, since he’s unlikely to trouble parliament again, but it matters what we thought we saw in him, and why.

Sorry, scratch that: I have lately come to abhor the journalistic formulation “we made the following mistakes”, which I hope isn’t the start of any deeper self-reflection. These are simply mistakes I made on my own.

I always claim to want Labour to be truly pluralistic; to discuss its project and purpose meaningfully between the constituency and parliamentary levels; to vote at party conference as if it matters, rather than have its values handed to it on the last day in a carefully manicured, ultimately meaningless speech. When it came to it, though, the promise of a candidate who obviated the messiness of pluralism by satisfying every wing just enough was too appealing.

There was also an internalised patriarchalism. I dismissed way too readily the voices that said it was ridiculous, in the year 2020, for the party of equality to have never had a female leader. That absurdity wasn’t really about whether any woman in the party was better suited to the job. It was about a failure, over decades, to reflect on where that preference for a middle-class white guy was actually coming from. What qualities of steadiness, credibility and intelligence was I projecting on to him? What cosplayed status quo-ism was I hoping would be sold to the rest of the voting public?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

It’s funny to be returning to the saying that George W Bush famously mangled in a very different political age: “Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me”. The Keir Starmer who fought the general election had already fooled his original supporters more times than they could count. It was obvious by the time he had his core team in place, with Morgan McSweeney at their helm, that it wasn’t even technocracy he was promising, it was a Blairite/Mandelsonian project much further to the right of what those politicians were flogging in the 90s. Perhaps I was hoping it was all just a feint to get into power, after which he’d rediscover his radicalism, or perhaps “hope” is just a pretty word for “I would prefer to believe than to participate”. So I’ll go along with Andy Burnham’s “hope in every heart” – it would be churlish not to – but it will be as well as, not instead of, comparing his actions with his promises.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist
