The 42 Best Deals From the REI Labor Day Sale

Wired September 02, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

REI's annual Labor Day Sale has come to feel like the end of summer to me. This year’s event is in full swing and ends on Labor Day, September 7. Many items are up to 40 percent off, and REI Co-op members save up to 20 percent on any REI Outlet item.

Many of the best REI deals are on gear from the company's house brand. But there are also good discounts on other brands, like Mountain Hardwear, Nemo Equipment, Big Agnes, and Coleman, among others. I’ve also pulled some deals from competing sales at Backcountry and other cottage industry retailers. Below, find the best deals on all our favorite tents, backpacks, sleeping bags, sleeping pads, cookware, outdoor apparel, and more. Be sure to check out our outdoor gear guides, like the Best Tents, Best Sleeping Bags, Best Sleeping Pads, Best Backpacking Tents, Best Merino Wool, and Best Base Layers.

Updated September 2, 2026: We've removed a few sold-out deals and added a dozen more deals on hiking boots, trail running shoes, sleeping pads, tents, and more.

Can’t You Just Put Links to All Your Outdoor Guides Right Here?

Sure. Here you go:

The REI Half Dome 2 is the best budget two-person backpacking tent. I’ve toted it on many backpacking trips and found it plenty sturdy, quick to set up, and capable of fitting two people along with their gear. It even comes with a footprint (which I never bother with, but it's nice to have it if you have to deal with pointy rocks).

The Big Agnes Copper Spur series is our top pick among freestanding ultralight tents. This is the bike-packing model, which features shorter pole segments that are easier to haul on a bike, but I really prefer it for the more subdued colors. The Copper Spur is a high-quality, well-designed tent that's lightweight, easy to set up, and roomy enough to be livable in the backcountry. The “awning” design (with trekking poles or sticks) is a nice extra.

Nemo's Dragonfly tents are roomy for the weight. There's a generous amount of mesh at the top, which provides some nice ventilation on warm summer nights and is perfect for falling asleep under the stars when the weather permits. The Osmo fabric is a blend of nylon and polyester that absorbs less water than pure nylon rainflies.

MSR's Groundhog stakes aren't cheap, but they're the best backpacking tent upgrade you can make. They're superstrong—I've never had one bend or pull out on me—and considering their strength, they're pretty lightweight. I suggest carrying a mix of stakes when backpacking—some of these, some carbon fiber pegs, and some shepherd hooks. That way, no matter the terrain, you've got something that'll work.

REI's Base Camp tent is my favorite car camping tent. It's a traditional dome tent design, with two crossed poles and two side poles, that hold up very well in wind. The floor is high-quality 150-denier polyester, which so far has not shown any signs of abrasion, despite quite a few nights on rough ground out West. Inside, there are loads of storage pockets, and the double doors make great vents in warmer weather, with huge windows that ensure you catch any whiffs of breeze on hot nights.

The Marmot Halo is my favorite all-weather four-person family tent. The low-profile design stands up better to wind, while the steep sidewalls maximize interior space. It also has a nearly full-length rain fly, which helps make this a real haven in a storm. The name comes from the unusual pole design. There are two cross poles, like every square, domed tent, but the side poles connect halfway up the tent body instead of at the ground. The only downside is that you can't stand up in it. If you want more room, the six-person version, which, with a 76-inch peak height, may be tall enough for you to stand up in, is also on sale.

My favorite barefoot sandals are 25 percent off right now. I always call these the barefoot equivalent of Chaco sandals. They're not as robust, and I'd still bring Chacos if I were white-water rafting, but for everything else these are perfect. Z-Trails flex and bend as you walk, giving your feet the freedom of movement you'd expect from a barefoot shoe, though these do have 10 mm of cushioning, which makes them a good option if you're just starting out with barefoot shoes. The even more minimal Z-Trek sandals are also on sale.

The best all-around barefoot shoe, the Prios are your classic sneaker reimagined for barefoot shoe enthusiasts. When you were a kid, you had just one pair of shoes: The Prios are that pair. The toe box is wide enough for my toes to splay out nicely, and the heel cup is snug with no slipping. The ground feel is great too, enough feedback to feel barefoot, but you're not going to wince when you hit a sharp stone.

Altra's Lone Peak shoes have carried countless thru-hikers to the finish line. The Lone Peak first came on the scene in 2011 and quickly built a cult following. They're light (11.5 ounces) and very comfortable in our testing. The reinforced toe and heel offer excellent protection against rough, rocky trails, and while they're much more padded these days than early versions, they're still zero drop.

Keen's Targhee Apex has finally found a look that isn't bad by Targhee standards. Perhaps more than any other shoe we've tested, these look like the trail-running Gorpcore icons they are. At just 0.75 pounds each, they are light without being fragile, and the generous footbed lets your feet spread comfortably on long days.

The La Sportiva Prodigio combines trail-running agility with boot-level protection, delivering surprising versatility on rugged terrain. They're one of our favorite light hiking boots. The fit is a little on the snug side—much like La Sportiva climbing shoes—but they should be fine even for wide feet thanks to the generous footbed width. At 1.65 pounds for the pair, these aren't terribly bulky.

This camp chair is the coziest way to hang out around the fire. It is somewhat huge, heavy, and awkward to fold up and carry, but so long as you have room for it in your vehicle, there's no better way to relax under the stars with your loved ones.

The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI brand gear is the company's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works well and has produced some great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example: It's comfortable (it does wobble a little side-to-side when you move) and less than half the price of competitors.

I've noticed that when people try to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter backpack, they struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which smashes anything soft down to about half the size of the same item in a regular stuff sack. This works well with sleeping bags and clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino wool.

The Flash 22 is one of the best-value day packs on the market, especially on sale. It's surprisingly comfortable despite the lightweight straps and minimal padding. It carries loads up to 15 pounds without straining the shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. Note that this deal is only on the patterned colors.

WIRED staffers have North Face duffels that have been going strong for 25 years, earning a spot in our Buy It for Life guide. They're big ol' bags (this one is 62 liters), capable of swallowing gear like a whale, and unlike all the other identical cases on the luggage carousel, they’re always easy to spot. This version is made of phthalate-free, recycled PVC and recycled nylon that’s treated with a non-PFC water-repellent (DWR) finish.

Now is a great time to score some new base layers and mid layers ahead of the cooler months, or pick up one of our favorite rain jackets.

Arc'teryx's Beta AR rain jacket is one of the burliest rain jackets I've tested. The Beta AR uses 40D fabric for most of the face, with reinforced 80D patches in high-wear areas, all of it with a Gore-Tex Pro 3L membrane. It's been the only Gore-Tex jacket I've tested that hasn't wetted out yet, and the pit zips provide excellent ventilation. At 1 pound, 0.3 ounces, it's not the lightest jacket, but you'd be hard-pressed to find anything else this durable at this weight.

This is an REI Outlet deal because it's been discontinued, which is a shame (hopefully that just means new colors are coming next year). REI's 100 percent merino base layers are some of the best values around, even at full price. On sale, they're a true steal. I like this half-zip for the extra ventilation the zipper provides, but if you prefer, the regular top (on sale for $30) is also on sale, as is the base layer bottom (on sale for $30).

Nothing says outdoors like a hatchet loop on your pants. Fjällräven Vidda Pro trousers give you that and great ventilation. The Vidda Pro uses Fjällräven's G-1000 fabric, a 65 percent recycled polyester and 35 percent cotton blend, with pockets everywhere and extras like ventilation zippers, reinforced knees (with openings for pads), and that sweet, sweet hatchet loop on the leg.

Our favorite backpacking sleeping bag, the Bishop Pass 15 offers the best warmth-to-weight ratio while packing down small and staying affordable. I have slept in this bag for more than two weeks, with nighttime temps ranging from 28 to 65 degrees Fahrenheit, and, yes, it was too warm in the heat, but on those warmer nights, I unzipped it and used it as a blanket. It isn't perfect, but it's a versatile bag.

REI's Magma line of down gear is some of the best value around. The Magma 15 sleeping bag has long been an affordable option that's perfect for shoulder-season trips when the temperature potentially swings lower than you expect (the comfort rating is 21). There are three lengths and three widths, which makes it easy to find a perfect fit for your body, and the 850-fill-power goose down (Bluesign-approved) packs down nicely and small. If you don't need the shoulder-season coverage, the Magma 30 is also on sale for $262 ($87 off), and it makes a great summer sleeping bag.

This down mummy bag has a spoon-shaped design for side sleepers and extra room in the elbows and knees so you can roll over onto your side without feeling like you're slipping into a straitjacket. It's built for temps down to 30 degrees Fahrenheit and has zippered gills you can open to avoid overheating when it's warmer.

The best budget ultralight quilt, the Magma Trail is a great value for the money. The lower price does mean that this one is a bit heavier (it uses 850-fill-power down), though at 24 ounces for the long, wide version I have, it’s competitive on the scale. The straps for attaching it to your sleep pad aren’t as nice as what you’ll get with something like the Enlightened Equipment's Revelation Quilt, but it’s just as warm and does a respectable job of keeping out drafts. There's even a zippered foot box with a drawstring for cooler nights.

Nemo's Pulse quilt uses RDS-certified, gold-infused 1,000-fill-power ExpeDRY down, which does a good job of shedding moisture from tent condensation and reportedly dries faster than standard down, though I've never figured out a good way to test this. The Karo Step baffle stitching keeps down well distributed, and at 12 ounces for the regular, this one is pretty dang lightweight.

This is our favorite sleeping bag for car camping. The REI Siesta is plenty warm and affordable. It's also not a mummy bag because you're not climbing Denali here. The rectangular cut makes for a much roomier, more comfortable sleeping experience. The 20-degree-Fahrenheit rating makes it warm enough for three seasons, and unlike most rectangular bags, the Siesta has a hood, which helps on those cold nights.

The Kindercamp makes a great car camping bag if you've got young children. Once your kids are about 4 feet tall, an adult sleeping bag works just fine. Prior to that, they'll benefit from a kids' sleeping bag like the Kindercamp, which is cut smaller so your little ones don't have to heat up a huge, adult-size sleeping bag to stay warm.

There are other good sleeping pads out there, but nothing compares to the Therm-a-Rest NeoLoft for comfort. This pad reinvigorated my love of backpacking by ensuring that I get a great night's sleep. It's cushy and comfortable, especially if you're careful not to overinflate it. The R-4.8 insulation keeps you warm down to about freezing, though I've used it in colder conditions by pairing it with a closed-cell foam pad.

The Z-Lite Sol weighs next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), folds up compact enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and will completely change your backpacking experience for the better. I am too old and too soft to sleep on just this anymore, but I use it as a chair, padding for a nap on the rocks, a table, extra padding on cold nights, and more. It's possibly the most versatile piece of gear I own.

If you want to feel like you never left your bed at home, this is the camping pad to get. You really have no idea how comfortable tent camping can be until you sleep on a Megamat. The firm, 4-inch-thick pad is both soft and surprisingly firm thanks to the closed-cell foam inside, which relieves pressure and feels about as close to the mattress in your bedroom as you're going to get in the woods.

Nothing says camping like roasting marshmallows over open flames and burning beans on the camp stove. Check out our guides to the best backpacking stoves and best camping stoves for more picks.

MSR's PocketRocket Deluxe is our top pick for a backpacking stove. It wins the title thanks to its larger burner area, which allows the flame to spread out for faster boil times and better fuel efficiency, especially with larger pots. It also fared better in the wind than smaller burners. The genius of the deluxe model is the small curved lip around the burner, which helps keep wind from getting to the base of the flame. It's a small design element, and one that you certainly want. During long-term testing, I found it more effective at maintaining a simmer in the wind, should you want to do any actual cooking.

You can put together a lighter cooking setup, but Jetboil's Stash is the lightest all-in-one system out there, and it does boil water a bit faster than the rest. The heat diffuser design speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I could only match indoors in still air), but the real appeal is how this kit packs down into itself and how simple it is to use.

Jetboil's larger all-in-one cooking system, the Flash, offers a larger-capacity 1-liter pot that combines an integrated pot and burner into an easy-to-use system. I prefer the more compact Stash above, but if you're cooking for two and are all-in on dehydrated meals, this stove is popular for good reason.

While I prefer the larger burner head of the Deluxe model above, the MSR PocketRocket 2 is lighter at 2.6 ounces compared to the Deluxe's 2.9. It still has wide enough arms to support just about any one- or two-person pot. It's simple to use, even while wearing gloves, and it's efficient. At 947-foot elevation, it boiled 1 liter of water in 3 minutes, 47 seconds. You can even get it to simmer, though the flame radius is small, so fancier cooking isn't easy.

MSR's WhisperLite series is probably the most popular backpacking stove ever made. They last forever (mine is over 30 years old and still works great), and this model, the Universal, can use just about any fuel you can imagine—white gas, kerosene, unleaded gasoline, and isobutane-propane canisters, to be precise. The only downside is that it can be fiddly compared to stoves like the Jetboil. But if you're headed out on a long trip, buying fuel as you go, this is the most flexible option out there.

This is by far the most compact two-burner stove I've tested. It's my pick for any situation where space is at a premium—whether that's canoeing or just because you have a small car. The burners are large, and with some practice, I could get a light, simmer-friendly flame. My main gripe is the windscreen, which is not the best. The Basecamp version, with fitted pots, is also on sale for $300 ($100 off).

My favorite stove in Coleman's current lineup, the Coleman Cascade 3-in-1 features heavy-duty cast-iron grates and comes with a cast-iron griddle and grill. It'll comfortably fit a 12-inch pan and a 10-inch pan side by side, and it's significantly sturdier and more robust than other Coleman stoves, making it worth the extra money if you use it often. That said, the much cheaper stove below will get you by if you're only using it a few nights a year.

This stove is ubiquitous at campgrounds for a reason. It's well-built, sturdy on a table, and just works. It's not the most powerful stove, and it lacks frills like push-button ignition, but it's capable of holding a low flame, simmering soups, and cooking scrambled eggs without browning them. It's also incredibly durable.

The MSR Gravity Autoflow filter is a must-have for backpacking with a group. To use this filter, scoop up 10 liters of water in the dirty water bag, attach the hose, connect your water bottle, and sit back and relax. The filter is good enough to keep you safe from all the usual protozoa and bacteria, and the flow rate is a solid 1.5 liters per minute when the filter is clean.

The MSR Guardian is our pick for trips with sketchy water sources because it filters down to 0.02 microns, which will even remove viruses. It is heavy at 22 ounces and may be overkill for trips in the US, but it's a great option for overseas adventures. I really like that it's designed to be self-cleaning, which makes field maintenance incredibly easy, and that it screws right onto a Nalgene bottle. Also, because it's a pump filter, it's very fast. You can crank out a couple of liters in hardly any time at all. The gravity-fed version is also on sale at Backcountry for $232 ($78 off).

If you snap a selfie in the woods and Instagram isn't around to see it, did it happen? You'll never have to answer that question if you've got one of our favorite action cameras or 360 cameras with you.

Insta360's X6 360 camera just launched—our review will be coming soon—but the X5 is still a great option, especially on sale. The twin 1/1.28-inch sensors capture 8K video, which means you can reframe your footage to fit rectangular video formats and still have nearly 4K clips sharp enough to mix with footage shot with your phone. The dynamic range is impressive, and the X5 also has great battery life.

If you're going to turn your action camera on yourself, consider the Ace Pro 2, our top pick for vlogging. It has a great lens and sensor co-engineered with Leica, is capable of recording 8K video at up to 30 frames per second (fps), and has some pretty darn nice color even in the default settings. My guess is that the Ace Pro 3 is coming pretty soon, but this is still a good deal.

Sure, phones have some of the features you'll get with a satellite messenger, but we still think you're better off with a dedicated device. Garmin's new inReach Mini 3 Plus now offers some of those phone features—like voice messaging—along with the emergency features and excellent service worldwide. It's also still tiny, well-built, and it has great battery life. A non-Plus model, which doesn't have a speaker and mic, is also on sale.

A Prop 65 Warning Doesn’t Mean What You Think

Wired September 02, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

My first encounter with a Prop 65 warning was on the back of my TV.

I was selling it on Facebook Marketplace, and when the buyer arrived to pick it up, he spotted a warning I had never noticed. “California Proposition 65 Warning: This product contains chemicals known to the state of California to cause cancer and birth defects or reproductive harm.” Neither of us had seen such a label before, and for a moment, he didn’t want the TV anymore. We did what anyone would do in this situation: We Googled it. He ended up taking the TV. I kept Googling.

California’s Proposition 65, officially called the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act, applies to a dizzying range of products, from food and cosmetics to electronics and household goods. Passed in 1986, the law turns 40 this year, yet that ominous little label still confuses the average consumer.

So, should you steer clear of all products with a Prop 65 warning? Not necessarily. Here’s what you need to know before you panic-buy a new TV.

In November 1986, California voters approved Proposition 65 by a landslide margin of about 63 percent to 37 percent. It’s a right-to-know law, meant to inform Californians about potential exposure to chemicals that may cause cancer or reproductive harm over a lifetime.

It doesn’t ban those chemicals; instead, it requires businesses to provide a warning when their products could expose people to a listed chemical at levels above specific thresholds.

“At that time, it was part of a broader effort to address a growing concern that the public had about toxic chemical exposure,” says Megan Schwarzman, environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health.

The idea is that consumers can use that information to make their own decisions. A warning might prompt someone to choose an alternative, use a product less frequently, or take other steps to reduce their exposure. Prop 65 also gives businesses an incentive to reformulate products or change manufacturing practices to avoid issuing a warning that may deter customers.

And because California is such a massive consumer market, products often need to comply with Prop 65 requirements even when they’re manufactured or sold by companies elsewhere. Some large retailers, such as Target and Amazon, also require their vendors to comply with Prop 65 warning requirements.

Prop 65 covers a broad range of products and potential exposures. You can find warnings on fortified foods, smartphones, and appliances. The law is concerned with exposure, not simply whether the chemical is detectable. California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) establishes the so-called safe-harbor levels for many listed chemicals. Generally speaking, a warning is required when anticipated exposure exceeds these levels.

The Prop 65 list contains both naturally occurring and synthetic chemicals that California has determined are known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Supplements, for example, can contain trace amounts of naturally occurring or environmental contaminants, including lead, cadmium, and arsenic. The list is updated at least annually, and chemicals can also be removed from the list as scientific evidence evolves.

Chemicals can be added to the Prop 65 list through four mechanisms: through California’s Labor Code; through evaluations from California’s Carcinogen Identification Committee (CIC) or Developmental and Reproductive Toxicant Identification Committee (DARTIC); through identification by certain authoritative bodies, like the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA); or through identification by a state or federal agency.

Mariana C. Stern, cancer epidemiologist and member of the CIC, says the committee includes epidemiologists, toxicologists, molecular biologists, and cancer scientists who review the available literature before deciding whether a chemical belongs on the list.

“We may spend the whole day trying to dissect one chemical,” Stern says. “It’s not uncommon that we end up deciding we don’t have enough evidence to add this compound to the list.”

But seeing a warning doesn’t necessarily mean a product contains a dangerous amount of a chemical, or even that the product itself has been tested. According to Schwarzman, “some companies have opted to warn rather than test or reformulate, but from our research, I believe that is much less common than when companies post a warning because of the actual presence of the chemical above a certain threshold.”

From a consumer standpoint, the ubiquity of Prop 65 labels also means that it can be harder to prioritize which ones actually warrant attention. “We definitely have a concern with over-warning,” says Tina Cox, section chief of the OEHHA’s Proposition 65 Implementation Program. “Any unnecessary warnings do make it difficult for consumers to identify where the real exposures are, and it does dilute the value of Prop 65 warnings.”

As a result, California has started trying to make them more useful by requiring short-form warnings to name at least one chemical, rather than relying on the generic “may cause cancer or reproductive harm” language. Businesses have until January 2028 to fully comply with the new requirement. The state is also conducting more outreach to help companies understand when a warning is required and when it is not.

Prop 65 was meant to inform consumers, not to tell them which products to buy. By the same token, a product without a warning isn’t necessarily free of hazardous chemicals.

“You’re never going to be zero exposure, even if you avoid all Prop 65 labels,” says air pollution scientist Shahir Fouad Masri. “If you have a product that doesn’t have a label, it’s one of two things: It was tested and it didn’t exceed Prop 65, and therefore it’s safe, or simply nobody ever sent it to the lab.”

That said, a Prop 65 warning is still useful information, and there are ways to reduce your exposure to these harmful chemicals. “Everybody has different risk tolerances and different priorities,” says Schwarzman. Consider how frequently you use the product and at what dose.

“Exposure from that one product, in many cases, is not going to cause cancer,” adds Cox, “but maybe over a lifetime of exposure, or exposure to similar products that have the same chemical, will increase your risk for cancer or reproductive toxicity.”

One example is holiday lights. Flexible plastic components can contain phthalates, which are added to PVC (polyvinyl chloride) to make it more pliable. Those chemicals migrate out of the plastic and come into contact with your hands or enter household dust. “My own choice around that is to handle them briefly and wash my hands,” says Schwarzman. “I don’t have my kids handle them, and I do make a different decision about that than something I’d be consuming on a daily basis.”

On a similar note, if you’re concerned about a warning on a tool, Masri suggests wearing gloves to reduce direct skin contact. There’s also a difference in dermal absorption rate. The skin on your hands, for example, is generally thicker and more calloused than the skin on your face, which means less absorption. So you might think differently about a screwdriver you occasionally handle with gloves than an LED mask you put directly on your face every day, where the potential for absorption is higher.

If you’re considering a product with a Prop 65 warning, don’t fret. Instead, look for more information.

Prop 65 is a right-to-know law meant to raise awareness and ensure that we, as consumers, have an impact on the type of products we’re exposed to in our daily lives. As Schwarzman puts it, “I want to encourage us all not to feel like the toxic things are inevitable, and there’s nothing we can do, because there often is something we can do.”

The Range Rover Electric Has Finally Arrived

Wired September 01, 2026

It feels like we have been waiting an age for the Range Rover Electric. First announced back in December 2023, JLR's luxury EV SUV was meant to hit the road in 2024, but extended development testing forced the carmaker to push its arrival back. Now it's finally here—one of WIRED's most anticipated rides—the first fully electric Range Rover.

The specs are as mighty as you would expect. Dual 260-kilowatt motors deliver “V8 levels of power” up to 542 horsepower and 850 newton-meters of torque (20 percent more than other motors of the same size, JLR claims). Inside, a double-stacked 118.5-kWh battery with 800-volt split-charging tech can recharge the cell from 10 to 80 percent in 22 minutes (or, if you prefer, 137 miles in 10 minutes). Max range is supposedly 372 miles (according to WLTP standards), and a claimed real-world distance of up to 333 miles.

The Range Rover Electric will launch from a standstill to 60 mph in 4.3 seconds, which is rapid considering the car's weight, though there's no official figure.

All this comes at a price, naturally—one that's high even for Range Rover. Available for order now, the UK entry-level Autobiography model is £154,070, or about $208,000, but this quickly climbs to £225,240 (north of $304,000) for the SV Black long-wheelbase model. It could go higher, too, as the “Ultra” models are listed as “price on application”—shorthand for “If you have to ask, you can't afford it.” However, US customers can buy a lower SE-spec Range Rover Electric from $138,00—add $2,550 for delivery and destination.

This brings us to the other reason the Range Rover Electric was supposedly delayed: the lukewarm response from wealthy buyers toward the luxury EV market. Indeed, sales of perhaps the Range Rover Electric's biggest rival, the electric Mercedes G-Wagen, have been woeful. Other brands, including Porsche and Audi, have suffered similar fates.

JLR is banking on a “Range Rover first, electric second” approach to separate the SUV's fortunes from what's gone before in luxe EVs. And the Range Rover's electric tech is perfectly suited for off-roading, as we found out last year.

JLR claims the traction management controls motor speed within 50 milliseconds and manages slip up to 100 times faster than on equivalent internal combustion systems. Single-pedal driving works on climbs up to 45 degrees. There's even 900-millimeter wading capability, for those worried about an electric SUV's ability to cross water. All in all, more than 300 patent applications have been filed for the Range Rover Electric, the most for a single vehicle in JLR’s history, apparently.

Inside, while the cabin is plush, the Range Rover seems to shun the move back to physical switchgear, sticking with a large central touchscreen and steering-wheel controls.

The long delays have meant the Range Rover Electric has benefited from extensive JLR testing. The company put live batteries through extreme vibration and shock testing in temperatures ranging from –40°C to +90°C. Physical tests saw the EV driven the equivalent of 38 times around the world, alongside more than 250,000 hours of virtual tests, more than on any previous Range Rover. Perhaps that's why JLR has the confidence to offer an eight-year or 100,000-mile warranty.

Today's reveal comes after JLR announced it's “the most car-like Range Rover ever created” in July. The Range Rover GT will be an all-electric grand tourer built on the company's Electrified Modular Architecture (EMA), the same platform that will underpin other midsized cars for the brand. The GT is still undergoing final testing, ahead of a full launch expected later this year.

OpenAI Is About to Release Its First AI Model With ‘Critical’ Cyber Abilities

Wired September 01, 2026

OpenAI announced Tuesday that its forthcoming AI model, Astra, is its first to reach the company’s threshold for what it calls “critical” cyber capabilities. OpenAI says it plans to publicly release a version of Astra “soon,” but will make the model’s advanced cyber capabilities available only to select partners in its Daybreak Blue early-access program at launch.

In a briefing with reporters, OpenAI safety and security leaders said the company has concluded that Astra reaches the critical cybersecurity capabilities outlined in its preparedness framework, which sets thresholds and protocols for when its AI models pose new levels of risk. The company says an AI model has reached its critical cyber threshold when it can independently find and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in real-world software. OpenAI leaders said the company has followed its procedure for this situation, which is to halt further development until appropriate safeguards and security measures can be implemented.

OpenAI previously said that it paused some training workloads related to the development of Astra and a future AI model for several weeks. Executives say the company has now resumed said work on Astra, and the future AI model, after putting additional safety and security controls in place. OpenAI says the multi-week pause was productive, and it is now confident that it can release Astra broadly in a safe way.

The announcement comes as Silicon Valley grapples with the advanced cybersecurity capabilities of cutting-edge AI models, and tries to assure users, lawmakers, and other companies that it can keep them under control. In July, OpenAI disclosed an incident in which agents running two of its models exploited vulnerabilities in what was supposed to be a siloed testing environment, gaining access to the internet and hacking the open source AI platform Hugging Face. (OpenAI notes that Astra was not one of the models involved in this case.)

Other AI companies, such as Anthropic and Meta, have disclosed similar incidents in recent weeks. On Monday, Anthropic also said it has paused some AI training workloads while it hardens its safety and security practices.

OpenAI says it’s implementing a multi-step approach to limit everyday users from accessing Astra’s advanced cyber capabilities, including a new “misalignment monitor.” If someone asks Astra to help them find an exploit in a real-world software system, for example, the model is supposed to refuse to answer. OpenAI says it has also made Astra more robust to jailbreaking attempts, and in tests it successfully refused unsafe queries at a significantly higher rate than previous models.

However, OpenAI notes in a blog post that its misalignment monitor may “occasionally flag legitimate activity as potential cyber misuse or unauthorized behavior, leading to it inadvertently being slowed, paused, or stopped.” OpenAI says the guardrail can be triggered in some cases even when a user is engaging in activities that don’t appear related to cybersecurity. When this happens, ChatGPT and Codex users may be asked to review the model’s action before proceeding, OpenAI said.

Partners in OpenAI’s Daybreak program—which includes digital infrastructure providers like Cisco, Cloudflare, and Palo Alto Networks—will get early access to a less restricted version of Astra with more robust cyber capabilities. The goal of the program is to ensure these companies can use advanced AI models like Astra to harden their defenses before similarly capable models are made broadly available. OpenAI leaders also said the company has been working closely with government partners to ensure they’re aware of Astra’s cyber skills and can get access to them.

Astra is not only capable of finding novel software vulnerabilities and developing ways to exploit them for hacking, but is also able to “chain” multiple exploits together, a technique used to bore deeper and deeper into a target system and gain access that wouldn’t be attainable using just one vulnerability.

According to figures from OpenAI, Astra outperforms industry leading AI models such as GPT-5.6 Sol and Anthropic’s Mythos on cybersecurity benchmarks such as ExploitBench, which Astra scored 100 percent on. However, these capabilities are broadly in line with the rising hacking abilities of AI models that OpenAI and Anthropic have been forecasting for months. In April, for example, Anthropic emphasized that Mythos Preview was able to autonomously develop exploit chains.

As the AI and cybersecurity industries have scrambled to adapt, though, many cybersecurity experts have emphasized that key digital security defenses and longstanding best practices are still durable. However, AI puts organizations and systems that haven’t fully implemented these protections at even more urgent risk.

The Diamond Moon and Other Astronomical Events to See in September 2026

Wired September 01, 2026

August set the bar high for stargazers, with two eclipses and the peak of the Perseids meteor shower. But it’s not time to put away your telescopes, with some lesser-known astronomical events set to arrive across the sky this month.

The Pleiades will appear next to the moon, Venus will reach its brightest point of the year, Neptune will be in its best position for spotting with a telescope, and as an encore to the Perseids, there will also be a smaller meteor shower.

Here are some dates worth marking on your calendar for the month to come.

September begins with an easy opportunity to spot two of the brightest objects in the night sky. Venus will appear near Spica, the most intense star in the constellation Virgo. Both objects will be visible to the naked eye.

The exact timing of Venus’ appearance is September 2 at 00:17 UTC. This means that, depending on the your location, the conjunction could occur in the afternoon or evening of September 1.

Milky way stars photographed with a wide-angle lens.

It should be easy to tell the two celestial objects apart. Venus will shine much more brightly, looking like a white dot that doesn’t twinkle as much as the stars. Spica will appear nearby as a considerably fainter bluish dot. The two will be approximately 1.5 degrees apart.

A handy trick is that 0.5 degrees in the sky is roughly the average diameter of a full moon. Therefore, once you find the brightest point in the sky—which will be Venus—you can find Spica about three moons away.

The moon will be accompanied by one of the most famous star clusters in the sky. On the night of September 3, it will appear approximately 1.1 degrees from the Pleiades—close enough to observe both objects in the same region. The moon will be about 59 percent illuminated, according to Star Walk’s calculations.

The Pleiades, also known as “the Seven Sisters” or M45, is a star cluster located in the constellation Taurus. Six or seven of its members are usually visible to the naked eye under good conditions, although the cluster contains hundreds of young stars. These stars were born at approximately the same time and remain gravitationally bound together.

Astronomical photograph of the Pleiades. From Earth, six or seven stars can usually be seen, but they form a gigantic cluster. The moon will appear next to them on September 3.

The proximity to the waning moon offers a good opportunity for spotting them. To the naked eye, they will appear as a small group of bright points next to the moon, as if they were diamonds. Binoculars will allow you to make out many more. The encounter will happen again on September 30, when the two objects will once more be separated by just one degree.

September also has its own meteor shower. The Epsilon Perseids will peak September 9 and 10, producing up to eight meteors per hour.

A meteor shower, captured in Spain.

The number of meteors is lower than that of the famous Perseids in August. However, this shower has one advantage: Its peak will occur just two days before the new moon, making the sky ideally dark for viewing.

Conditions will be especially favorable from the northern hemisphere, and, as with any meteor shower, it is recommended to find a dark location away from light pollution.

Venus is usually one of the easiest objects to spot in the night sky, but toward the end of September it will shine even brighter. The planet will reach an apparent magnitude of approximately -4.8. By comparison, the full moon has a magnitude of -12.7, and Sirius—considered the brightest star in the sky—barely reaches -1.46.

Look for the planet after sunset, near the western horizon. Viewing conditions will be best from the southern hemisphere.

Unlike the other events on this list, the equinox isn’t something we can go out and observe directly. Instead, it’s an astronomical moment that marks a specific point in Earth’s orbit and, with it, the change of season.

The September equinox will occur on September 23 when the Sun crosses the equator as it moves southward. The event marks the astronomical beginning of fall in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere.

Spotting Neptune is considerably more challenging than spotting other planets. The most distant planet in the solar system (sorry Pluto) is forecasted to reach opposition on September 26. This means that Earth will be approximately between Neptune and the Sun.

This positioning means Neptune will remain visible for much of the night and will be at one of its closest distances to our planet for the year. Therefore, September offers one of the best opportunities in 2026 to try to spot it.

One of the few great photos we have of Neptune.

It’s too faint to be seen with the naked eye. You’ll need a telescope and to know its position among the stars of Pisces. Even then, it will appear as a tiny bluish disk.

September will end with a particularly famous full moon. The full moon closest to the September equinox is traditionally called the Harvest Moon. The term does not describe a distinct physical phenomenon, nor does it mean that the moon will change color, size, or brightness. It’s a traditional name related to the harvests of the northern hemisphere.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Sonos Has New Devices, a New OS, and Yes, a New App

Wired September 01, 2026

Sonos has a new app. Stop me if you’ve heard this one before.

The smart speaker company, long a darling of the audio industry, undid much of the goodwill it earned with its multiroom speakers through a bevy of software updates that broke its app in 2024. Almost all app users hated it, citing the loss of features like volume control and accessibility tools meant to help blind people use the wireless speaker system. Sonos eventually owned up to the mistake, considered bringing back the old app again, then booted its CEO and marched its new leaders out to apologize profusely to win back the company’s furious customers.

Now, Sonos says it has a brand-new app update, infused with lots of generative AI features. The company also announced a new soundbar and its second pair of over-the-ear headphones. Sonos representatives say it doesn’t want to be seen as a speaker company anymore, but as something bigger and more holistic.

“For years people have been seeing us as a speaker company,” says Brandon Holley, the interim hardware lead at Sonos. “What we actually are is an audio operating system.”

The company is calling that operating system Sonos 27, and it manifests in a few ways. First and foremost: updates to the Sonos app.

Sonos knows that the words “new Sonos app” might strike fear in the hearts of its users.

“When I say that out loud, I know exactly what comes to mind,” Sid Patel, vice president of software at Sonos, tells WIRED. Patel says the app was developed with a “customer-centric feedback listening approach” that involves reaching out to the community and being active in forums like Reddit. New features to make the app easier to use will include improved tab navigation, better room sorting, and changes to volume knobs on the app itself. In the fall, Sonos will release system health views that let you diagnose connection issues for each product.

The big feature is Sonos 27voice, the company’s generative AI integration, which is being released in early access. It lets you talk to the speakers like you would Amazon’s Alexa or a Google Home speaker, allowing you to request music based on your mood. It also has a Model Context Protocol, which can connect to your AI service of choice if you want to ask ChatGPT to play music on your speakers.

The company is highlighting its Sonos Custom Agents, which let users customize their agents to do various tasks throughout the system, like triggering speakers in a certain room at a certain time. You can also change the voices used if maybe you’d like the AI in your kitchen to sound like a fancy French chef, or have your bathroom speaker talk to you like a pirate.

“Obviously AI is something that's very hot these days, clearly,” Patel says. “So we have integrated various pieces of AI into our system.”

When asked what products Sonos 27 and its AI features would work with, a Sonos representative wrote via email that Sonos 27 will work in Sonos’ S2 app, but not the S1 app—the version that controls some older Sonos equipment. So owners of older Sonos hardware won't be able to access these new AI features.

“Sonos 27 is designed to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities, so not every product will support every new feature,” the representative wrote. “We want to be transparent about those limitations while continuing to support products with security and ongoing updates for as long as the hardware allows.”

Despite the stated effort to be transparent, Sonos says it won’t release details about compatibility or upgrade paths for each product until “a later date.”

Sonos Fabric

Sonos has an official name for the network its products use to sync across rooms: Sonos Fabric.

“Sonos Fabric is the name of the magic that has existed for what Sonos was built on,” Patel says. “The idea of, you have one speaker, two speakers, three speakers, and how they magically work together in a home theater setup or a bonded setup or group.”

Two new features are coming to that newly christened technology. One is what Sonos calls portable surround, which enables users to take devices from one room to another and have them sync there. So if you have a main soundbar by your TV but want to bring in another couple of speakers from other rooms to act as surround sound speakers for movie night, the Sonos products can detect their location and moderate which audio to play where.

Second is the ability to switch audio between the speakers and headphones, which Sonos calls Headphone Linking.

Sonos Ace Ultra

Sonos’ first pair of over-ear headphones arrived in 2024, right during the height of the Sonos app woes. The Sonos Ace were very good, except the headphones didn’t work within Sonos’ speaker ecosystem. Sonos wants to fix that problem with its follow-up headset, the Sonos Ace Ultra.

It has 35 hours of battery life and can connect to devices via USB-C and 3.5 mm. More importantly, it can connect to other Sonos speakers via Wi-Fi. The Ace Ultra runs on Sonos Fabric, which means it can connect to your wider Sonos system and let you switch playback between speakers and the headphones

“With a single push of a button, you'll be able to suck music into your headphones,” Patel says.

Sonos Beam Ultra

Sonos introduced a new soundbar, called the Beam Ultra. It’s an upgrade of the company’s existing Sonos Beam with nine drivers, four more than the past Beams. They’re also upward-firing drivers that bounce the sound off your ceiling for better acoustics. The Beam Ultra has AI-enabled features, like AI speech enhancement that aims to make dialog more discernible in loud scenes. The Beam Ultra can connect via Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and wired HDMI eARC.

This is a lot of change for Sonos, something the company hasn’t always handled gracefully. Sonos’ home systems already aren’t the easiest to set up, sometimes requiring separate apps for older products. The company may be rejiggering itself as an “audio operating system,” but its software has long been the source of its troubles with getting its products to work right. Will AI smarts fix that? Maybe for its newer devices. But anyone with an existing system may still struggle.

The AI features on products and in the Sonos 27 app will be opt-in, meaning you can avoid them entirely. “That really is our new approach to our app release,” Patel says. “We're going to bring our customers along. We're going to listen more.”

That would be a good plan. Sounds like Sonos’ speakers will be listening more, too.

Using High-Energy Laser, US Shoots Down Drones Near Mexico Border

Wired September 01, 2026

This week, the US Army used a high-energy multipurpose laser to shoot down three drones near the US-Mexico border, which official reports claimed were “posing a physical threat to US military personnel and CBP partners,” referring to Customs and Border Patrol.

The operation took place between the night of August 25 and the early morning of August 26 in the vicinity of the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and was led by the Joint Task Force Southern Border (JTF-SB), which operates under US Northern Command. Authorities confirmed that, during the operation, agents used technology derived from the Army’s High-Energy Multipurpose Laser (AMP-HEL) system, a military program focused on implementing high-energy lasers for new defense capabilities.

Available information suggests that this initiative began in September 2025, when AeroVironment, a company specializing in defense technology, delivered the first two functional prototypes of these laser-based weapons to the US Armed Forces. Two new, improved systems were delivered as the program was expanded in December of the same year. According to the manufacturer, this particular platform, called the Locust Laser Weapon System, is designed to be mounted on military vehicles, as the Army has done with the versions its received.

Operating at 20 kilowatts, the Locust system relies on an extremely concentrated beam of light that, in various phases, allows for the detection, tracking, illumination, damaging, or destruction of targets at a distance. Locust and other high-energy laser (HEL) systems typically use sensors, cameras, radars, or other means to locate an object. Once identified, the system focuses the light beam on the target with great precision, even when it is moving. It then uses an additional electrical energy charge to increase the beam’s power and convert it into heat. This ultimately damages or disables the drone, the exact outcomes depending on factors such as distance, exposure time, and the target’s characteristics.

In addition, Locust’s most recent versions—such as the one delivered to the military last December—include radar and command-and-control systems. These make it easier to integrate the weapon into a more complex mobile defense platform, rather than using it as a stand-alone device.

The exact location of the operation remains unknown. Nor is there any concrete information regarding the origin of the neutralized drones or the entities responsible for their operation. However, Curtis Taylor, commander of JTF-SB, suggested that the aircraft could be linked to criminal cells involved in drug trafficking and operations in Mexican territory.

“Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners. By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance. We also greatly appreciate the support of our Mexican Army partners as we work together to combat this threat to the border region,” the major general stated in a press release.

The official statement also does not specify the exact models from the AMP-HEL program that were used in the operation. However, the international press has linked the action to the campaign against illegal immigration and drug cartels that President Donald Trump has been waging since he began his second term.

During his election campaign, Trump promised to combat both issues by implementing drastic measures, especially along the US-Mexico border. To that end, his administration has deployed a wide variety of technologies, HEL systems being just part of the growing toolkit.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

The Best Folding Phones

Wired September 01, 2026

Samsung

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

You may be scoffing as you read this. The best folding phones? Really? Aren’t those just gimmicks? I'm here to tell you they're pretty darn useful. And yes, there are quite a few now, so you have options. Folding phones are an evolution of the traditional single-screen slab of glass we've all been using for nearly two decades—and we might even see a folding iPhone in 2026.

They largely come in two forms: a folding flip phone or a folding book-like phone, enabling you to either relive the glory days of small phones or expand your multitasking options while on the go. A folding phone is a personal decision—arguably even more than a traditional smartphone, since it hinges (heh) on what style you prefer. We have tested almost all of them, and these are our favorites.

Check out our other mobile buying guides, including the Best Android Phones, Best iPhones, Best Cheap Phones, Best Samsung Phones, Best Google Pixel Phones, Best Motorola Phones, Best Phones With a Headphone Jack, and Best Phones You Can't Buy in the US.

Updated August 2026: We've added the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Motorola Razr Ultra (2026), Motorola Razr (2026), Honor Magic V6; mentions of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Z Flip8, Motorola Razr Fold, Motorola Razr+ (2026), and Oppo Find N6; removed some older devices; and updated prices.

Samsung

Samsung

Amazon

Best Buy

The Galaxy Z Fold8 features fresh proportions for a form factor that feels just right and purpose-built. It is shorter and wider than the Galaxy Z Folds you might be used to, yet when you open it up, it feels even more tablet-like than ever. The crease is significantly less obvious than previous models, and the Fold8 is lighter and easier to handle than the larger Fold8 Ultra. You lose a little bit of screen real estate, but it's marginal.

The front 5.5-inch screen has a nice 10:16 aspect ratio that doesn't cause ridiculous letterboxing. I also found I opened the inner 7.6-inch screen far more often than with the Ultra, and you can comfortably have three apps side by side in split-screen mode. The Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset ensures the smoothest of rides with apps and games. The Fold8's 4,800-mAh battery (Samsung's first with silicon-carbon battery technology) lasts about five to six hours of screen-on time.

Where the Fold8 loses ground compared to the more expensive Ultra is the camera. The Fold8 has a 50-megapixel main sensor and a 50-megapixel ultrawide, with two 10-megapixel selfie cameras on the outer and inner screens. The Ultra adds a more powerful 200-megapixel main camera and a 10-megapixel telephoto offering 3X optical zoom, making it the better choice for photographers. That said, the Fold8 still takes great photos and will serve just fine for most folks.

If you've been on the fence about foldables, the Fold8 could be the tablet-phone combo to tempt you down. It's pricey at $1,900 (the Ultra is $200 more), but there are already offers popping up, and we'll see more as we head into the holiday season.

Motorola

Amazon

Motorola

Flip phones are perfect if you want something that comfortably fits in your pocket or a small clutch. Motorola's Razr Ultra isn't just compact, but it's also the most fashionable smartphone today. You can buy it with suede-like Alcantara or a sustainably sourced wood on the back—both look and feel fantastic. It's also reasonably durable, with an IP48 rating for some dust protection, a titanium-reinforced hinge, and Gorilla Glass Ceramic for more durable displays.

Not much has changed over last year’s Razr Ultra 2025. You get the same Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite chipset, 512 GB of storage, and 16 GB of RAM. The 4-inch OLED screen on the front lets you add multiple widget panels, so you don't need to open the phone as frequently. Once you do, though, you'll enjoy a super-bright, colorful 7-inch AMOLED screen. The big upgrade is the 5,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery, which can easily last two days between charges and is impressively huge for a phone this small.

The 50-megapixel main camera delivers great photos, and there's a reliable 50-megapixel ultrawide and a 50-megapixel selfie camera. While it's a good camera, it still doesn't quite match candybar phones from the likes of Google and Apple. Still, I love being able to take a selfie with the phone closed and see a preview with the front screen, and my wife loves it when I take a picture of her because she can see a preview of herself on the other side of the phone and can correct my poor angle. Video capture is also good, with Dolby Vision support that makes clips look sharp, colorful, and not too grainy in low light.

You'll hear a lot about Motorola's AI features on this phone—there's even a dedicated “AI” button—but the long and short of it is that most of these features aren't very helpful. Pay Attention is the only one I've found myself using due to the nature of my job; it starts a recording with real-time transcription and an AI summary at the end, but most flagship phones can do that these days. Don't buy it for Moto AI, buy it because it's a flipping-cool Razr.

Motorola

Amazon

Motorola

You can get a cheaper folding phone if you're willing to make a few sacrifices. The regular Razr flip phone has a similar design to the Ultra, but with slightly smaller screens. It also makes do with a slightly souped-up MediaTek chipset and less RAM, which means slower performance, but nothing too frustrating. It has the same titanium-reinforced hinge as the Ultra and an IP48 dust- and water-resistance rating.

The camera is still solid, offering pleasing shots in good conditions, but it struggles a little with low light and high-contrast scenes. The outer display is smaller, but still customizable. Battery life is good and should last a couple of days when you need it to.

The fact that you only get three Android upgrades is disappointing, and the Razr has the same unimpressive Motorola AI features as the Ultra. But weighing up the package at this price, the Razr is the most affordable, but still worthwhile, way to try a folding phone.

Google

Amazon

Best Buy

A polished update to Google’s Pixel line, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold brings several minor improvements. One of the few folding devices with a proper IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating plus the ability to withstand 10 years of folding, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold may be your most durable option. It's also the only folding phone with Qi2 25W wireless charging support, meaning you can magnetically stick it to MagSafe or Qi2 wireless chargers.

Even with a slimmed-down body, it's noticeably thicker and heavier than Samsung’s folding options, which makes it more cumbersome to use. Despite a smaller battery than last year's model, it has enough stamina to get through most days, and that's mostly because the new Tensor G6 chipset is more efficient. Google added floating Bubbles for better multitasking, so you can have an expandable chat floating over two other apps in split-screen mode. There are also enhancements for Gemini, including some useful contextual pop-ups in chats to add links to your calendar for events or open destinations in Maps.

Despite the “Pro” in the name, the Fold lacks most of the Pro features available in the cheaper Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL. You do get the new HiLight feature, a group of color LEDs in the camera module’s flash that light up different colors based on who is calling or while you chat to Gemini. But you miss out on a much more powerful camera system and features like instant Night Sight, 120X digital zoom, and better video capture. You can still capture excellent photos on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, but they're not the best that Google offers. That's a bitter pill when you're coughing up $1,900.

Honor

Amazon

Despite the sizable camera bump, the otherwise super-svelte Honor Magic V6 (4.1 mm open, 8.8 mm closed) is a lovely foldable that's easy to handle and feels close to a regular phone when closed. It brings better battery life, faster charging, and greater durability over last year's Magic V5, and also has a versatile camera and a responsive fingerprint sensor in the power button. Honor’s MagicOS is packed with potentially useful foldable and AI features, but also some bloatware.

The biggest enhancement this year is the long-lasting 6,660-mAh silicon-carbon battery, and Honor is promising better durability than before, with an IP68/69 rating for water resistance. There’s also a snazzy new red finish. The Honor Magic V6 is the best book-like foldable for folks in the UK, Europe, or other markets where the phone is sold, though you can always import it into the US. Read more in our Best Phones You Can't Buy in the US guide.

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra for $2,100: The Z Fold8 Ultra is a refined release with a 6.5-inch cover display that opens to an expansive 8-inch screen that feels like two 6.5-inch displays side by side. It's fast and smooth, with a 5,000-mAh battery, but it's the camera that earns it the “Ultra” title. It's an impressive combo, including a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and a 10-megapixel telephoto lens that supports 3X optical zoom. Sadly, it lacks Qi2 support for magnetic wireless charging, and the camera module makes it rock when lying flat on a surface. But the main reason it misses out on a place above is that the smaller Fold8 is so much easier to handle.

Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 for $1,200: We haven't had a chance to spend much time with the Flip8 yet, but based on what we have seen, it's a close second to Motorola's Razr Ultra. It is the lightest and thinnest flip phone in the world with a redesigned chassis. It has a 4.1-inch cover screen, and it flips open to become a 6.9-inch candy bar. It's also more durable than ever and boasts the same excellent chipset and performance as Samsung's larger Fold models. The 4,300-mAh battery is solid, but the camera system is relatively basic, comprising a 50-megapixel main shooter backed by a 12-megapixel ultrawide.

Motorola Razr Fold

Motorola Razr Fold for $1,900: The first book-style foldable from Motorola is good, but not great. The front screen feels very much like a normal phone, and you can open it to enjoy the vast 8.1-inch display inside. Sadly, the Razr Fold lacks the top-end processor of the year, which is disappointing at this price. The highlight is the massive 6,000-mAh battery, which can stretch to nearly three days of use. Thankfully, it does come with seven years of software updates (unlike Motorola's Flip family). Motorola has also added a telephoto lens to the capable, triple 50-MP camera. But, overall, we prefer Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Motorola Razr+ 2026 for $1,100: The awkward middle child in the Razr lineup lacks the bells and whistles or top-notch specs of the Ultra, but still costs more than $1,000. You can get very close to the same experience from the cheaper Razr and save hundreds. Even battery life is unimpressive, because it has the smallest capacity of the Razr family. The cover glass isn’t the ceramic glass mixture as on the Razr Ultra. I found out the hard way after dropping the phone once, roughly a 4-foot drop onto asphalt, and the front screen shattered. Get a screen protector!

Oppo Find N6

Oppo Find N6 for $1,929: With an 8.12-inch internal display, the Find N6 is a beautifully engineered folding phone that’s impossibly slim and light. Despite its promise of being creaseless, the fold is still discernible. You’ll hardly notice it when the screen is on, though you’ll feel it if you use the optional stylus. Performance is impressively slick, with enough stamina to see you through a busy day, and the camera system is excellent. It’s a big step up from last year’s N5, with a 200-MP main shooter, 50-MP telephoto, and 50-MP ultrawide. The global model can use familiar Google apps, but you’ll have to import it, as this phone won’t officially be released in the West.

Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold for $1,799: The only reason to consider the Pixel 10 Pro Fold right now is if you see it on sale. Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold is superior, but the 10 Pro Fold isn't far behind this year's release. It's still a reasonably slim device with a large front screen that feels like a normal phone, an excellent 8-inch inner screen, and a triple-camera system that delivers great results, though not as great as the Pixel 10 Pro series. Read our Best Pixel Phones guide for more.

Xiaomi Mix Flip for $899: Xiaomi’s first flip phone has a lovely design with excellent displays inside and out, long battery life with fast charging, and flagship-level performance, which makes a nice change, as flip phones often have middling specs. It also boasts a solid dual-lens camera, opting for telephoto instead of ultrawide alongside the capable main shooter, which is more useful for most folks. The software lets the party down a little; there’s no IP rating, and it is pricey, but I had fun with this flip phone.

Things to Know Before Buying

Folding phones are more fragile than normal phones. Folding phones have more parts than a traditional smartphone, not to mention a hinge. Companies advertise how many folds these devices have been tested for—usually around 200,000 or 500,000 folds—but a single drop can be incredibly damaging. They are not as dust-resistant, and some aren't as water-resistant (only the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is IP68-rated in the US), so you'll want to be especially careful. Use a case, and it may be worth investing in the manufacturer's device care policy.

Don't remove the built-in screen protector. Most of these folding phones have a film over the inner screen. You might be tempted to remove it, but don't—it can damage the display. The packaging usually includes instructions not to remove it and how to care for your device.

There's a small learning curve to the software. Flip-style folding phones are fairly straightforward, but book-like folding phones that double as tablets have new multitasking tricks that will take some getting used to if you want to make the most of them. I recommend taking some time to run through these features so you understand how they work.

They're expensive. Do you need one? Nobody needs a folding phone. If you think you'll benefit from one, know they're frequently discounted during big sale events like Black Friday, and you can also knock a few hundred dollars off if you trade in an eligible device.

Which Type of Folding Phone Is for You?

Folding flip phones are for people who want a compact device. Think of a normal phone you can fold in half. That's pretty much what you get, plus a screen on the front to monitor widgets and texts. This does mean you can flip the phone to answer a call and flip it shut to end one—super cool. You can put the phone at a 90-degree angle, and some apps will adapt to show controls on the bottom and important details at the top, like in video calling apps or when watching videos on YouTube, though this depends on the phone. Folding flip phones typically have mediocre battery life, and their cameras aren't as good as their non-folding counterparts.

Folding book-like phones are for people who want the big-screen experience. Are you constantly watching full-length movies on your phone? Or do you always find yourself jumping back and forth between two apps? Then these are for you. They have good battery life and better cameras (though not as good as non-folding phones), but they're far more expensive. These include the short-lived triple-screen folding devices like Samsung's Galaxy Z TriFold. They're thick and heavy, though we're seeing newer models that are surprisingly thin. Still, you may have a hard time fitting them in your pockets.

Is Now a Good Time to Buy?

If you're team Android, this is a good time to buy. Samsung and Google just updated their foldables, and Motorola released its first big foldable in the summer and won't announce the Razr 2027 lineup until the spring. For folks outside the US, we probably won't see new foldables from Honor or Oppo until the spring, too.

If you're considering an iPhone, Apple is likely to unveil a new folding phone soon, so you might want to wait and see what it looks like.

My Favorite Folding Features

Whichever style you go for, my favorite feature of folding phones is the ability to see the viewfinder on the external screen and snap a selfie with the high-quality rear cameras—just set the phone down slightly folded so it stays upright, and there's usually a button you can click in the camera app to send the preview to the external screen. You can usually trigger the shutter hands-free with a palm gesture. (Motorola's Razr Ultra lets you start and stop video recordings with hand gestures, too!) It's excellent when traveling if you want to take a photo of yourself next to a point of interest.

Many of these phones offer similar functionality with translation—Samsung and Google, for example, let you show your words translated on the external screen so the person you are speaking to can see it, and then they can tap a button on the screen to have the phone start translating their words, which you'll see on the internal screen. It's a much nicer system than using Google Translate on a candy bar phone.

Review: Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless

Wired September 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

We’ve waited almost four years for a new pair of Sennheiser Momentum wireless over-ear headphones. That’s eons in a world where Sony, Apple, and Bowers & Wilkins have been busy launching stellar Bluetooth headphones like the Sony WH-1000XM6, Apple AirPods Max 2, and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3.

Plenty has happened in the intervening years—not least, Sennheiser’s consumer division being sold to hearing aid company Sonova, which is currently looking to sell it on. Thankfully, the Momentum 5 is a hugely enjoyable pair of premium headphones with some unexpectedly good features, and not the product of a troubled homelife.

The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless look good. They strike a middle ground between premium cans (AirPods Max 2, Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3) and more lightweight ones (Bose QuietComfort Headphones, Sony WH-1000XM5). The 10.3-ounce build is mainly plastic, and the ear cups are basic, but the denim trim on the top of the comfortable headband adds fun texture. They are not head turners like the Nothing Headphone (1), but they are still nice to look at, and come in blue denim (pictured), black, and white.

Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

They are, however, very comfortable, with a great level of squish to the earpads. Massive ears (like mine) have room to flap, and the headband doesn’t add any uncomfortable pressure. No over-ear headphone is perfect to wear with glasses, but I happily wore these for hours. When temperatures hit 95 degrees Fahrenheit my ears got sweaty, but so did the rest of me, to be fair.

The Momentum 5 Wireless get up to 57 hours of battery with ANC on, according to Sennheiser. That’s almost double what the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 can do. It’s three hours shy of the older Momentum 4, and 13 hours less than the similarly priced Marshall Monitor III ANC.

I didn’t perform an exact test on the 57-hour battery claim, but it seems fairly accurate in my real-world use thus far. I have been using the Momentum 5 daily for the past month, and they are still at about 50 percent charge.

The more interesting story to me is that the battery can be easily replaced. Remove the left ear pad, unscrew four Phillips-head screws, lift the cover, and the battery can be unplugged and swapped out in seconds.

iFixit has been showing us how to replace batteries in electronics for years, but this is the first time I’ve seen a headphone brand actively encourage consumers to do it themselves. I think Sennheiser embracing our right to repair is worth celebrating, even if, at the time of publication, the replaceable battery isn't available for purchase.

The Momentum 5 Wireless supports SBC, AAC, aptX, aptX HD, aptX Lossless, and aptX Adaptive codecs, plus multipoint connectivity. Plug in using either the 3.5-millimeter jack or the USB-C port to get digital lossless audio (up to 24-bit/96 kHz).

Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The Sennheiser Smart Control Plus app is where you can customize ANC levels, transparency, an eight-band EQ, connection preferences, and Dolby Atmos. You can also save sound profiles based on your location, maxing out ANC when you hit the office, for instance.

Controls on the headphones themselves are touch controls on the right ear cup, and they work fine: as in, they didn’t annoy me. A tap pauses music, swipes adjust volume and skip tracks, while a double tap toggles between ANC and transparency modes.

Active Noise Cancellation comes via eight microphones, and it is good, verging on great. It works well on public transport, provides a cocoon in cafés, and gifts solitude in a shared office. If you’ve never used Sony or Bose ANC headphones, you’ll be delighted with the Momentum 5s, but if you’re switching from those two brands, you might find these a bit of a letdown. We’re talking small margins here, but the Momentum 5 just lacks that eerily quiet sealed-off feeling of the WH-1000XM6 or Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen).

Call quality is good too, and the wind-reducing mics kept my voice front and center, but it’s not the reason I’d buy these headphones.

I tested the Momentum 5 Wireless using the best and worst playback resolutions from Spotify—both over Wi-Fi and cellular. I also listened to Qobuz hi-resolution recordings and my own digital music library. And no matter what I played, the headphones offered me a smooth, refined, and expressive performance.

They’re not “high-fidelity” in the sense that the extreme edges of a recording are not exposed, and they happily make poor-quality output sound enjoyable. That said, you’ll get a bit more out of them by listening to higher-fidelity sources. And if you’re still playing the lowest-resolution audio playback on Spotify (or don’t even know what I am talking about), you don’t need to spend $399 on a pair of headphones.

Mixing it up between the pop of Olivia Rodrigo’s excellent new album, the twang of Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band, via Wu-Tang, and more of the Police than I’m comfortable admitting, the Sennheiser made every genre enjoyable to listen to and were totally agreeable. They’re not neutral, with plenty of relaxed warmth to the sound profile.

Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Listening to the Sennheisers side by side with the B&W Px7 S3, I noticed a little lack in punch and drive by comparison. The opposite is true when listening to them against the AirPods Max 2, however, with the Sennheiser’s classy midrange cutting through the mix with real authority. This was also the case when comparing them with the now discontinued Momentum 3 Wireless from 2019 (although I wish Sennheiser would bring back the sumptuous leather earpads at least as an add-on).

They are bass-forward, though, and anyone leaning toward acoustic or classical would do well to tweak the EQ via the app. The sound is clean overall, with a tight thump, although not a patch on the taut rumble from the more expensive AirPods Max.

The Momentum 5 Wireless are long overdue, but at $399, they face stiff competition from more mainstream competitors like Sony, Bose, Apple, and Bowers & Wilkins, all of whom have launched serious good over-ear headphones recently. This hasn’t left a lot of room for Sennheiser to compete in, but, sensibly, the brand hasn’t tried to win every battle.

The ANC is very good (but not spookily quiet), and the design is classy (but not indulgent). Sound is warm, expressive, and easy to enjoy for long periods of time, even if the bass might need taming in the EQ. But importantly, Sennheiser has created a headphone with superb battery life, easy wired and hi-res listening, an impressive codec list, and an easily replaceable battery you can swap yourself.

They are not the most exciting headphones in any one area, but they are comfortable, considered, likable, and impressively repairable.
